lessons.headline: Choose roles or choose a group
lessons.intro: A named job makes the person doing it important. An ordinary pair has no first member. Decide which kind of choice you need before multiplying.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film shift from ordering at a stall to choosing two helpers. Ask whether swapping the two chosen people creates a new outcome in each problem.
lessons.recap: Multiply along a chain of choices. Check whether swapping two selections really creates another outcome.

example.prompt: From Kim, Jo and Lin, how many pairs can carry a banner together?
steps: List KJ, KL and JL. Each pair already includes both banner carriers.
Writing JK too would count the first pair again. There are 3 pairs.

questions.title: Two flags
questions.prompt: A signal uses one of four flags at the top and a different one below. How many signals can be made?
questions.hint: Fill the upper position first.

questions.title: One duet
questions.prompt: Six singers choose two of their number for a duet. Both sing the same part. How many duets are possible?
questions.hint: How often would listing a first and a second singer count a duet?

questions.title: Design panel
questions.prompt: Choose two of four painters and one of three engineers for a panel. How many panels can be made?
questions.hint: Choose the painters as an unordered pair.

questions.title: Photo assignment
questions.prompt: A team of three is chosen from five pupils. One of the three will take a photo of the other two. How many different team-and-photographer choices are there?
questions.hint: Try choosing the photographer before choosing the pair in the picture.

lessons.headline: Start with the clue that fixes a place
lessons.intro: A puzzle may describe many possible orders. Put in any clue that fixes one place, then use neighbouring and earlier-or-later clues around it.
lessons.bridge: When the paintings must be put in order, watch how a pair that must stay adjacent shrinks the possible positions.
lessons.recap: Place fixed entries, then test remaining positions against all the clues, including exclusions.

example.prompt: Three books sit on a shelf. The red book is between the other two and the green book is at the right. Where is the blue book?
steps: Red is in the middle and green uses the right position.
Only the left position remains for blue.

questions.title: Who stands in the middle?
questions.prompt: Dara, Eli and Faye stand in three places. Dara is next to both other people and Faye stands to the left of Dara. Who is on the right?
questions.hint: Only the middle place has two neighbours.

questions.title: Room assignments
questions.prompt: Three clubs, Art, Band and Chess, each meet in a different room numbered 5, 6 and 7. Art cannot use the smallest room number. Chess must use a larger number than Art. Which room number is Band using?
questions.hint: Place the ordered pair before filling the spare room.

questions.title: Two seats apart
questions.prompt: Four children sit in seats 1 to 4: Faye, Gus, Hiro and Ira. Faye is exactly two seat numbers before Gus. Ira is in seat 1. Which seat number belongs to Hiro?
questions.hint: Write every possible pair for the two numbered seats.

questions.title: Place the end pieces
questions.prompt: Five distinct cards in a row read Jia, Kir, Liv, Mo and Nia in some order. Liv must be exactly in the middle. Kir immediately follows Jia. Nia is before Jia. Which position from the left must Kir occupy?
questions.hint: Can the consecutive pair straddle the occupied middle?

lessons.headline: Read one floor at a time
lessons.intro: A view from the side can hide cubes. Imagine lifting off one horizontal floor at a time, or label each floor position with the height of its complete stack.
lessons.bridge: In the film’s six-stack model, look for the difference between what a silhouette requires and what it merely allows.
lessons.recap: Add complete stack heights or add horizontal floors. In either method, include hidden cubes.

example.prompt: Two stacks beside each other are 3 and 1 cubes high. How many cubes are on the second floor or higher?
steps: The first stack contributes 2 cubes above its bottom. The other contributes none.
There are 2 above the bottom floor, out of 4 altogether.

questions.title: Shelves of cubes
questions.prompt: A fully packed box has 5 unit cubes across, 4 deep and 3 layers high. How many cubes fill it?
questions.hint: Find one floor of the box.

questions.title: The top-view numbers
questions.prompt: A plan shows four stack heights: 5, 3, 4 and 5. Each stack is solid down to the floor. How many cubes are above the bottom layer?
questions.hint: Each nonempty stack contributes one cube to the bottom.

questions.title: A square stair tower
questions.prompt: A tower has solid square floors. From the top down their side lengths are 1, 2, and so on up to 6 cubes. How many cubes does the tower contain?
questions.hint: The floor with side i uses a square number of cubes.

questions.title: Match two silhouettes
questions.prompt: Four nonempty stacks form a 2-by-2 square. From the front, the maximum heights in the two columns are 4 and 3. From the side, the maxima of the two rows are also 4 and 3. What is the minimum total number of cubes?
questions.hint: Can one tall stack satisfy two maxima at once?

lessons.headline: Use the line total
lessons.intro: A grid with equal row or column sums gives a short equation every time a line is almost full. After placing a value, check the other lines it touches.
lessons.bridge: Watch the two given corner values in the magic square. Notice how filling one line supplies information to its neighbours.
lessons.recap: Find a line with one unknown, solve it, and transfer the result into the crossing line.

example.prompt: A row must total 12 and currently reads 3, blank, 5. Find the missing number.
steps: The known entries use 8.
The missing number is 12 − 8 = 4.

lessons.videoTitle: Magic grids, symbolic rules and consistency

questions.title: Complete a line
questions.prompt: Each row of a number grid totals 17. One row begins with 3 and 5. What is its third entry?
questions.hint: Subtract both entries from the line total.

questions.title: Identical counters
questions.prompt: A triangle and two circles have total value 24. The triangle has value 6. What value must each identical circle have?
questions.hint: Subtract the triangle before dividing.

questions.title: Opposite corners
questions.prompt: In a 3-by-3 magic square each line totals 51 and the central cell is 17. The top-left cell is 14. What is the bottom-right cell?
questions.hint: Use the one diagonal joining these cells.

questions.title: The centre of the grid
questions.prompt: A 3-by-3 magic square uses the numbers 4 through 12 once each. Every row, column and main diagonal has the same total. What number belongs in the centre?
questions.hint: The four lines through the centre count the centre four times and every other entry once.

lessons.headline: Explain why a list is complete
lessons.intro: Finding one solution and showing that it is the only solution are different tasks. Choose a bounded feature, list its possible values in order and show which pass.
lessons.bridge: In the rectangle puzzle, follow the list of factor pairs and notice where the speaker can stop without overlooking another solution.
lessons.recap: Name the first and last cases and the step between them, so another solver can see what the list covers.

example.prompt: How many positive-integer pairs x ≤ y have xy = 6?
steps: The smaller member cannot exceed 2 because 3 × 3 is too large.
The candidates x = 1, 2 lead to (1,6) and (2,3). These are all the possibilities.

lessons.videoTitle: Proving all cases and unique solutions

questions.title: Bound the list
questions.prompt: How many multiples of 5 lie between 14 and 29, inclusive?
questions.hint: List multiples in steps and check both neighbours of the list.

questions.title: Count unordered pairs
questions.prompt: Two different positive integers have sum 11. Count the possible pairs, counting a reversed pair as the same.
questions.hint: Give each pair a single representative by choosing its smaller member.

questions.title: Only one rectangle
questions.prompt: A rectangle has area 35 square units and its longer whole-number side is two units longer than its shorter side. What is its shorter side?
questions.hint: Test products x(x + 2) in increasing order.

questions.title: A parity condition on pairs
questions.prompt: Two positive integers add to 10. Count the unordered pairs with odd product. Equal numbers are allowed.
questions.hint: For an odd product, first determine both parities. List only the smaller entry.

lessons.headline: Grow the whole recipe
lessons.intro: A ratio gives a recipe you can resize. Draw one box for each part, then use the size of a single box to find either ingredient.
lessons.bridge: Ask how the bead quantities and the wall drawing both preserve a ratio when the physical units look quite different.
lessons.recap: Check your new recipe by dividing both amounts by the same number. They should return to the original pair.

example.prompt: A string of flags has two green flags for every three yellow flags. It has 8 green flags. How many are yellow?
steps: Two green parts make 8 flags, so each part represents 4 flags.
Three yellow parts make 3 × 4 = 12 flags.

figure.alt: The green group has two equal parts and the yellow group has three. The two green parts together stand for eight flags.

questions.title: Soup for six
questions.prompt: A soup uses 2 cups of lentils for every 5 cups of stock. How many cups of stock go with 6 cups of lentils?
questions.hint: How many times larger is the lentil amount?

questions.title: All the tiles
questions.prompt: A wall has 56 tiles, blue and white in the ratio 3 to 5. How many are white?
questions.hint: How many parts represent all 56 tiles?

questions.title: A taller map
questions.prompt: A plan uses 2 cm to represent 7 m. A garden boundary is 12 cm long on the plan. What is its real length in metres?
questions.hint: Count the pairs of centimetres first.

questions.title: Matching a second batch
questions.prompt: A box contains 14 copper and 21 silver beads. Another box contains 10 copper and 9 silver beads. How many silver beads must be added to the second box so both boxes have the same copper-to-silver ratio?
questions.hint: Reduce the first box to its smallest whole-number ratio.

lessons.headline: Trace the cut edge
lessons.intro: Perimeter measures the length of a boundary. When two pieces meet, the joined edges are hidden inside. A cut can expose new edges, even when it removes very little material.
lessons.bridge: As the film cuts a hole and then a corner from a board, predict which cut will change the boundary and trace the new edges.
lessons.recap: Trace every boundary the question includes. A join removes two copies of its length.

example.prompt: Two tiles of side 2 cm meet along a whole edge. How far is it around their outline?
steps: Separately the two squares have 8 cm of perimeter each. The 2 cm join hides one edge from each square.
The outline measures 16 − 4 = 12 cm. The joined rectangle is 4 cm by 2 cm, which gives the same result.

lessons.videoTitle: Perimeter, shared edges and boundary effects

questions.title: The projecting porch
questions.prompt: A 8 m by 5 m hall has a square porch of side 3 m attached outside along one whole porch edge. What is the perimeter in metres of the combined floor plan?
questions.hint: Trace the old edge covered by the porch.

questions.title: Corner of the label
questions.prompt: A 8 cm by 5 cm label loses a 3 cm by 2 cm rectangle from a corner. What is the perimeter of the remaining L-shape in centimetres?
questions.hint: Pair the missing outside edges with the two fresh cut edges.

questions.title: Silk round a window
questions.prompt: A 12 by 8 cm fabric panel has a rectangular 3 by 2 cm window cut entirely inside. How many centimetres of ribbon trim every cut edge and the outside?
questions.hint: Trace each closed boundary separately.

questions.title: Recover the joins
questions.prompt: A single patch of 20 unit square tiles has total exposed boundary 24 units. How many pairs of tiles share a full edge?
questions.hint: Start with four edges per tile and count what vanishes at one join.

lessons.headline: Use an easier outline
lessons.intro: Area counts the space a region covers. Sometimes one subtraction from a larger rectangle is shorter than cutting the region into several pieces.
lessons.bridge: Watch where the two shaded rectangles overlap. Decide which tiles would get counted twice if you simply added their areas.
lessons.recap: Check that pieces cover the region exactly once and that you report square units.

example.prompt: A rectangle covers 4 by 3 squares. Two squares at its upper-right corner are white and all others blue. How much is blue?
steps: The whole rectangle has 4 × 3 = 12 squares.
Remove the two white squares to leave 10 blue squares.

questions.title: Cover the L
questions.prompt: A sheet is 11 cm by 7 cm. A rectangular 4 cm by 3 cm corner is cut away. What area of sheet is left in square centimetres?
questions.hint: Complete the original rectangle in your sketch.

questions.title: A sliding top corner
questions.prompt: A triangle uses the entire 22 cm bottom edge of a rectangle as its base. Its top vertex can slide along the opposite side 7 cm above it. What area, in square centimetres, does the triangle always cover?
questions.hint: What changes when the vertex slides? What stays fixed?

questions.title: Two painted bands
questions.prompt: A sign is 11 columns by 7 rows of unit squares. Paint the leftmost 4 columns and the top 3 rows. How many different squares receive paint?
questions.hint: Draw the small rectangle that receives two coats.

questions.title: The kerb cuts a corner
questions.prompt: A rectangular lot is 12 m by 14 m. A straight kerb cuts off one corner, meeting the two adjacent sides 5 m and 6 m from that corner. How many square metres remain?
questions.hint: Which two lengths form perpendicular legs of the missing triangle?

lessons.headline: Give each outcome an address
lessons.intro: Split a count by a feature that every allowed outcome has exactly once. Inside a case you can multiply choices. Across disjoint cases you add.
lessons.bridge: In the exhibit puzzle, find the rule that tells you which row to use before choosing individual exhibits. Check where exhibit B is permitted.
lessons.recap: Try to place one example in two cases. If you can, repair the case rule before adding.

example.prompt: A lunch is one sandwich or one soup with a roll. There are three sandwiches, two soups and two rolls. How many lunches are offered?
steps: The sandwich case gives 3 lunches. The soup case gives 2 × 2 = 4.
Every lunch belongs to just one case, so there are 7.

questions.title: Odd or even row
questions.prompt: A two-character tag starts with A or B. An A tag ends in one of 1, 3 or 5. A B tag ends in one of 2 or 4. How many tags exist?
questions.hint: Count tags separately for each first letter.

questions.title: Exactly one special card
questions.prompt: Two shelves have 3 and 4 different cards. Each shelf has exactly one gold card. Pick one card from each shelf. How many pairs have exactly one gold card?
questions.hint: Separate which shelf contributes gold.

questions.title: A single vowel
questions.prompt: A three-letter sign uses different letters from A, E, M, N, P. How many signs have exactly one vowel, in an end position?
questions.hint: Fix the vowel's position.

questions.title: Parcel route
questions.prompt: A courier chooses three different stops, in order, from P, Q, R, S, T. P must be visited. If P is last, Q must be first. How many routes are allowed?
questions.hint: Separate the three possible positions of P.

lessons.headline: Which angles fill the line?
lessons.intro: Angles measure turns. Start with a straight line, a full turn or a triangle whose total is known. Mark only the angles belonging to that total.
lessons.bridge: When the exterior angle appears, follow its value into the two remote angles. Watch how the bisectors use that information together.
lessons.recap: Use a geometrical reason for every total before subtracting.

example.prompt: A ray splits a straight angle into 48° and an unknown angle. Find the unknown angle.
steps: Together the two parts make a half-turn of 180°.
Subtracting the known part gives 180 − 48 = 132°.

questions.title: A straight sightline
questions.prompt: Three adjacent angles on one side of a straight line have sizes 26°, 52° and a missing angle. How many degrees is the missing angle?
questions.hint: A straight angle totals 180°.

questions.title: Reflecting beacon
questions.prompt: Two rays from a beacon to two posts form the equal sides of an isosceles triangle. The inside angle at one post is 26°. What is the angle between the rays at the beacon, in degrees?
questions.hint: Which angles stand opposite the equal sides?

questions.title: The outside turn
questions.prompt: One exterior angle of a triangle is 70°. One of its two remote interior angles is 26°. How many degrees is the other remote angle?
questions.hint: Connect the exterior angle to the triangle’s interior sum.

questions.title: The inside bisectors
questions.prompt: In triangle ABC an exterior angle at A is 102°. The internal angle bisectors from B and C meet at P. What is angle BPC in degrees?
questions.hint: Work with B + C rather than trying to determine each angle.

lessons.headline: A cell is bounded by lines
lessons.intro: Grid questions may ask about cells, intersections or outlines. Trace the object you are counting before choosing dimensions. A row of cells has a line at each end.
lessons.bridge: When the film counts rectangles containing cell A, pause and point to all the possible boundary lines before it introduces cell B.
lessons.recap: Convert cells to boundary lines only in the dimensions where the question asks about lines.

example.prompt: A row has three square cells. How many vertical grid lines touch the row?
steps: There are two outside boundaries and two dividers.
Four lines make three spaces. Any rectangle uses two of these lines as sides.

questions.title: Four boundary lines
questions.prompt: A rectangular grid has 5 columns and 4 rows of unit squares. How many rectangles with sides along grid lines can you draw, including squares?
questions.hint: Choose two vertical lines and two horizontal lines.

questions.title: Two marked borders
questions.prompt: On a 5-column, 4-row grid, count all grid-line rectangles with their top edge on the top of the grid and their left edge on the far left.
questions.hint: Which two edges are still free?

questions.title: Through a marked cell
questions.prompt: A 5-column by 4-row grid has a star in column 3, row 2, counting from the left and bottom. How many grid-line rectangles include the entire starred cell?
questions.hint: The left and right sides must enclose that cell. Likewise the top and bottom.

questions.title: One marker inside
questions.prompt: A 5 by 4 cell board has two markers in row 2 from the bottom, in columns 3 and 4 from the left. How many grid-line rectangles cover the whole marker cell in column 3 but exclude the other marker cell?
questions.hint: First count rectangles around the required cell. Then tighten the sides to enclose both.

lessons.headline: Find the partners in a mirror
lessons.intro: A reflection pairs positions at equal perpendicular distances from its mirror. Positions on the mirror stay where they are.
lessons.bridge: In the coloured-board puzzle, follow one chosen cell through both mirrors. Look for cells that need fewer partners than the others.
lessons.recap: Test both distance and side of the mirror. Count points on the mirror separately.

example.prompt: On a number line, reflect 2 across the mark at 5. Where is its partner?
steps: The point 2 is three units to the left of 5.
Go three units to its right to reach 8. The two positions have midpoint 5.

questions.title: Mirror in a line
questions.prompt: A pin at (7, 4) is reflected across the vertical line x = 4. What is the x-coordinate of its image?
questions.hint: Measure the horizontal distance to the mirror.

questions.title: A half-turn on the board
questions.prompt: Rows and columns of a 5 by 5 board are numbered from 1. A piece starts in row 3, column 4. What column contains it after turning the whole board through 180°?
questions.hint: Pair columns from opposite edges.

questions.title: Palindromic row
questions.prompt: A row of 5 flags is coloured using red or yellow. The colours look the same when read from either end. How many different patterns are possible?
questions.hint: Pair the outside positions and keep track of the centre.

questions.title: Two fold lines
questions.prompt: A square quilt has 7 rows and the same number of columns. Its colour pattern is mirrored across the middle row and across the middle column. How many cell colours can be chosen independently?
questions.hint: Choose one representative from each pair of reflected rows and columns.

lessons.headline: Keep the constraint on the page
lessons.intro: To maximise an area, list what must stay fixed while the sides vary. With a fixed rectangular perimeter the neighbouring sides have a fixed sum.
lessons.bridge: At the wall-side pen, count the fenced sides on the picture before working out which dimensions might give the greatest area.
lessons.recap: List legal dimensions and compare their areas. Check which sides actually need fencing.

example.prompt: A rectangle has perimeter 12 m and whole-metre sides. Which area is largest?
steps: The adjacent sides add to 6. The possible pairs are 1 and 5, 2 and 4, or 3 and 3.
Their areas are 5, 8 and 9 m². The largest is 9 m².

lessons.videoTitle: Optimising areas and lengths under constraints

questions.title: Share the fencing
questions.prompt: A rectangle has whole-metre side lengths and perimeter 22 m. What is its greatest possible area in square metres?
questions.hint: Keep the side sum fixed and compare pairs near its middle.

questions.title: Tile a compact plaza
questions.prompt: Make a rectangle from exactly 30 unit square tiles. Its sides must follow tile edges. What is the least possible perimeter?
questions.hint: Compare factor pairs starting near the square root.

questions.title: Wall at the back
questions.prompt: A gardener has 20 m of wire for three sides of a rectangular garden against a straight wall. The two end fences have equal whole-metre lengths. What is the largest area in square metres?
questions.hint: Let the two end fences use 2x. How much closes the front?

questions.title: Space for a sign
questions.prompt: A frame has perimeter 20 cm and whole-centimetre sides. Its length must exceed its width by at least 4 cm. What is the largest permitted area in square centimetres?
questions.hint: Find the closest allowable pair with the required side sum.

lessons.headline: Add the work finished in one minute
lessons.intro: Two machines can work on the same job. Find what each finishes in one minute before putting their work together.
lessons.bridge: Watch the labelling machine for just its first minute. See how that one-minute fraction lets two differently paced machines share the next batch.
lessons.recap: Check the units on a rate. If the answer tells you batches per minute, its reciprocal tells you minutes per batch.

example.prompt: One machine finishes a batch in 6 minutes. A second takes 3 minutes. What fraction can they finish together in one minute?
steps: The first completes 1/6 and the second 1/3.
Together they finish 1/6 + 2/6 = 1/2 of a batch per minute.

figure.alt: A batch split into sixths. Machine A completes one sixth per minute and machine B completes two sixths per minute.

questions.title: Half an hour's work
questions.prompt: A printer makes a full set in 40 minutes. What fraction of a set does it make in 30 minutes?
questions.hint: Put minutes worked over minutes needed.

questions.title: Two spouts
questions.prompt: Two spouts fill an empty tub in 15 minutes and 10 minutes respectively when working alone. How many minutes do they take together?
questions.hint: How much of a tub do both fill in one minute?

questions.title: Joining late
questions.prompt: A painter can paint a wall in 12 hours alone. She works for 3 hours, then a second painter with the same rate joins her. How many more hours do they need? Give an exact fraction or decimal.
questions.hint: How much wall remains when the second painter arrives?

questions.title: A secret speed
questions.prompt: A tap and a pump together fill a pool in 8 hours. The tap alone takes 24 hours. How many hours does the pump need alone?
questions.hint: Subtract the tap's contribution from the combined rate.

lessons.headline: What does the silhouette force?
lessons.intro: A front view tells you the height of the tallest stack in each column of sight. Shorter stacks behind it can change without changing the outline.
lessons.bridge: Watch the row and column maxima in the film’s model. Can one tall stack account for two of those maxima?
lessons.recap: Distinguish a required maximum height from a count of all the cubes behind a view.

example.prompt: Two nonempty stacks line up behind each other. Their common silhouette is 3 cubes high. What is the smallest possible total?
steps: At least one stack must have height 3.
Give the other its minimum height 1. The least total is 4 cubes.

questions.title: Two ways to hide a shorter stack
questions.prompt: Two nonempty solid stacks stand one behind the other. The front stack has height 4 and the back stack cannot rise above it. How many different positive back-stack heights leave the front silhouette unchanged?
questions.hint: List the heights that do not exceed the visible stack.

questions.title: Two rows, one silhouette
questions.prompt: Two rows each have four nonempty columns of cubes. Viewed from the front, the four maximum heights from left to right are 2, 6, 3, 1. What is the greatest possible total number of cubes?
questions.hint: Both stacks behind a silhouette column may reach the displayed height.

questions.title: Leanest skyline
questions.prompt: A model has two rows of four nonempty stacks. Its front view shows maximum heights 6, 5, 1, 2 from left to right. What is the least number of cubes possible?
questions.hint: Only one stack in each pair must reach the maximum.

questions.title: Reconstruct the storeroom
questions.prompt: Six nonempty stacks form a front row and a back row of three. The back heights from left to right are 4, 1, 2. The front silhouette shows column maxima 4, 3, 2. Altogether there are 14 crates. How many different front rows fit every clue?
questions.hint: The middle front stack is forced. Work out the sum needed from the two end stacks.

lessons.headline: Reserve a gap for neighbours
lessons.intro: Two objects that have to touch can travel as a block. Two objects that must stay apart can use gaps between other objects. Draw the row before deciding which view is shorter.
lessons.bridge: Watch how the film keeps track of A beside B. When a second pair is introduced, sketch a row in which both pairs touch.
lessons.recap: Check the order inside a block as well as its place. At the ends of a row there are gaps too.

example.prompt: Place A and B together in a row with C. How many orders are possible?
steps: The block AB can go before or after C.
Either A or B may lead the block. There are 2 × 2 = 4 orders.

questions.title: Ordered block
questions.prompt: Line up A, B, C and D with A immediately before B. How many orders are possible?
questions.hint: Treat AB as one labelled object.

questions.title: An end gap
questions.prompt: In how many orders of A, B, C and D are A and B at opposite ends?
questions.hint: First decide who takes the left end.

questions.title: Keep the black flags apart
questions.prompt: Three different white flags and two identical black flags form a row. The black flags cannot touch. How many rows are possible?
questions.hint: Arrange the white flags and mark their four gaps.

questions.title: Cabin assignments
questions.prompt: Five different guides stand in a row. Ari must stand next to Bao, and Chen cannot occupy either end. How many rows are possible?
questions.hint: Start with the Ari–Bao block and remove the rows with Chen on an end.

lessons.headline: Classify a cube by its position
lessons.intro: Paint reaches only exposed faces of the large solid. A corner, an edge away from a corner and the middle of a face have different numbers of painted faces.
lessons.bridge: Pay attention when the film leaves the top unpainted. Predict what that changes at the top corners and along the vertical edges.
lessons.recap: Decide which outside faces were painted and classify positions before multiplying.

example.prompt: A 3-by-3-by-3 cube is painted all over and taken apart. Which small cube has no paint?
steps: Every cube on the outside lies on at least one big face.
Only the centre cube sits one layer in from all six surfaces.

lessons.videoTitle: Painted faces, boundary and hidden cubes

questions.title: The clean core
questions.prompt: A solid cube 5 small cubes along each edge has all six outside faces painted. How many small cubes get no paint?
questions.hint: Trim one layer from opposite sides in each direction.

questions.title: Two painted faces
questions.prompt: All faces of a solid 5 by 5 by 5 unit-cube block are painted. How many small cubes have paint on exactly two faces?
questions.hint: Keep the edges but remove both corners from every edge.

questions.title: Just one colour mark
questions.prompt: All six outside faces of a solid 5 by 6 by 4 cuboid of unit cubes are painted. How many unit cubes have exactly one painted face?
questions.hint: Count the interior of each large face, excluding its border.

questions.title: The bottom stays clean
questions.prompt: A cuboid 5 cubes wide, 6 deep and 4 high has its four sides and top painted. How many small cubes get paint on exactly two faces?
questions.hint: Separate vertical edge columns from the border of the top.

lessons.headline: Unfold the box in your head
lessons.intro: A box’s capacity counts cubic units inside. Its net counts square units of card on the surface. Sketch the base and a rectangle for each wall before adding areas.
lessons.bridge: When the film turns a volume into an open box, watch which measurement it can fix immediately and which face is missing from the card net.
lessons.recap: List actual panels when calculating card. For capacity, multiply the base area by the height.

example.prompt: A box with a 3 by 2 cm base is 1 cm high and has no lid. What card area does it use?
steps: The base contributes 6 cm². Two long walls add 6 cm² and two short walls add 4 cm².
The five panels total 16 cm².

lessons.videoTitle: Nets, surface area, volume and 3D views

questions.title: Fill from the base
questions.prompt: A rectangular tank with base 4 cm by 6 cm holds 72 cm³ when full. How many centimetres deep is it?
questions.hint: One centimetre of height adds one base-area of volume.

questions.title: Read a folded net
questions.prompt: A closed cuboid has side lengths 4, 6 and 3 cm. What area of card, in square centimetres, makes its net, ignoring tabs?
questions.hint: Each different rectangle appears twice.

questions.title: Wrapping the walls
questions.prompt: A rectangular gift has base 4 cm by 6 cm and height 3 cm. A paper band exactly covers its four upright faces, with no overlap. What is the area of the band in square centimetres?
questions.hint: Unroll the four walls into one strip.

questions.title: A light open crate
questions.prompt: An open rectangular crate must hold 60 cm³ and be exactly 3 cm high. Its base sides are positive whole centimetres. What is the smallest possible card area, in square centimetres, ignoring tabs?
questions.hint: The base area is fixed. Which factor pair uses the least wall?

lessons.headline: Put back the total behind the mean
lessons.intro: An average tells you how the total would look if it were shared equally. Multiplying the mean by the number of observations recovers that total.
lessons.bridge: When the film combines two group means, pause before the calculation and work out what total each group contributes.
lessons.recap: Before combining or changing averages, write down both the total and the count.

example.prompt: Four tubs contain an average of 7 marbles. Three tubs hold 3, 6 and 10. What is in the last tub?
steps: The four tubs hold 4 × 7 = 28 marbles altogether.
The three known counts total 19, leaving 9 in the last tub.

lessons.videoTitle: Averages, weighted means and simple distributions

questions.title: Missing lap
questions.prompt: Three lap times average 42 seconds. Two times are 39 and 44 seconds. What was the last time in seconds?
questions.hint: Work backwards from the three-lap total.

questions.title: A further test
questions.prompt: Five quiz scores average 12. A sixth score is 18. What is the new mean?
questions.hint: The number of scores also changes.

questions.title: Two crews
questions.prompt: Three rowers average 50 kg, and two others average 60 kg. What is the mean mass of all five rowers in kg?
questions.hint: Convert each mean into a crew total.

questions.title: Damaged logbook
questions.prompt: Seven daily counts average 16. A smudge hides two of the counts. The other five total 74, and the larger hidden count is 6 more than the smaller. What is the smaller count?
questions.hint: Recover their combined total before using the difference.

lessons.headline: Add the ways into a point
lessons.intro: When every step moves right or up, the last step into a grid point has just two possible directions. Label a point with the number of routes that reach it.
lessons.bridge: Follow the two closed intersections. Notice which route totals become zero and which neighbouring totals can still grow.
lessons.recap: Place 1 at the start and 0 at any blocked point, then work across the grid in an order that respects the steps.

example.prompt: A grid point has two ways in from the left and three ways in from below. How many routes reach it?
steps: Every arriving route has exactly one last step. The two groups cannot overlap.
Add their totals: 2 + 3 = 5.

questions.title: Arrival tally
questions.prompt: A walker starts at (0,0), finishes at (4,3) and uses only unit steps right or up. How many routes are possible?
questions.hint: The last move comes from the left or from below.

questions.title: First two instructions
questions.prompt: A walker starts at (0,0), finishes at (4,3) and uses only unit steps right or up. The first two steps must be different. How many routes fit?
questions.hint: Where do both allowed starts leave the walker?

questions.title: Closed crossroads
questions.prompt: A walker starts at (0,0), finishes at (4,3) and uses only unit steps right or up. The intersection (2,1) is closed. How many routes can still be used?
questions.hint: Write zero on the blocked point before adding incoming routes.

questions.title: Two loading bays
questions.prompt: A warehouse robot goes from (0,0) to (3,3), one unit east or north at a time. It must scan exactly one of the loading bays at (1,2) and (2,1). How many routes can it take?
questions.hint: Compute the number through each bay. Could a legal route visit both?

lessons.headline: Build a rectangle from four choices
lessons.intro: Two different vertical lines and two different horizontal lines give exactly one rectangle. Restrictions fix some of those choices or rule out certain pairs.
lessons.bridge: In the film’s marked-cell problem, look for the moment when choosing four boundary lines counts a rectangle exactly once.
lessons.recap: Give every rectangle one left, right, top and bottom boundary. Put restrictions on those choices before multiplying.

example.prompt: A square is divided into two horizontal strips by one full line. How many grid-line rectangles are there?
steps: The left and right sides are fixed. Choose two horizontal lines from the three.
The three choices give each single strip and the full square: 3 rectangles.

questions.title: One fence already built
questions.prompt: A rectangular pen occupies the full height of a 3-column by 2-row grid. Its width must be at least two cells. How many choices of pen are possible along the grid lines?
questions.hint: Only the pair of vertical sides remains to be chosen.

questions.title: A moving two-by-two window
questions.prompt: A window must cover exactly two neighbouring columns and two neighbouring rows of a 6 by 5 grid. How many different positions can it occupy?
questions.hint: Count possible locations of its lower-left cell.

questions.title: Square frames in a window
questions.prompt: A window has 6 columns and 5 rows of square panes. How many square outlines, of any size, can be traced along its straight bars?
questions.hint: Count positions for each possible side length.

questions.title: Add a vertical line
questions.prompt: A grid has 6 existing vertical lines and 6 horizontal lines. One more full vertical line is drawn to the right. How many additional grid-line rectangles are created?
questions.hint: Every new rectangle must use the new line as one side.

lessons.headline: Use both clues at once
lessons.intro: A total tells you what two amounts make together. A gap tells you how unlike they are. Removing the gap leaves two matching amounts.
lessons.bridge: Pause at the two numbers that add to eighteen and differ by four. Watch how the same habit of keeping both clues becomes useful when the objects are notebooks and rulers.
lessons.recap: Check both clues, even if your first calculation already gives the stated total.

example.prompt: Two bowls hold 22 cherries altogether. One has 4 more. How many cherries are in the smaller bowl?
steps: Set aside the extra four. Eighteen cherries now make two equal groups.
Each group contains 9. The original bowls held 9 and 13.

figure.alt: Two bowls share the same base number of cherries. The larger bowl has an additional four.

questions.title: Equal first
questions.prompt: Two boxes contain 32 stones altogether and contain equal numbers. How many are in either box?
questions.hint: Split the total equally.

questions.title: A longer ribbon
questions.prompt: Two ribbons total 41 cm. One is 7 cm longer. How long is the shorter ribbon in centimetres?
questions.hint: Remove the surplus length.

questions.title: Three heights
questions.prompt: Three models stand on a table. Their heights total 69 cm. The middle one is 3 cm taller than the smallest and the tallest is 6 cm taller than the smallest. What is the tallest height in centimetres?
questions.hint: Remove both extras to leave three equal heights.

questions.title: The changed lead
questions.prompt: Two runners collect 50 flags between them. If the leader hands 3 flags to the other runner, the leader still has 2 more. How many flags did the leader collect originally?
questions.hint: Work out the two holdings after the handover.

lessons.headline: Let the first uncovered cell decide
lessons.intro: A tiling covers every cell once with no overlap. Start at an exposed corner: one possible placement may force the next piece, turning a large problem into a shorter strip.
lessons.bridge: When the first domino goes sideways in the two-row board, pause and locate the piece that must go beside it.
lessons.recap: Find a corner with few options. Count complete continuations separately for each legal first placement.

example.prompt: How many ways do dominoes cover a fixed strip one cell high and four cells long?
steps: The first cell must pair with its right-hand neighbour.
The remaining two cells also pair. There is one complete tiling.

questions.title: Doubled strips
questions.prompt: Tile a 2-row board of width 5 with dominoes on adjacent squares. If every domino lies across a whole column, how many dominoes are needed?
questions.hint: Count filled cells and divide by each domino’s area.

questions.title: The extra colour
questions.prompt: A checkerboard strip has three rows of 9 squares. Its top-left square is black. How many black squares does it contain?
questions.hint: The first and third rows match.

questions.title: The first empty column
questions.prompt: How many distinct domino tilings does a fixed 2-row board of width 5 have? Rotating the whole board does not identify tilings.
questions.hint: One upright domino fills the first column, or two horizontal ones fill the first two.

questions.title: An odd panel with an extension
questions.prompt: A 3-by-9 board has two more squares immediately to the right of its bottom two rows, one in each row. What is the greatest number of nonoverlapping dominoes it can hold?
questions.hint: Use the odd area for a bound, then show a placement that reaches it.

lessons.headline: Test the speaker and the claim together
lessons.intro: In a truth-teller puzzle, a statement and its speaker must agree: a truthful speaker’s full claim is true, and a liar’s full claim is false. Try writing one short row for each possible world.
lessons.bridge: As Noor and Oli describe the next speaker, mark whether each link means “same type” or “different type”. Check the final claim only after following those links.
lessons.recap: Test the whole statement against the assigned speaker type. Then recheck every claim in the surviving case.

example.prompt: Pia says “The coin is in the jar.” You know Pia always lies and that the coin is in the jar or the bag. Where is it?
steps: Her claim about the jar must be false.
The bag is the only remaining location, so the coin is in the bag.

questions.title: A true observation
questions.prompt: Every person either always tells the truth or always lies. Dara calls Eli a liar. We know Dara always lies. Is Eli truthful? Answer yes or no.
questions.hint: Evaluate what the sentence would say if it were true.

questions.title: A claim about two people
questions.prompt: Every person either always tells the truth or always lies. Ira says, “Jia is a liar and Kir is truthful.” We know Jia is truthful. Can Ira be truthful? Answer yes or no.
questions.hint: What is required for a sentence containing “and” to be true?

questions.title: Two claims in sequence
questions.prompt: Every person either always tells the truth or always lies. Faye says Gus is truthful. Gus says Hiro is a liar. If Hiro is truthful, how many of these three lie?
questions.hint: Start with the person whose type is given.

questions.title: Who called whom truthful?
questions.prompt: Every person either always tells the truth or always lies. Hiro calls Ira truthful. Ira calls Jia truthful. Jia says Hiro and Ira are the same type. How many are truthful?
questions.hint: The first two descriptions link what types can agree.

lessons.headline: Decide what a legal move means
lessons.intro: Route counting begins with the permitted connections. Squares that touch only at a corner can be close on paper and still be forbidden neighbours.
lessons.bridge: Watch how the film moves from neighbours on a board to red and blue stops. What stays fixed about the colour of the next stop?
lessons.recap: Draw connections explicitly when a side, bridge or colour determines the next possible stop.

example.prompt: On a two-row, three-column board, how many side-neighbours does a corner cell have?
steps: From that corner there is one step along the row and one into the next row.
There are 2 side-neighbours. The diagonally touching cell is excluded.

questions.title: Three next-door neighbours
questions.prompt: Cells in a 5-column by 4-row board are neighbours only across a full side. How many cells have exactly three neighbours?
questions.hint: Separate corners, edges away from corners, and the interior.

questions.title: A bridge for each pair
questions.prompt: A 5 by 4 array of islands has one short bridge for each pair of horizontally or vertically adjacent islands. How many bridges are built?
questions.hint: Count horizontal connections in one row before counting vertical ones.

questions.title: Alternating stations
questions.prompt: There are 4 red stations and 4 blue stations. Every red station joins every blue station. Starting at a specified red station, take two moves without revisiting the start. How many different ordered routes are possible?
questions.hint: Choose the middle station first.

questions.title: Every station exactly once
questions.prompt: Each of 4 red stations is connected to every one of 4 blue stations, with no same-colour links. Starting at a fixed red and ending at a fixed blue, how many ordered routes visit all stations once?
questions.hint: The colours force the positions. Fill each colour’s remaining slots.

lessons.headline: Count equally likely outcomes
lessons.intro: Probability compares favourable outcomes with all possible outcomes. The outcomes in your list must have equal chances. Two different labels need not appear equally often.
lessons.bridge: At the spinners, notice what one square of the outcome table represents. At the bag of counters, ask what replaces those squares as the equally likely outcomes.
lessons.recap: Identify what the random action actually selects. Count that unit both above and below the fraction bar.

example.prompt: A bag holds three yellow counters and one green counter. One counter is drawn at random. What is the chance of green?
steps: Use individual counters as outcomes. There are four equally likely choices.
One is green, so the probability is 1/4.

questions.title: Purple sectors
questions.prompt: A fair spinner has eight equal sectors, three purple. What is the probability of purple? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Count equal sectors.

questions.title: Even total
questions.prompt: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability that the number of heads is even, including zero? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: List the four ordered toss pairs.

questions.title: Different colours
questions.prompt: A bag contains two red and three blue counters. Two are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that they have different colours? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Count unordered pairs of individual counters.

questions.title: Which platform?
questions.prompt: A train chooses one of three platforms with equal probability. It then chooses one of the exits at that platform with equal probability. The platforms have one, two and three exits respectively. What is the probability of one particular exit on the three-exit platform? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Both the correct platform and the correct exit are needed.

lessons.headline: Count digits in their own columns
lessons.intro: A printed label can use the same digit twice. Make a tally for each place, then add the tallies to count every printed copy.
lessons.bridge: The film moves from adding the digits of 386 to counting printed threes. Decide which question needs the positions of the digits and which can ignore them.
lessons.recap: Say whether the question wants labels or copies of a digit. A label with two copies counts once for the first question and twice for the second.

example.prompt: On the labels 20 through 23, how many copies of the digit 2 appear?
steps: All four labels have a 2 in the tens place.
The label 22 also has a 2 in the units place, so the total is 5.

lessons.videoTitle: Digit sums and counting digits in ranges

questions.title: A short shelf
questions.prompt: Labels run from 31 through 35. How many copies of the digit 3 appear?
questions.hint: Look at tens and units separately.

questions.title: At least one
questions.prompt: Among 20 through 29 inclusive, how many labels contain at least one 2?
questions.hint: A label needs to qualify only once.

questions.title: First month
questions.prompt: A calendar numbers the days 1 to 31. How many copies of the digit 2 appear?
questions.hint: Count days ending in 2 and days beginning with 2 in the twenties.

questions.title: A print order
questions.prompt: A machine prints every label from 99 to 122 inclusive. How many copies of the digit 1 does it use?
questions.hint: The change to three-digit labels opens a new column.

lessons.headline: Use how far each value is from the mean
lessons.intro: At the mean, shortfalls exactly balance excesses. When values cluster around a convenient number, working with the differences can be quicker than adding the original values.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film turn a group mean back into a total. As a second check, consider which group pulls the combined mean towards its own value.
lessons.recap: Subtract a common starting value, average the smaller differences, then restore the starting value.

example.prompt: Four trays hold 18, 22, 19 and 21 counters. What is their mean?
steps: Relative to 20 the differences are −2,+2,−1,+1.
They cancel, so the mean is exactly 20.

lessons.videoTitle: Averages, weighted means and simple distributions

questions.title: A close set
questions.prompt: What is the mean of 48, 53, 51, 50 and 48?
questions.hint: Measure each number from 50.

questions.title: Balance the fourth
questions.prompt: Four packets average 26 g. Three weigh 24, 25 and 30 g. How many grams is the fourth?
questions.hint: Their differences from 26 must sum to zero.

questions.title: Shift a reading
questions.prompt: Eight temperatures average 15 degrees. One temperature is raised by 4 degrees and another is lowered by 2 degrees. What is the new average? Give an exact number.
questions.hint: How much has the whole total changed?

questions.title: Find the outlier
questions.prompt: Nine observations average 41. Eight of them average 39. What is the ninth observation?
questions.hint: Each of the eight is collectively below the overall mean.

lessons.headline: Read a total or read a change
lessons.intro: A cumulative reading includes everything recorded up to that point. Subtract successive readings to find what happened during an interval. Read the time labels as carefully as the values.
lessons.bridge: In the film’s time chart, point to the two readings you would subtract. Then check the time between them before comparing rates.
lessons.recap: Name both endpoints and their units. A point tells you a total and a difference tells you a change.

example.prompt: A turnstile count is 8 at 9 am, 14 at 10 am and 23 at 11 am. How many people enter between 10 and 11?
steps: Use the two readings at the ends of this interval: 14 and 23.
The later total already contains the earlier 14. Subtract to find 9 new arrivals.

figure.alt: Turnstile readings are 8 at 9 am, 14 at 10 am and 23 at 11 am.

questions.title: Morning gate
questions.prompt: A counter shows 35 at 8 am, 46 at 9 am and 64 at 10 am. How many people pass between 8 and 10?
questions.hint: Use just the start and end readings.

questions.title: Highest hourly gain
questions.prompt: At hours 0,1,2,3,4 a tank meter reads 4,13,20,35,41 litres in total. What is the greatest gain in a single hour, in litres?
questions.hint: Compare four differences.

questions.title: Find the blank
questions.prompt: A meter reads 12 at noon, an unknown amount at 1 pm and 39 at 2 pm. The second hour's gain is twice the first hour's gain. What is the 1 pm reading?
questions.hint: Split the total gain in the ratio 1 to 2.

questions.title: Two scanners
questions.prompt: Scanner A's total rises from 40 to 96 over four hours. Scanner B's rises from 15 to 63 over three hours. How many more items per hour does the faster scanner process on average?
questions.hint: Convert changes to rates over the stated durations.

lessons.headline: Divide a job into convenient units
lessons.intro: Call the complete job a number divisible by the individual completion times. Rates that look awkward as fractions can then become whole numbers of work units.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film choose thirty imaginary pieces for the machines' batch. How many pieces does each machine finish each minute, and why does their total work still represent one batch?
lessons.recap: Changing the number of imaginary units should change neither the real time nor the fraction of the job completed.

example.prompt: Two sorters finish a box in 4 minutes and 6 minutes alone. Imagine the box has 12 equal work units. How many units does the pair finish per minute?
steps: The sorters complete 3 and 2 units per minute.
Together they complete 5 of the 12 units each minute.

figure.alt: A box split into twelve equal units. The four-minute sorter completes three units in a minute. The six-minute sorter completes two.

questions.title: The filing team
questions.prompt: Two clerks handle 3 and 5 files per minute. How many minutes do they need for 96 files together?
questions.hint: Count the files done by both each minute.

questions.title: A head start
questions.prompt: A packer can complete a batch alone in 18 minutes. After 6 minutes a second packer joins, working at twice the first packer's rate. How many more minutes does the batch need?
questions.hint: Use 18 units for the batch.

questions.title: A short overlap
questions.prompt: Machine A makes a set in 10 minutes and B makes the same set in 15 minutes. They run together for 3 minutes. Then B stops. How many further minutes does A need?
questions.hint: Count the fraction both machines complete together.

questions.title: Whose contribution?
questions.prompt: Two scanners finish a stack together in 12 minutes. The first could scan the stack alone in 20 minutes. The stack has 150 pages. How many pages did the second scanner scan?
questions.hint: Find the first scanner's share over the actual working time.

lessons.headline: Mark step zero before cycling
lessons.intro: If a full group of moves returns a device to its starting state, only the leftover moves affect its final display. Write down the starting display at step zero so that step numbers line up.
lessons.bridge: Follow the pointer from its starting direction. Notice how the machine later needs an extra step before its repeating section begins.
lessons.recap: Subtract the starting index before reducing by the repeat length. A zero remainder takes you back to the state at the start of the cycle.

example.prompt: A dial shows A, then B, then C, then A again. Starting at A, what does it show after 8 presses?
steps: Each group of 3 presses returns to A.
Eight presses are two full groups and two more, taking A to B to C.

questions.title: Quarter turns
questions.prompt: A pointer starts at north and turns clockwise by a quarter turn per press. After 19 presses how many extra quarter turns beyond complete rotations affect its direction?
questions.hint: Divide 19 by the period.

questions.title: Starting on blue
questions.prompt: A light cycles red, blue, green in that order and starts on blue. After 20 changes, which colour shows? Answer red, blue or green.
questions.hint: Write the cycle beginning at the actual starting colour.

questions.title: A labelled rail
questions.prompt: A trolley occupies positions 0 through 6 around a loop and advances 2 positions on each signal, wrapping after 6. Starting at 0, which numbered position does it occupy after 25 signals?
questions.hint: Compute the total advance modulo 7.

questions.title: Inspection rounds
questions.prompt: An inspector visits sites A, B, C and D in that repeating order, one per day, with A on day 1. How many times does she visit C during the first 39 days?
questions.hint: Find the day numbers for C, including the incomplete last cycle.

lessons.headline: Distinguish a notch from a missing corner
lessons.intro: Imagine running a finger around the outline before and after a cut. Match the parts of the two journeys and measure just the change.
lessons.bridge: Watch the enclosed hole and the missing outer corner separately. Try tracing both loops before comparing their lengths.
lessons.recap: A corner cut can replace edges of equal length. At a notch or hole, count the extra sides explicitly.

example.prompt: A 5 by 4 rectangle loses a 1 by 1 corner. How much does its perimeter change?
steps: Two unit edges disappear. The cut exposes two new unit edges further in.
The change is zero. The shape has less area but still has perimeter 18.

lessons.videoTitle: Perimeter, shared edges and boundary effects

questions.title: The V in the pennant
questions.prompt: A pennant has a perimeter of 30 cm. Replace a straight 6 cm part of its edge with an inward V made of two 5 cm sides. What is its new perimeter in centimetres?
questions.hint: Cross out the original edge before adding the new pair.

questions.title: The loading bay
questions.prompt: A 21 m by 8 m rectangular yard has a 3 m wide entrance cut 4 m into the middle of a long edge as a rectangular notch. How long is the new boundary in metres?
questions.hint: Compare the mouth of the notch with the back of the notch.

questions.title: Two alterations to a sign
questions.prompt: A sign starts with 40 cm of exposed edge. On one side a straight 5 cm segment becomes two sloping sides measuring 3 and 4 cm. Elsewhere another 5 cm segment becomes a rectangular recess, 3 cm deep and 5 cm wide. What is the new perimeter in centimetres?
questions.hint: Measure each replacement path and compare it with the length it took away.

questions.title: Recover the inner fence
questions.prompt: A 12 m by 9 m exhibition lawn surrounds a rectangular flower bed completely inside it. All boundaries together measure 52 m. The bed is 2 m wide. How long is it in metres?
questions.hint: Subtract the outer fence before halving the bed perimeter.

lessons.headline: A route keeps some history
lessons.intro: If a walk cannot revisit a stop, arriving somewhere does not erase the earlier moves. Keep enough information to recognise when a tempting next step would go back.
lessons.bridge: In the alternating route, keep a record of which red or blue stops have already been used when deciding the next move.
lessons.recap: Record visited stops when repetition is forbidden. If a route must use bridges instead, track which bridges have been used.

example.prompt: A path goes through A, B, C in that order. Start at A and never revisit a vertex. After moving to B, how many next stops are available?
steps: B connects to both A and C, but A has already been used.
Only C is still allowed, leaving one choice.

questions.title: No second visit
questions.prompt: Four stations form the undirected links AB, BC, CA and CD. A walker starts at A and must make exactly three moves without visiting any station twice. How many routes are possible?
questions.hint: Try each possible first move and keep track of the stations already used.

questions.title: Along a ring
questions.prompt: On a ring of 10 labelled stops, each stop joins its two immediate neighbours. Starting at a specified stop, visit all the others exactly once using 9 moves. How many different ordered routes are possible?
questions.hint: Count the first step, then check how many later choices remain.

questions.title: Corner-cutting shortcuts
questions.prompt: A 6 by 3 rectangular array of points has a diagonal link between points in adjacent rows and adjacent columns whenever they are opposite corners of a unit square. How many distinct diagonal links are there?
questions.hint: Count the little squares between the points, not the points.

questions.title: The closed first link
questions.prompt: Every red station joins every blue one among 5 labelled stations of each colour, except that the link from the designated red start to blue station B is closed. The designated blue finish is different from B. How many alternating routes visit every station exactly once from start to finish?
questions.hint: In a route that visits the start only once, when could the closed link be used?

lessons.headline: Treat a remainder as a position
lessons.intro: After making full groups, a remainder tells you how far you are beyond the last multiple. Sometimes it is quicker to count the short distance up to the next multiple.
lessons.bridge: In the film's number beginning with 58, decide which clue restricts the last two digits and which clue checks the whole number.
lessons.recap: Check the adjusted number by division. A remainder of 3 does not necessarily mean you must add 3.

example.prompt: What is the least number to add to 38 to reach a multiple of 7?
steps: Thirty-eight is 3 above 35, so it is 4 below 42.
Adding 4 completes the next group of 7.

questions.title: The last packet
questions.prompt: How many counters are left after 73 counters are put into as many full packets of 8 as possible?
questions.hint: Find the largest multiple of 8 at most 73.

questions.title: Complete the row
questions.prompt: A theatre has 94 chairs. What is the fewest extra chairs needed to make rows of 12 with none left over?
questions.hint: Compare 94 with the next multiple.

questions.title: A shared leftover
questions.prompt: A number between 60 and 80 leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 5 and by 7. What is the number?
questions.hint: Take away the common remainder before comparing multiples.

questions.title: Back to the depot
questions.prompt: Depot stops occur at road markers 3, 10, 17 and every 7 kilometres thereafter. How many depot stops have marker numbers from 45 to 100 inclusive?
questions.hint: Find the first and last numbers in that interval that are 3 past a multiple of 7.

lessons.headline: Notice which faces were painted
lessons.intro: “On the outside” and “painted” can describe different positions when a solid has unpainted faces. Mark the painted directions before removing any outer layers.
lessons.bridge: Look at the top of the cuboid in the film. A piece there can still get paint on its sides, even though its top is clean.
lessons.recap: Remove a layer from a clean-core calculation only on a side that was painted.

example.prompt: A 4-by-3-by-2 block has only its top painted. How many unit cubes have paint?
steps: Only the top layer touches that face.
The layer has 4 × 3 = 12 cubes. The lower layer has none.

lessons.videoTitle: Painted faces, boundary and hidden cubes

questions.title: Paint only the standing walls
questions.prompt: A block is 6 cubes wide, 7 deep and 5 high. Paint only its four vertical sides. How many unit cubes have no paint?
questions.hint: The top and bottom need no layer removed.

questions.title: Two colours on opposite ends
questions.prompt: A straight solid bar has a square cross-section 6 units on each side and length 8. Paint one end red and the opposite end blue. How many unit cubes have red paint and no blue paint?
questions.hint: The length determines whether the two end layers coincide.

questions.title: Three adjoining sides
questions.prompt: A cuboid is 6 by 7 by 5 unit cubes. Paint three outside faces that all meet at one corner. How many cubes get some paint?
questions.hint: Which smaller cuboid gets none of the three colours?

questions.title: The two-colour display case
questions.prompt: A block is 7 cubes wide, 5 deep and 4 high. Paint its top red and all four upright sides blue. How many individual cubes have a red face and exactly one blue face?
questions.hint: Look down on the red layer. Which positions have just one neighbour outside the footprint?

lessons.headline: Count the labels that escape
lessons.intro: Sometimes counting labels with at least one target digit is easier by counting those that avoid it. Decide whether a leading zero is permitted before choosing the digits.
lessons.bridge: Watch the list of labels ending at 442. Count a digit in each of its positions, even when the same label contributes more than once.
lessons.recap: Check that “no occurrence” and “at least one occurrence” cover every label exactly once. Printed numbers and fixed-width codes have different rules about zero.

example.prompt: How many two-digit codes from 00 to 99 contain a 7?
steps: There are 100 codes. If neither position shows 7, each has nine choices.
Subtract the 81 codes with no 7. The other 19 contain at least one.

lessons.videoTitle: Digit sums and counting digits in ranges

questions.title: The unmarked list
questions.prompt: How many two-digit whole numbers have no digit 8?
questions.hint: Count choices in the tens position separately.

questions.title: One four only
questions.prompt: How many two-digit whole numbers contain exactly one digit 4?
questions.hint: Separate a leading 4 from a trailing 4.

questions.title: A fixed-width locker code
questions.prompt: A locker code has three positions, each showing 0, 1, 2 or 3. Leading zero is allowed. How many codes show at least one zero?
questions.hint: Count all codes and those using only 1, 2 and 3.

questions.title: Codes with two sevens
questions.prompt: A three-digit display uses all digits 0–9 and allows leading zeros. How many displays have exactly two 7s?
questions.hint: Choose the position that does not contain 7.

lessons.headline: Keep each fraction with its group
lessons.intro: Different groups can have different sizes. Find the number selected in each group before you combine them.
lessons.bridge: When the film shows starred cards, point to the group named by each fraction. Notice when the denominator changes to the size of both groups together.
lessons.recap: A fraction of the combined group needs the combined size as its denominator. A fraction of one group keeps that group's size.

example.prompt: A tray holds 12 oat biscuits, half iced, and 8 fruit biscuits, one quarter iced. How many biscuits are iced?
steps: Half of 12 gives 6 oat biscuits. One quarter of 8 gives 2 fruit biscuits.
Add the actual numbers: 6 + 2 = 8 iced biscuits.

questions.title: On the two shelves
questions.prompt: One shelf holds 15 books, one third hardbacks. Another holds 20, one half hardbacks. How many hardbacks are there altogether?
questions.hint: Work on one shelf at a time.

questions.title: What fraction wears a cap?
questions.prompt: Six of 8 juniors and 2 of 12 seniors wear caps. What fraction of all the players wear caps? Give an exact fraction.
questions.hint: Count all the cap wearers, then all the players.

questions.title: The blank label
questions.prompt: There are 24 large envelopes and 16 small ones. Half of the large ones and some of the small ones are stamped. There are 18 stamped envelopes in total. What fraction of the small envelopes are stamped?
questions.hint: Remove the stamped large envelopes first.

questions.title: A third overall
questions.prompt: A nursery has 18 green pots, two thirds flowering. It adds yellow pots, each containing a plant without flowers. How many yellow pots are needed for exactly one third of all pots to be flowering?
questions.hint: Which number stays fixed as pots are added?

lessons.headline: Distinguish today's amount from the total so far
lessons.intro: In a doubling sequence, the last amount can be almost as large as all earlier amounts put together. A question about one day and a question about the running total need different calculations.
lessons.bridge: Watch the difference between the amount required on one day and the running total. In the budget example, it is the running total that must fit.
lessons.recap: Label the last term and the running total separately. A budget must cover every completed day, including the first.

example.prompt: A project uses 3, 6 and 12 counters on its first three days. How many have been used by the end of day 3?
steps: Day 3 alone uses 12.
Over all three days the amount is 3 + 6 + 12 = 21.

lessons.videoTitle: Doubling, geometric growth and finite sums

questions.title: The fifth patch
questions.prompt: A pattern uses 3 tiles in its first patch, doubling the number in every new patch. How many tiles are in the fifth patch?
questions.hint: The first patch precedes four doublings.

questions.title: All the patches
questions.prompt: Five patches contain 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 tiles. How many tiles do they contain altogether?
questions.hint: Add all five terms.

questions.title: First day recovered
questions.prompt: Four daily amounts double from one day to the next. Together they total 75. How large is the first amount?
questions.hint: Measure each day in copies of the first amount.

questions.title: Enough envelopes
questions.prompt: A stall uses 5 envelopes in its first hour, then twice the previous hour's amount. It has 150 envelopes. How many complete hours can it run?
questions.hint: Check running totals on both sides of the budget.

lessons.headline: Read the centre twice
lessons.intro: In a magic square, one cell can belong to more than one line. Write each full line separately to make sure the shared entry is counted with the right frequency.
lessons.bridge: Watch the main diagonals share the centre cell. Notice how using the same number on both lines narrows the list of possible corner values.
lessons.recap: Opposite entries on a line through the centre add to the line total minus the centre.

example.prompt: The diagonal of a magic square reads 7, 5, blank, with a line total of 15. What is the blank?
steps: The first two values total 12.
The third must be 3. The opposite corners then sum to 10.

lessons.videoTitle: Magic grids, symbolic rules and consistency

questions.title: Both diagonals
questions.prompt: Each of the two main diagonals in a 3-by-3 number grid totals 18. Together its four corner entries add to 24. What number is in the centre?
questions.hint: Add both diagonals and track how often they pass through the centre.

questions.title: Change one entry
questions.prompt: A 3-by-3 magic square has three row sums, three column sums and two main diagonal sums. If only the centre entry increases by 2, how many of these eight sums increase?
questions.hint: Trace every full line that passes through the centre.

questions.title: Read the ring
questions.prompt: In a 3-by-3 magic square every row, column and main diagonal has sum S. Its eight outer entries together total 48. What is S?
questions.hint: Call the centre c. Compare the three row sums with the four lines through the centre.

questions.title: A changed set of tiles
questions.prompt: Take a 3-by-3 magic square with line total 15. Replace each number x with 2x + 4. What is the new line total?
questions.hint: Count how many times the added constant occurs in one line.

lessons.headline: Count the frames around a cell
lessons.intro: A marked cell puts the left boundary on one side and the right boundary on the other. It also constrains the lower and upper edges. These choices determine a unique frame.
lessons.bridge: When two marked cells enter the grid, compare the frames surrounding the first cell with those that also surround the second.
lessons.recap: To include one mark and exclude another, count all frames around the first mark and subtract the ones around both.

example.prompt: There are three cells in one row. How many whole-cell subrectangles contain the centre cell?
steps: The left edge can be before cell 1 or before cell 2. The right edge can be after cell 2 or after cell 3.
The two pairs of choices give 2 × 2 = 4 frames.

questions.title: Cover the corner seal
questions.prompt: A seal is on the upper-left cell of a 4-column by 3-row sheet. A rectangular label must cover exactly two adjacent cells, including the seal. How many placements fit?
questions.hint: The second cell must share a whole side with the corner cell.

questions.title: Exactly one sticker
questions.prompt: Five cells form a row, with stickers in the second and fourth cells. How many uninterrupted strips of whole cells contain exactly one sticker?
questions.hint: Count strips around the second sticker that stop before the fourth, then use the mirror image.

questions.title: The strip of tickets
questions.prompt: Tickets form a 3-column by 3-row sheet. A rectangular cut-out must contain both middle-row corner cells, and it must leave at least one row of the sheet untouched. How many cut-outs are possible?
questions.hint: The two marked tickets force the width. Count possible selections of consecutive rows.

questions.title: Rectangles with unequal sides
questions.prompt: A board is 7 cells wide and 6 cells tall. How many grid-line rectangles have different width and height?
questions.hint: Count every rectangle, then remove squares of each possible side length.

lessons.headline: Count two kinds in one collection
lessons.intro: When you know the item count and a second total, pretend all the items are of the simpler kind. The excess tells you how many items must change kind.
lessons.bridge: Think of the film's notebooks and rulers as different kinds sharing two totals. Watch what the combined shopping bills reveal before you separate their prices.
lessons.recap: Rebuild the collection. Its number of items and its second total must both match.

example.prompt: There are 6 coins, each worth 2 or 5 cents. Together they are worth 18 cents. How many are 5-cent coins?
steps: Six 2-cent coins would give 12 cents. The actual total is 6 cents higher.
Each replacement gains 3 cents, so exactly 2 coins are worth 5 cents.

questions.title: Two kinds of tile
questions.prompt: Eight tiles are numbered either 1 or 3. Their numbers sum to 18. How many tiles show 3?
questions.hint: Start with eight 1s.

questions.title: Count what was asked
questions.prompt: A tray has 13 biscuits costing either 2 or 5 tokens each. The tray costs 44 tokens. How many biscuits cost 2 tokens each?
questions.hint: Find the expensive count, then its complement.

questions.title: An empty seat
questions.prompt: A hall sets out 10 benches, each with 3 or 5 seats. Exactly one seat is empty and 39 people are seated. How many five-seat benches are there?
questions.hint: Find total capacity before counting bench types.

questions.title: A penalty as well as a reward
questions.prompt: A quiz has 16 questions. Each correct answer earns 4 points and each wrong answer loses 1. All are answered and the score is 39. How many answers are correct?
questions.hint: Changing a wrong answer to correct changes the score by more than four.

lessons.headline: Count what escaped
lessons.intro: A question asking for at least one often has one simple alternative. Start with all outcomes and remove those in which the event never happens.
lessons.bridge: As the film lists numbers to exclude, watch what happens to a number divisible by more than one of the listed divisors.
lessons.recap: Write the exact opposite of the condition. Subtract from a total that uses the same definition of an outcome.

example.prompt: Three switches can each be on or off. How many settings have at least one switch on?
steps: There are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 settings.
Only all-off is forbidden, so there are 7.

questions.title: A string of lamps
questions.prompt: Four separate lamps can each be on or off. How many settings light at least one lamp?
questions.hint: Count all settings and remove one.

questions.title: One striped token
questions.prompt: A bag has three distinct striped and four distinct plain tokens. How many unordered pairs contain at least one striped token?
questions.hint: Remove the pairs containing two plain tokens.

questions.title: Skipping a colour
questions.prompt: A three-letter signal uses R, G or B at each position. How many signals use R at least once?
questions.hint: How many signals use only G and B?

questions.title: Both ticket types
questions.prompt: A wallet has four different bus tickets and five different train tickets. How many sets of three tickets contain both types?
questions.hint: Exclude the all-bus sets and all-train sets.

lessons.headline: Price one extra metre of width
lessons.intro: A wall or an internal divider changes how much material each extra metre of depth costs. Label all fenced sides before writing an equation.
lessons.bridge: When the film fixes the total fencing at the wall, watch what happens to the available front each time both ends grow by a metre.
lessons.recap: Count every copy of a repeated side and check that your chosen lengths use the stated material.

example.prompt: A pen has 10 m of wire for its front and two equal ends. Each end is 2 m. How long can the front be?
steps: Both ends together use 4 m.
The single front gets the remaining 10 − 4 = 6 m.

lessons.videoTitle: Optimising areas and lengths under constraints

questions.title: A wall shorter than the pen
questions.prompt: An 8 m by 4 m rectangular pen touches a straight stone wall along just 6 m of an 8 m side. The rest of the pen boundary needs wire. How many metres of wire are required?
questions.hint: Mark the unfenced section on just one side.

questions.title: Allow for the gate
questions.prompt: A garden uses a wall along its entire back. The two sides are each 6 m deep. The front is closed by a 4 m gate and wire. Exactly 32 m of wire is used along the two sides and front. How long is the front in metres?
questions.hint: The gate uses up front length but uses none of the 32 m of wire.

questions.title: Two square runs
questions.prompt: Two equally sized square dog runs sit side by side against a long wall. The wall forms both backs. Wire forms the fronts, outer sides and the one shared divider, except for a 2 m gate in one front. With 67 m of wire, what is the largest combined floor area in square metres if each square side is a whole number of metres?
questions.hint: Count lengths of wire equal to a square side, including the divider just once.

questions.title: A divided pen against a wall
questions.prompt: A wall forms the back of a rectangular pen. The front needs one fence, and two ends plus a dividing fence each run the same distance straight out from the wall. With 36 m of fencing and whole-metre lengths, what is the maximum total area?
questions.hint: One metre of extra depth costs three metres of fence.

lessons.headline: Compensate around a round number
lessons.intro: An awkward product can be close to a very simple one. Replace a factor with a convenient round number and keep track of the correction you owe.
lessons.bridge: Look at 108 × 92 in the film. Which pieces from breaking around 100 cancel, and which small piece still has to be removed?
lessons.recap: State what you added or removed before calculating its value. A correction to one factor changes the product by a whole row or column.

example.prompt: Find 29 × 8 without long multiplication.
steps: Thirty groups of 8 make 240.
Remove one extra group of 8 to get 232.

questions.title: Near fifty
questions.prompt: What is 49 × 12?
questions.hint: Use fifty groups, less one group.

questions.title: Ninety-seven sets
questions.prompt: A printer makes 97 copies of a 24-page booklet. How many pages does it print?
questions.hint: Begin with 100 copies.

questions.title: Two rounded figures
questions.prompt: A club buys 98 packs at $24 each. The treasurer estimates the bill using 100 packs at $25 each. By how many dollars is the estimate too high?
questions.hint: Correct one rounded figure at a time, using the packet count at that step.

questions.title: Which rectangle gains?
questions.prompt: Rectangle A measures 198 by 202 metres and rectangle B measures 199 by 201 metres. How many square metres larger is B than A?
questions.hint: Both pairs are centred on 200.

lessons.headline: Use the difference between the parts
lessons.intro: A ratio can tell you the size of a share even when only the difference between two amounts is known. Compare the unequal ends of two bars.
lessons.bridge: Follow the red and blue counters towards the end of the film. Which amount stays fixed as counters move, and which difference changes?
lessons.recap: Read carefully whether a stated quantity is a total, one amount or a difference. Each corresponds to a different number of ratio parts.
