example.prompt: Two teams have scores in the ratio 5 to 3. Their scores differ by 8. What is the lower score?
steps: The difference of 2 shares is worth 8, so each share is worth 4.
The lower score is 3 shares, or 12. The higher score is 20, exactly 8 more.

figure.alt: The higher score is five equal parts and the lower is three. The two extra parts account for the difference of eight.

questions.title: The longer rope
questions.prompt: Two lengths of rope are in the ratio 7 to 4. Their lengths differ by 18 m. How long is the longer rope in metres?
questions.hint: Match 18 to the gap in parts.

questions.title: Before cutting
questions.prompt: A cord is cut in the ratio 5 to 2. The longer part exceeds the shorter by 21 cm. What was the length of the uncut cord in centimetres?
questions.hint: The uncut cord contains both shares.

questions.title: Same addition
questions.prompt: Two pots contain 18 and 30 counters. Add the same number of counters to each until the smaller and larger amounts are in the ratio 2 to 3. How many go into each pot?
questions.hint: Adding equally preserves the difference.

questions.title: One fence, two plans
questions.prompt: On one plan a fence is 6 cm long. The same fence is 9 cm long on a second plan. A gate is 4 cm long on the second plan. How long is the gate on the first plan, in centimetres? Give an exact fraction.
questions.hint: Use the fence to compare the two drawings, in the direction you need.

lessons.headline: Build scores from a common starting point
lessons.intro: A lead measures the difference between scores. Write each score as the lowest score plus its own extra, making sure every lead refers to the right opponent.
lessons.bridge: In the film's three-score puzzle, the highest leads the middle, not the lowest. Follow both leads back to the lowest score before adding the extras.
lessons.recap: Write who leads whom beside each margin. Check relative claims by subtracting the final scores in the named order.

example.prompt: Kai has 2 points more than Jo. Dee has 3 more than Kai. How much more than Jo does Dee have?
steps: Moving from Jo to Kai adds 2.
Moving on to Dee adds another 3, so Dee leads Jo by 5.

figure.alt: Jo has a baseline amount. Kai has the baseline plus two. Dee has the baseline plus two and another three.

lessons.videoTitle: Winner margins, shared totals and linear rules

questions.title: Who leads last?
questions.prompt: Mira beats Eli by 8 points, and Eli beats Nia by 5. By how many points does Mira beat Nia?
questions.hint: Trace a path from Nia to Mira.

questions.title: Opposite directions
questions.prompt: Jo beats Pat by 9 and Kim beats Pat by 4. What is Jo's lead over Kim?
questions.hint: Both leads use Pat as their base.

questions.title: Three scores, one sum
questions.prompt: The silver team scores 2 more than bronze and gold scores 5 more than silver. The scores total 63. How many points does gold score?
questions.hint: Express each score above bronze.

questions.title: A scoring correction
questions.prompt: The result sheet gives A a 7-point lead over B. A basket worth 3 points was credited to A but should go to B. By how many points does A now lead?
questions.hint: Both teams' scores change.

lessons.headline: Read sideways dominoes in pairs
lessons.intro: In a board two rows high, once a horizontal domino begins at the first open column the other row must match it. One paired block uses two whole columns.
lessons.bridge: The film specifies the number of upright dominoes. Before its count begins, translate the remaining width into paired sideways blocks.
lessons.recap: Describe tilings using whole upright columns and forced double-column blocks. Keep individual domino counts distinct from block counts.

example.prompt: Can a two-row board of width 3 be covered entirely with horizontal dominoes?
steps: Each row would need to be split into pairs of adjacent cells.
A row of length 3 has one cell left over, so such a tiling is impossible.

questions.title: The lone upright
questions.prompt: A board 2 cells high and 7 cells long is tiled with dominoes. Exactly one domino is vertical. In how many different columns could it stand?
questions.hint: On each side of this domino the remaining columns must pair up.

questions.title: One local turn
questions.prompt: Four upright dominoes fill a 2-by-4 board, one per column. Choose two adjacent uprights and replace them by two horizontal dominoes covering the same cells. How many different finished tilings can one such change produce?
questions.hint: Which pairs of columns can be selected?

questions.title: Exactly four horizontal pieces
questions.prompt: A fixed 2-by-8 rectangle is tiled with dominoes. Exactly four individual dominoes lie horizontally. How many tilings are possible?
questions.hint: At the left edge of any horizontal pair, its partner is forced.

questions.title: A seam must be crossed
questions.prompt: A 2-by-8 board is tiled with dominoes. How many tilings have a domino crossing between columns 5 and 6?
questions.hint: Either forbid the seam entirely, or fix the pair crossing it.

lessons.headline: Follow the changing gap
lessons.intro: For objects moving on one straight line, follow the distance between them. Speeds that both close a gap add. A pursuer gains only the difference between the two speeds.
lessons.bridge: In the film's delayed start, mark the second runner's starting instant. Measure the first runner's lead at that instant before using the difference of their speeds.
lessons.recap: Sketch both arrows. For a chase, include the distance already covered during any head start.

example.prompt: A runner at 7 m/s follows another at 5 m/s. The gap starts at 12 m. When will it close?
steps: Each second the faster runner gains 2 m.
A 12 m gap takes 6 seconds to close.

figure.alt: At the start, the trailing runner is twelve metres behind. Both run in the same direction, with speeds seven and five metres per second.

lessons.videoTitle: Relative speeds, timed movement and meetings

questions.title: Face to face
questions.prompt: Two people 84 m apart walk straight towards each other at 3 and 4 m/s. How many seconds until they meet?
questions.hint: How far does the gap shrink each second?

questions.title: The moving target
questions.prompt: A cyclist starts 60 m behind another. They go in the same direction at 8 and 5 m/s. How many seconds until the faster cyclist catches up?
questions.hint: Both move forward during each second.

questions.title: A later start
questions.prompt: Lena runs off at 4 m/s. After 15 seconds Finn leaves from the same spot at 7 m/s in her direction. How many metres does Finn run before catching her?
questions.hint: Measure the gap at Finn's start.

questions.title: Return to the whistle
questions.prompt: Two cyclists leave a whistle together in opposite directions on a 180 m circular track at 7 m/s and 5 m/s. After how many seconds do they first meet again?
questions.hint: Together they have to account for one complete lap.

lessons.headline: Allow for the choice you just made
lessons.intro: Multiplication works when you know how many options remain at each stage. A restriction can change that number, so choose a starting point that makes the remaining choices easy to see.
lessons.bridge: When the film builds a team from the artists, builders and coders, notice how the number of coders allowed changes the available team patterns.
lessons.recap: If the next choice depends on the first, count the valid options in each branch before joining the totals.

example.prompt: A badge has a red, blue or green rim and a different centre colour from the same list. How many badges are there?
steps: For each of the 3 rims, exactly 2 colours remain for the centre.
The parts have different positions, so multiply 3 × 2 = 6.

questions.title: Route out and home
questions.prompt: Four paths join a hut to a lake. Walk out on one and back on a different one. How many routes are possible?
questions.hint: Direction distinguishes the two trips.

questions.title: Fruit portion
questions.prompt: A bowl holds three different fruits chosen from five kinds. How many possible sets omit the apple kind?
questions.hint: Remove apple from the available kinds first.

questions.title: Workshop pair
questions.prompt: There are four art workshops and three science workshops. A pupil books two different workshops, with at least one science workshop. How many unordered bookings are possible?
questions.hint: Separate bookings with one science workshop from those with two.

questions.title: Costume teams
questions.prompt: Seven actors include Kai and Mo. A company selects four actors and gives one selected actor the lead. Kai must be in the four and Mo cannot be the lead. How many choices are possible?
questions.hint: First give every team its possible leads, then remove the forbidden assignments.

lessons.headline: Work with an angle sum
lessons.intro: Two angles can be hard to find separately but easy to use together. An exterior angle of a triangle gives the sum of the two remote interior angles.
lessons.bridge: In the bisector puzzle, keep the two remote angles together. Watch where their half-sum becomes a known angle total in another triangle.
lessons.recap: Look for the sum a later step needs. It may already be known even if neither individual angle is.

example.prompt: One angle of a triangle is 60°. What do the two other angles add to, and what do half of each add to?
steps: The two angles total 180 − 60 = 120°.
Half of each together gives half of 120°, or 60°.

questions.title: The propped easel
questions.prompt: An isosceles triangular easel has its two equal base angles on the floor. Extending the floor beyond one foot makes an exterior angle of 112° with the sloping side. What is the angle at the top, in degrees?
questions.hint: Find the inside angle at that foot, then use the other equal base angle.

questions.title: Two angles differ
questions.prompt: Two angles of a triangle differ by 8°. The third is 116°. How many degrees is the smaller of the first two?
questions.hint: Remove the third angle and the extra eight degrees.

questions.title: One crease in a triangle
questions.prompt: A paper triangle has angles A = 34° and B = 42°. A crease from A to a point M of side BC bisects angle A. What is angle AMB in degrees?
questions.hint: Look at the small triangle containing A, M and B.

questions.title: Bisect the outside angle
questions.prompt: In triangle ABC, angle B is twice angle A. The exterior angle at C is 96°. Extend side BA past A and bisect the resulting exterior angle at A. How many degrees are between this bisector and side AC?
questions.hint: Use the exterior angle at C to identify three equal angle parts.

lessons.headline: Let group sizes set their influence
lessons.intro: If one group is larger, its mean should count more heavily. Picture one copy of each group's mean for every member of that group.
lessons.bridge: Watch how many copies of each group's mean contribute to the combined total. Predict which of the group means the answer will be closer to.
lessons.recap: A combined mean lies between its group means. It should lie closer to the larger group's mean when the sizes differ.

example.prompt: Two jars average 9 seeds each and six others average 13. What is the overall mean?
steps: The jars contain 2 × 9 + 6 × 13 = 96 seeds.
Share the total among all eight jars to get 12 per jar.

lessons.videoTitle: Averages, weighted means and simple distributions

questions.title: Teams of unequal size
questions.prompt: Four pupils average 8 points and six average 13 points. What is the combined mean?
questions.hint: Count all ten pupils.

questions.title: Missing group mean
questions.prompt: A group of 12 averages 17. Five of its members average 10. What is the mean of the other seven?
questions.hint: Take away the smaller group's total.

questions.title: Recover a count
questions.prompt: Three science teams average 12 points each. Some maths teams average 18 each. Together the teams average 16. How many maths teams are there?
questions.hint: Balance the science teams' shortfall against the maths teams' excess.

questions.title: Unlabelled crates
questions.prompt: Two crate sizes have mean masses of 14 kg and 20 kg. Fifteen crates together average 18 kg. How many are from the 20 kg group?
questions.hint: Compare with a total based entirely on 14 kg.

lessons.headline: Count the gaps between term numbers
lessons.intro: A constant increment is added once per step, starting after the first term. Term number and number of increments are different counts.
lessons.bridge: In the theatre example, look for how the first and last rows work as a pair. Count the spaces between rows before calculating the last row.
lessons.recap: Mark the starting term and its number. Count the gaps to the requested term, then check the rule on a nearby term.

example.prompt: The first shelf holds 6 books and each shelf holds 3 more than the one before. How many are on shelf 5?
steps: From shelf 1 to shelf 5 there are four increases of 3.
Start at 6 and add 4 × 3 to get 18 books.

questions.title: The twelfth tile
questions.prompt: A line of tiles has numbers 7, 11, 15 and continues adding 4. What number is on tile 12?
questions.hint: How many increases separate tiles 1 and 12?

questions.title: Countdown marks
questions.prompt: The first mark reads 72 and every later mark reads 5 less. What does the ninth mark read?
questions.hint: Use eight decreases.

questions.title: Find its row
questions.prompt: A display has 9 counters in row 1, 15 in row 2 and 6 more in each later row. Which row has 81 counters?
questions.hint: Convert the extra counters into a number of gaps.

questions.title: Reverse the labels
questions.prompt: Seats in one row are marked in increasing steps of 7. The fifteenth seat is labelled 112. What label is on the fourth seat?
questions.hint: Count the gaps back from seat 15.

lessons.headline: Treat immediate neighbours as a block
lessons.intro: “Before” leaves room for a gap. “Immediately before” means two objects have adjacent places in a specified order. Draw a bracket around those objects before fitting them into the row.
lessons.bridge: During the short-film schedule, bracket the two films that must be consecutive. Then test that whole block against the end-position clue.
lessons.recap: Keep the order inside a fixed block and slide the whole block through the available positions.

example.prompt: In four slots, B must immediately follow A and A is second. Which slot is B in?
steps: A is at position 2. “Immediately” permits no intervening slot.
B must occupy position 3.

questions.title: Two seats apart
questions.prompt: Four children sit in seats 1 to 4: Ira, Jia, Kir and Liv. Ira is exactly two seat numbers before Jia. Liv is in seat 1. Which seat number belongs to Kir?
questions.hint: Write every possible pair for the two numbered seats.

questions.title: Who stands in the middle?
questions.prompt: Gus, Hiro and Ira stand in three places. Gus is next to both other people and Ira stands to the left of Gus. Who is on the right?
questions.hint: Only the middle place has two neighbours.

questions.title: The timetable window
questions.prompt: Three talks Liv, Mo and Nia start at different whole hours from 6 through 9 inclusive. Mo is two hours after Liv; Nia is strictly between them. How many schedules are possible?
questions.hint: List possible start times of the first talk only.

questions.title: A short screening schedule
questions.prompt: Four distinct films named Jia, Kir, Liv and Mo fill four successive slots. Kir immediately follows Jia. Liv is later than Kir. How many complete schedules are possible?
questions.hint: Treat the consecutive pair as one item when listing orders.

lessons.headline: A reversed digit changes its job
lessons.intro: In AB the digit A contributes ten times A, while in BA it contributes just A. This gives a reliable equation for a reversal even if the symbols look much alike.
lessons.bridge: When AB becomes BA in the film, write the two different values of the same digit A. Watch how the digit-sum clue narrows the possible digits.
lessons.recap: A positive two-digit reversal difference is a multiple of 9. The digit sum and any leading-zero rule then limit possible answers.

example.prompt: A two-digit number has tens digit 5 and units digit 2. By how much does it exceed its reverse?
steps: The values are 52 and 25.
Their difference is 27, or 9 times the digit difference of 3.

questions.title: Read the places
questions.prompt: A two-digit number has digits 8 and 3, with 8 in the tens place. What is the difference between the number and its reverse?
questions.hint: Build both numbers first.

questions.title: Reverse a gap
questions.prompt: A two-digit number exceeds its reverse by 54. By how much does the tens digit exceed the units digit?
questions.hint: Use the place-value weights in the difference.

questions.title: Find the original
questions.prompt: A two-digit number exceeds its two-digit reversal by 27. Its digits sum to 11. What is the original number?
questions.hint: Convert 27 to a digit difference.

questions.title: Two clues in the code book
questions.prompt: A two-digit number AB and its reverse BA are both two-digit. Their sum is 99. A exceeds B, and the product of the digits is 14. What is the larger number?
questions.hint: Which factor pair of 14 can be two digits that sum to 9?

lessons.headline: A rate can take work away
lessons.intro: A leaking tank combines a rate that adds water with one that takes it away. Count the net change per minute, using the same volume unit for both.
lessons.bridge: In the film, track the two pumps until one stops. Both pumps there add water. For the practice problems, use the same one-minute accounting when a drain takes water away.
lessons.recap: Draw arrows into and out of the container. Apply the net rate only while both processes run.

example.prompt: Water enters a tub at 9 litres per minute and drains at 3 litres per minute. How much water accumulates in 4 minutes?
steps: The net gain is 9 − 3 = 6 litres each minute.
In 4 minutes the tub gains 24 litres.

questions.title: A dripping barrel
questions.prompt: Rain enters a barrel at 11 litres per hour and a leak loses 4 litres per hour. How many litres are gained in 6 hours?
questions.hint: Find the hourly gain.

questions.title: Can it fill?
questions.prompt: A pipe alone fills a tank in 5 hours. A drain alone empties a full tank in 10 hours. Starting empty with both running, how many hours does it take to fill?
questions.hint: Subtract full-tank rates.

questions.title: A plug inserted
questions.prompt: Water enters an empty 96-litre tank at 8 litres per minute. An open drain removes 2 litres per minute for the first 4 minutes, then closes. How many minutes from the start until the tank is full?
questions.hint: Separate the open-drain and closed-drain times.

questions.title: Hidden leak
questions.prompt: A pipe delivers 12 litres per minute into a 90-litre tank. With a leak, the empty tank takes 10 minutes to fill. How many litres per minute escape?
questions.hint: Compare the measured fill rate with the pipe's rate.

lessons.headline: Track the entire display
lessons.intro: A machine can contain two rhythms. It returns to its first display only when both components return together. List the return times of each part or use a common multiple.
lessons.bridge: Follow the two dials in the film and write down when each first returns. Decide what must be true for the whole display to return at once.
lessons.recap: A display repeats when every component matches at the same time. Different starting offsets also have to be respected.

example.prompt: One lamp flashes on every third beat and a second on every fourth. Both flash on beat 0. On which positive beat do they first flash together?
steps: The first lamp returns at 3,6,9,12. The second at 4,8,12.
Their first positive common beat is 12.

questions.title: Quiet bells
questions.prompt: Two bells ring every 5 and 8 minutes. They ring together at noon. How many minutes until their next simultaneous ring?
questions.hint: Find the first common positive multiple.

questions.title: A shared factor
questions.prompt: Two dials return to their marks every 6 and 9 presses. Both start at their marks. How many presses until both return together for the first time?
questions.hint: The product can exceed the first common multiple.

questions.title: Out of phase
questions.prompt: A blue light flashes on beats 2,6,10,… and a red light on beats 1,4,7,… . On which positive beat do they first flash together?
questions.hint: Compare beats belonging to the two lists, keeping their offsets.

questions.title: Three gears
questions.prompt: Three marks return to their start every 4, 6 and 9 turns respectively. All start aligned. From turn 1 through turn 100, at how many turns are all the marks aligned?
questions.hint: Find the full display’s period before counting returns.

lessons.headline: Read the scale before the height
lessons.intro: A bar can start above zero. Its top still gives the value on the axis. To compare two values subtract their readings, and to compare ratios use the full readings.
lessons.bridge: As the film reads its cumulative chart, notice how a total is taken from the axis. Keep the same habit when your own chart starts above zero.
lessons.recap: Write the axis values in a tiny table before calculating. A truncated baseline preserves differences but can distort visual ratios.

example.prompt: A water-level chart starts its axis at 20 cm. The tops for Monday and Tuesday are at 24 and 28. How much deeper is Tuesday?
steps: Use the two axis values at the tops.
28 − 24 = 4 cm. The visible bar lengths of 4 and 8 do not make the water twice as deep.

figure.alt: Two bars measured on an axis starting at 20 cm reach 24 cm on Monday and 28 cm on Tuesday.

questions.title: Find the top
questions.prompt: The axis of a bar chart starts at 40 points. A bar extends 13 points above it. What value does its top show?
questions.hint: Add the baseline.

questions.title: A cut-off axis
questions.prompt: A graph starts at 50. Bar X rises 10 units above that baseline and Y rises 25. What is Y's value divided by X's value? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Use the true readings, not the displayed lengths.

questions.title: A chart key
questions.prompt: On a pictogram one full square stands for 8 trays. Friday shows 5 full squares and a quarter square. Saturday shows 4 full squares and three-quarter square. How many more trays does Friday show?
questions.hint: First convert the fractions of a symbol.

questions.title: The changed scale
questions.prompt: A graph begins at an unknown baseline. A bar representing 86 units is 9 grid steps high. One representing 62 is 3 grid steps high. What is the baseline?
questions.hint: Use the difference to find the units per step.

lessons.headline: Which amount is left?
lessons.intro: After part of a collection is removed, the rest becomes the whole for the next instruction. Label the amount beside every fraction.
lessons.bridge: In the film's box of chalk, pause after the first class takes its share. The next fraction acts on the chalk you can still see in the box.
lessons.recap: Write the remainder as a fraction of the original whole. Multiplying the successive remaining fractions also provides a check.

example.prompt: A baker has 18 rolls. She sells a third, then gives half the remainder to a neighbour. How many rolls does she give away?
steps: She sells 6, leaving 12. The second instruction refers to those 12.
Half of 12 is 6, so 6 rolls go to the neighbour.

lessons.videoTitle: Parts and wholes, including remaining fractions

questions.title: The last jug
questions.prompt: A jug contains 24 cups of juice. A quarter is poured out. How many cups remain?
questions.hint: What fraction stays in the jug?

questions.title: Two deliveries
questions.prompt: A bicycle courier delivers half of 36 parcels, then one third of the parcels still aboard. How many are still aboard?
questions.hint: Find the number on the bicycle after the first delivery.

questions.title: Paper from the roll
questions.prompt: A class uses one quarter of a roll, then one third of what is left. It has 8 m left. How long was the roll in metres?
questions.hint: Find the fraction left after both cuts.

questions.title: From the opening supply
questions.prompt: On Monday a shelter uses one fifth of its original feed. On Tuesday it uses one quarter of the remainder. What fraction of the original supply does it use over both days?
questions.hint: Find Tuesday's amount as a fraction of Monday's opening supply.

lessons.headline: Undo the last operation first
lessons.intro: A sequence of reversible moves has a different order when retraced. Begin at the result and undo the move closest to it.
lessons.bridge: Follow the film's machine from its output back to its input. When counters are added after a fraction is removed, see which action has to be undone first.
lessons.recap: For each undoing, name both the operation and the quantity it acts on. Then replay the original sequence.

example.prompt: A machine doubles a number and adds 5, giving 19. What entered?
steps: Undo the last move by subtracting 5 to get 14.
Undo the doubling by halving 14 to get 7. Forward checking gives 19.

questions.title: The subtraction machine
questions.prompt: A machine adds 8, then subtracts 3, ending at 21. What was its input?
questions.hint: Undo the subtraction first.

questions.title: Three before double
questions.prompt: A machine adds 3, then doubles. Its output is 22. What was the input?
questions.hint: Which step acted on the whole bracket?

questions.title: Two passages
questions.prompt: Every time a token goes through a gate, its score triples and then loses 2. After two passages it shows 46. What was its score initially?
questions.hint: Undo one entire passage at a time.

questions.title: The missing starting load
questions.prompt: A lift drops off half its passengers, then picks up 3. At the next floor 4 leave. There are now 8. How many passengers were on board initially?
questions.hint: Start with the 8 and reverse the stops.

lessons.headline: Separate corners from edge interiors
lessons.intro: An edge count often includes its two corner cubes, but corners may belong in a different paint category. Decide where the edge starts and stops.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film sort the painted pieces by where they sit. Compare a vertical edge cube with its two endpoints when the top is left clean.
lessons.recap: Separate corner, edge-interior, face-interior and central positions so each cube belongs to one category.

example.prompt: A cube edge is 5 small cubes long. How many edge cubes are away from both corners?
steps: Two of the five positions are endpoints.
Removing those leaves 5 − 2 = 3 edge-interior cubes.

lessons.videoTitle: Painted faces, boundary and hidden cubes

questions.title: A cube on one painted edge
questions.prompt: A solid cube has edge length 8 unit cubes. One large edge is marked from corner to corner. How many of its unit cubes touch a corner of the large cube?
questions.hint: An edge has two endpoints, whatever its length.

questions.title: One face, one border
questions.prompt: The front face of a large painted cube is a 6-by-6 square of unit faces. How many unit faces lie on the border of this front face, counting its corners once?
questions.hint: Subtract the central square or count the edges without repeating corners.

questions.title: Infer the cube size
questions.prompt: After a solid cube is painted all over and separated into unit cubes, exactly 150 pieces have paint on just one face. How many unit cubes lay along one original edge?
questions.hint: Each big face has a square interior of singly painted pieces.

questions.title: Which parcel took the edge cubes?
questions.prompt: A 5-by-5-by-5 cube is painted before being split into its 125 unit cubes. All cubes with two or three painted faces go into parcel A. How many more cubes go into the other parcel than into parcel A?
questions.hint: Parcel A contains corners and edge interiors. Keep their counts disjoint.

lessons.headline: Treat an incomplete block separately
lessons.intro: A full run of ten labels gives one of each units digit. A full run of one hundred has a regular tens column too. Use those blocks first, then count only the unfinished tail.
lessons.bridge: In the film's run of labels to 289, watch how often a five visits each column. Try counting the final incomplete block before the film does.
lessons.recap: Write both endpoints of each block. A neat-looking interval of ten numbers can still cross the boundary between two tens digits.

example.prompt: How many copies of 6 appear in the units column on labels 10 through 34?
steps: The complete blocks 10–19 and 20–29 each have one.
The partial block 30–34 has none. The units count is 2.

lessons.videoTitle: Digit sums and counting digits in ranges

questions.title: Complete and incomplete
questions.prompt: In the units column only, how many 5s appear on labels from 1 to 63?
questions.hint: List the units-five labels in steps of 10.

questions.title: Last partial decade
questions.prompt: In the tens column only, how many 6s appear on the labels 43 to 65 inclusive?
questions.hint: Find the part of the sixties actually included.

questions.title: A crossing at one hundred
questions.prompt: On labels 80 through 160 inclusive, how many copies of the digit 0 appear? Ordinary numbers have no leading zero.
questions.hint: Count the units and tens columns separately.

questions.title: The even rack
questions.prompt: A warehouse prints only the even labels from 20 to 68 inclusive. How many copies of the digit 6 does it print?
questions.hint: List the units-six labels, then count even labels in the sixties.

lessons.headline: Fix the smallest choice
lessons.intro: A short list is convincing when you can explain where any possible answer would go. Put the smallest number first and work upwards in order.
lessons.bridge: For the three labelled boxes in the film, identify the choice held fixed in one row. See how the bounds on the other boxes determine where that row stops.
lessons.recap: Choose an ordering rule and a stopping rule. The first prevents repeats and the second tells you when the list is complete.

example.prompt: Which pairs of different positive integers add to 8?
steps: Start with 1 + 7, then 2 + 6, then 3 + 5.
The next pair would repeat 4. Starting with 5 would reverse a pair already listed. There are 3 pairs.

questions.title: Two stamps
questions.prompt: Two different stamps have whole-number values from 1 to 7 cents. How many pairs total 9 cents?
questions.hint: Start with the smaller stamp.

questions.title: Corner labels
questions.prompt: Choose two different labels from 0, 2, 5 and 7. How many different sums can you make?
questions.hint: Write the sums in order and check for equal results.

questions.title: Tripod rods
questions.prompt: A tripod uses three different rod lengths from 1 to 7 cm. How many choices have a total length of 12 cm?
questions.hint: Group the triples by their shortest length.

questions.title: Mosaic frame
questions.prompt: A rectangular mosaic uses 48 identical square tiles with no gaps. Both sides must be at least 3 tiles long. A turn of the whole rectangle gives the same design. How many designs are possible?
questions.hint: List possible shorter sides until they would exceed the longer side.

lessons.headline: Compare areas through height
lessons.intro: Triangles can look quite different and still have matching areas. Look for a common perpendicular height before trying to measure their sloping sides.
lessons.bridge: The film measures shaded rectangles by their footprints. Watch how it accounts for their shared area before moving on to regions with triangular edges.
lessons.recap: A common height lets you use the ratio of the bases. For the portion left over, account for the whole region.

example.prompt: Two triangles have bases 3 cm and 6 cm on the same line and share a vertex 4 cm above it. How do their areas compare?
steps: Their areas are half of 3 × 4 and half of 6 × 4.
The second has twice the area of the first because the height is the same and its base is twice as long.

questions.title: A sail divided into panels
questions.prompt: Three triangles share a top point and have consecutive bases of 2 m, 3 m and 4 m on one straight line. Their total area is 45 m². What is the area of the triangle on the 3 m base?
questions.hint: All three perpendicular heights are equal. Compare the bases.

questions.title: One tile wide
questions.prompt: A mosaic is 12 tiles wide and 8 tiles tall. Its border is exactly one tile wide on every side, including the corners. How many tiles are in the border?
questions.hint: What rectangle is left after lifting off the border?

questions.title: Shared altitude
questions.prompt: Two triangles have their bases on the same straight line and share their opposite vertex, 8 cm above the line. Their base lengths are 24 cm and 10 cm. By how many square centimetres do their areas differ?
questions.hint: Compare just the change in the base.

questions.title: Recover the base
questions.prompt: A triangle sits inside a 24 cm by 16 cm rectangle. Its base lies on the bottom and its opposite vertex is on the top. The uncovered area is 304 cm². How many centimetres long is the triangle base?
questions.hint: Recover the triangle area, then undo half-base-times-height.

lessons.headline: Follow what stays in the bag
lessons.intro: In a series of draws, the first result can change the second probability. Keep both the total number of objects and the number of favourable objects up to date.
lessons.bridge: Watch the counters come out of the bag. Before the next draw, say how many counters of each colour remain on that particular branch.
lessons.recap: Write the second fraction using the contents that remain on that branch. Combine different successful orders only after their probabilities are known.

example.prompt: A bowl contains two plums and one pear. Two pieces are taken without replacement. What is the chance both are plums?
steps: The first plum has probability 2/3. After drawing it, one plum remains among two pieces.
Both draws must succeed, so multiply 2/3 by 1/2 to get 1/3.

questions.title: Two green draws
questions.prompt: Four green and two white counters are mixed. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability of two green? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Update the number of green counters after a green draw.

questions.title: Putting it back
questions.prompt: A bag holds one gold and two silver discs. A disc is drawn uniformly, replaced and the bag mixed before another draw. What is the probability of two golds? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Does the first draw change the second bag?

questions.title: One red left out
questions.prompt: Three red and three blue socks are mixed. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that at least one is red? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Count the complementary event.

questions.title: First repeat
questions.prompt: A box holds two tokens of each of three colours. Three tokens are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that the first two differ in colour and the third matches one of those two? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: After two different colours, list the four remaining tokens by colour.

lessons.headline: Test what each domino must cover
lessons.intro: Colour neighbouring grid squares differently, as on a chessboard. A domino covering two squares that share an edge always uses one of each colour.
lessons.bridge: In the domino film, test one move on a board with two alternating colours. What does every domino cover, and what mismatch makes a full covering impossible?
lessons.recap: Unequal colour counts can prove impossibility. Equal counts are a first test; a proposed covering still needs a construction.

example.prompt: Can two dominoes cover all four cells of a 2-by-2 square?
steps: The board has two cells of each colour, so the colour test permits a covering.
Place one horizontal domino in each row. This construction confirms the covering is possible.

questions.title: A chequered strip
questions.prompt: A strip has seven alternating black and white squares, beginning with black. How many black squares does it contain?
questions.hint: List the odd-numbered positions.

questions.title: One colour short
questions.prompt: A board has 9 blue and 7 gold squares. Every domino covers one of each. What is the greatest number of dominoes that the colour counts alone allow?
questions.hint: Each domino needs a gold square.

questions.title: One hole in a square
questions.prompt: A 3-by-3 board is coloured with its four corners black. One square is removed and the remaining eight can be tiled with dominoes. What colour was removed? Enter black or white.
questions.hint: Count the colours before the removal.

questions.title: Cross-shaped island
questions.prompt: Five unit squares form a plus sign: one centre cell with four neighbours, one on each side. What is the maximum number of ordinary dominoes that fit without overlap?
questions.hint: Which cell would every legal domino need?

lessons.headline: What stays fixed when items move?
lessons.intro: A transfer can change both holdings without changing the total. Use a second clue about the final holdings, then trace the transfer back.
lessons.bridge: The film reconstructs three boxes from overlapping two-box counts. Notice how a known combined amount helps pin down an unknown holding before you return to transfers.
lessons.recap: Label each number as before or after. Do not pair a final ratio or difference with an opening amount.

example.prompt: Two jars share 30 beads. After a transfer they are equal. What does the total alone tell you?
steps: Each final jar contains 15.
If 4 moved from A to B, then A originally had 19 and B had 11.

questions.title: Back to the first jar
questions.prompt: After 5 marbles move from jar A to jar B, the jars each have 18. How many did A start with?
questions.hint: Undo the change to A.

questions.title: Twice as much
questions.prompt: Two boxes contain 42 cards. After a transfer A has twice as many as B. How many are in B after the transfer?
questions.hint: Divide the final total into shares.

questions.title: From first to second
questions.prompt: Two bags contain 54 counters. Moving 6 from A to B gives B 4 more than A. How many did A hold originally?
questions.hint: Work out the final holdings first.

questions.title: The same transfer twice
questions.prompt: Two boats carry 60 crates altogether. After moving 4 crates from A to B and then 4 more the same way, B contains twice as many as A. What was the original lead of A over B? Enter a negative number if A originally had fewer.
questions.hint: Find the final pair and reverse both moves.

lessons.headline: Restore the part counted twice
lessons.intro: Two lists may overlap. Adding their lengths counts anything common to both twice. Look for an easy way to measure the overlap.
lessons.bridge: Follow the tennis and swimming lists in the film. Then look for the very same overlap problem among its lists of multiples.
lessons.recap: Use a small example to decide what the overlap means. In a divisibility list its step is the least common multiple.

example.prompt: From 1 to 12, how many numbers are multiples of 2 or 3?
steps: The two lists contain 6 and 4 numbers. Multiples of 6 are in both.
Remove the 2 duplicate entries. There are 8 numbers altogether.

questions.title: Club noticeboard
questions.prompt: Of 28 children, 15 play chess, 11 code and 6 do both. How many do at least one?
questions.hint: The 6 belong to both of the first counts.

questions.title: Shared beep
questions.prompt: A bell beeps every 4 minutes and a buzzer every 6 minutes, starting together at time zero. At how many distinct times from minute 1 through minute 30 does something sound?
questions.hint: Find the multiples of 4 or 6 in the stated interval.

questions.title: Only one badge
questions.prompt: From 1 to 60, how many numbers are divisible by exactly one of 4 and 5?
questions.hint: Common multiples belong to neither allowed case.

questions.title: Recover the overlap
questions.prompt: At a fair, 46 people each visit at least one of two tents. The art tent gets 31 visitors. Exactly 15 people visit both tents. How many visit the music tent only?
questions.hint: Which visitors have never entered the art tent?

lessons.headline: Build a mirror from its free half
lessons.intro: A palindrome reads the same in both directions. Choose only the independent places, then reflect them to fill the matching positions.
lessons.bridge: Watch how the film builds a palindrome by choosing some digits and reflecting them. Look for which digit in a five-digit palindrome is used just once.
lessons.recap: Mark the mirrored pairs before trying digit choices. For an odd length, the centre digit is unpaired.

example.prompt: What four-digit palindrome begins with 54?
steps: The fourth digit must match the first, and the third digit must match the second.
The result is 5445; its first two digits determine the entire number.

questions.title: Complete the reflection
questions.prompt: A five-digit palindrome starts with 482. What is the whole number?
questions.hint: The centre digit is not repeated.

questions.title: Last digit fixed
questions.prompt: How many four-digit palindromes end in 5?
questions.hint: Use the form ABBA.

questions.title: Limited display
questions.prompt: A five-place display uses only 0, 1 and 2. Leading zeros are allowed. How many displayed strings are palindromes?
questions.hint: Count the choices up to and including the centre.

questions.title: A missing digit sum
questions.prompt: A five-digit palindrome starts with 4 and has digit sum 25. Its centre digit is 3. What is the number?
questions.hint: Remove the contribution from the outside digits and the centre.

lessons.headline: Count time between events
lessons.intro: For repeated events, the interval starts at one event and ends at the next. The first event fixes the start of the clock.
lessons.bridge: The sensor in the film gives its first flash after a full interval. Compare that clock with a question that starts timing at the first flash itself.
lessons.recap: Mark the first event and the last. Count the gaps between them before multiplying by the gap length.

example.prompt: A bell strikes at 0, 3 and 6 seconds. How long from its first strike to its third?
steps: There are two gaps of 3 seconds.
The elapsed time is 6 seconds.

questions.title: Bird calls
questions.prompt: A bird calls every 5 seconds. How many seconds pass from call 1 to call 9?
questions.hint: Draw the first three calls and count their gaps.

questions.title: How many posts?
questions.prompt: A cyclist passes a post at 0 seconds and then a post every 4 seconds. Including the first and last, how many posts does she pass by 28 seconds?
questions.hint: Translate elapsed time into gaps first.

questions.title: A quicker bell
questions.prompt: A bell takes 24 seconds from its second stroke to its eighth stroke. At the same pace, how long from its first to its twelfth stroke, in seconds?
questions.hint: How many gaps are between strokes 2 and 8?

questions.title: A row of lamps
questions.prompt: A light flashes at 10:00:00 and every 18 seconds afterwards. How many flashes occur strictly after 10:01:00 but no later than 10:03:00?
questions.hint: List the first and last allowable multiples of 18 seconds.

lessons.headline: Work back one move
lessons.intro: To count routes to a destination, sort them by their final move. The routes ending with a one-step move come from one earlier landing, and those ending with a two-step move come from another.
lessons.bridge: At the broken rung, watch which earlier landing counts still contribute to the next square. A forbidden landing can be jumped over.
lessons.recap: For a last-move recurrence, label the starting position with one empty route, give forbidden landings zero, and identify all possible predecessors.

example.prompt: A frog starts on 0 and hops forwards by 1 or 2. How many routes reach 3?
steps: The routes ending with a 1 come from the two routes to 2.
The route ending with a 2 comes from 1. Adding gives 2 + 1 = 3 routes.

questions.title: Land on four
questions.prompt: A frog hops 1 or 2 spaces forwards from 0. How many different ordered hop sequences land exactly on 4?
questions.hint: Calculate the route counts for 0,1,2,3 first.

questions.title: First larger jump
questions.prompt: A robot moves forwards by 1 or 3 squares. How many ordered routes from 0 land on 5?
questions.hint: Classify by the final move.

questions.title: Two broken rungs
questions.prompt: A robot can move forwards 1 or 2 rungs. It must skip rungs 3 and 7. How many routes from rung 0 land on rung 9?
questions.hint: Enter zero at each broken rung. A jump may pass over it.

questions.title: The password strip
questions.prompt: A strip of length 6 is filled exactly with red pieces of length 1 and blue pieces of length 2. Only colours and positions matter. How many fillings contain at least one blue piece?
questions.hint: Count all fillings by their final piece and remove the all-red strip.

lessons.headline: Find a bound before testing
lessons.intro: A bound cuts down the search and makes a completeness argument possible. For a factor pair, only the smaller factor needs to be tested up to the square root.
lessons.bridge: Listen for the reason the rectangle’s factor search is complete. A bound on the smaller side can replace many unproductive trials.
lessons.recap: Prove your stopping point first and distinguish a valid example from a unique solution.

example.prompt: A rectangle has area 20 and integer sides. Can the shorter side exceed 4?
steps: If the shorter side were at least 5, both sides would be at least 5.
The area would then be at least 25. Testing shorter sides 1 through 4 is enough.

lessons.videoTitle: Proving all cases and unique solutions

questions.title: Stop the square search
questions.prompt: A carpenter tests square boards with positive whole-centimetre sides. Each board must have area below 60 cm². What is the largest side length she needs to test?
questions.hint: Find the last square below the limit and the first square above it.

questions.title: The last admissible stair
questions.prompt: A staircase has rows of 1, 2, 3, … counters. A complete staircase must use fewer than 30 counters. How many different positive numbers of complete rows are possible?
questions.hint: Compare consecutive staircase totals near 30. Check which side of the inequality includes equality.

questions.title: Test the last possible digit
questions.prompt: A two-digit code has digit sum 8 and its tens digit is exactly two less than its units digit. How many valid codes are there?
questions.hint: Let the tens digit be t. Can 2t + 2 equal the specified total?

questions.title: Check every triangle
questions.prompt: An isosceles triangle has positive whole-number sides and perimeter 14. Its two designated equal sides have length x. How many possible values of x are there?
questions.hint: The third side must be positive and shorter than twice x.

lessons.headline: A bound needs a placement
lessons.intro: Dividing the board area by the size of a tile gives an upper bound on how many tiles could fit. Shapes and gaps decide whether that many can actually be placed.
lessons.bridge: In the film’s domino puzzle, first use area to check the number of pieces. Then notice why the first open column still constrains their positions.
lessons.recap: For a packing maximum, present a reason no greater count can fit and a legal arrangement reaching your count.

example.prompt: What is the largest number of dominoes that fit in a straight strip of five unit cells?
steps: Each domino uses two cells, so three dominoes would need six.
Two do fit, covering cells 1–2 and 3–4. That construction attains the bound.

questions.title: A gap in a shelf
questions.prompt: A shelf of nine unit spaces has its fourth space blocked. Each tray needs two adjacent free spaces. What is the greatest number of trays that fit?
questions.hint: Treat the runs of free spaces separately.

questions.title: The plus-shaped counter
questions.prompt: A counter has five square cells shaped like a plus sign: one centre with one cell adjoining each of its four sides. What is the maximum number of non-overlapping dominoes it holds?
questions.hint: Which cell would any domino have to use?

questions.title: Join a chain of squares
questions.prompt: A strip of 6 unit squares in one row has a new unit square attached along a whole edge at the right-hand end, extending the same row. How many exposed edge units did the original strip have?
questions.hint: Work backwards from the extended rectangle and remove the net gain of two.

questions.title: Do not cross the seam
questions.prompt: A 2-by-13 floor has a seam after column 6. Dominoes may touch but cannot cross it. How many tilings cover the floor?
questions.hint: The choices on opposite sides can be made separately.

lessons.headline: Count the ends, then the links
lessons.intro: A handshake has two participants. If you let each person count their handshakes, the total counts each meeting twice. Think about the number of owners of each object.
lessons.bridge: In the festival problem, count the same bookings once from the rooms and once from the helpers. Identify the number of bookings belonging to one helper.
lessons.recap: A division is justified by a fixed number of reports per object. Name the reporters before dividing.

example.prompt: Six children each exchange a high-five with every other child once. How many high-fives occur?
steps: Each child reports five high-fives, for thirty reports.
Two children report the same high-five. Divide by two to get 15.

questions.title: Bridge ends
questions.prompt: A network of bridges has 18 bridge ends on its islands. Every bridge joins two distinct islands. How many bridges are there?
questions.hint: Count the ends per bridge.

questions.title: Short schedule
questions.prompt: Seven runners each race each other runner once in a two-person race. How many races take place?
questions.hint: Each race appears in two runners' schedules.

questions.title: Unknown island
questions.prompt: Five islands have 3, 3, 2, 2 and an unknown number of bridge ends. There are 7 bridges in total. How many ends are on the fifth island?
questions.hint: How many ends must all islands have together?

questions.title: The sign-up board
questions.prompt: Each of 12 pupils joins exactly two clubs. Four clubs each have 5 pupils, and all remaining memberships belong to a fifth club. How many pupils are in that club?
questions.hint: Count pupil–club memberships in two ways.

lessons.headline: Change between a plan and its layers
lessons.intro: From a numbered plan of heights, a position belongs to layer k exactly when its height is at least k. This test even works when the upper floors have different shapes.
lessons.bridge: In the six-stack model, follow one height through each horizontal layer. Compare the number of occupied positions with the silhouette height it produces.
lessons.recap: For each layer, count the stacks that reach it. Summing those layer counts reproduces the total.

example.prompt: Four stacks have heights 1, 3, 3 and 2. How many cubes are in the third layer?
steps: Only stacks at least 3 cubes high reach it.
Two stacks qualify, each contributing one cube to that layer.

questions.title: Find the third floor
questions.prompt: The top view of a model records stack heights of 1, 4, 3, 2, 4 and 1. How many occupied positions appear on the third horizontal layer counted from the table?
questions.hint: A stack reaches layer 3 if its height is at least 3.

questions.title: Above the flood line
questions.prompt: Five solid stacks have heights 7, 3, 3, 7, 3 cubes. Water hides the lowest 4 layers. How many individual cubes remain above water?
questions.hint: A short stack can contribute zero, never a negative number.

questions.title: An erased height
questions.prompt: A plan has two rows and three columns of solid stacks. Four stacks have height 3, one has height 3, and one height is unreadable. The model contains 22 cubes. What was the missing height?
questions.hint: Subtract every known column, including repeated heights.

questions.title: Solid staircase
questions.prompt: Each tread of a staircase is 3 cubes wide and one cube deep. The solid columns below the 7 successive treads have heights 1 to 7. How many cubes are used?
questions.hint: Slice along the width to see identical stair profiles.

lessons.headline: Give the front position its own rule
lessons.intro: When digit cards form a number, zero can sit inside it or at the end. It cannot start a number that is supposed to have the full number of digits.
lessons.bridge: In the film's three-digit numbers, keep an eye on zero. Ask why a choice allowed in the last place might fail in the first place.
lessons.recap: Choose the most restricted place early. After each choice, cross out any digit that cannot be used again.

example.prompt: How many two-digit numbers can you make using two different cards from 0, 3 and 8?
steps: The tens digit has two choices, 3 or 8.
Whichever you use, two cards remain for the units. There are 4 numbers: 30, 38, 80 and 83.

questions.title: From three cards
questions.prompt: Using the cards 0, 6 and 9 once each, what is the smallest three-digit number?
questions.hint: Choose the smallest legal hundreds digit first.

questions.title: Count full-length numbers
questions.prompt: Choose three distinct digits from 0, 1, 2 and 4. How many three-digit numbers can be formed?
questions.hint: There are three choices for the hundreds place.

questions.title: When zero must appear
questions.prompt: Using three distinct digits chosen from 0, 1, 2 and 4, how many three-digit numbers contain 0?
questions.hint: Subtract the numbers made without zero from all full-length numbers.

questions.title: A zero and a boundary
questions.prompt: A display shows three different digits chosen from 0, 3, 5 and 8. It shows an ordinary number greater than 500 that ends in 0. How many numbers fit?
questions.hint: Fix the units place before choosing the hundreds digit.

lessons.headline: Choose a common basis for comparison
lessons.intro: Two offers can use different descriptions of a saving. Compare the final prices for the same item, or the price per equal amount.
lessons.bridge: Use the film's two teams to practise making unlike totals comparable. Then notice which price is the base for the second percentage change.
lessons.recap: Before calling one offer better, ask whether both calculations used the same item, amount and starting price.

example.prompt: A $60 jacket is reduced by a quarter. How much does it cost now?
steps: A quarter of $60 is $15.
Subtract the saving from the original price: $60 − $15 = $45.

questions.title: Percent to dollars
questions.prompt: A $90 kit has a 20% discount. What is the price after the discount, in dollars?
questions.hint: Find 10% first.

questions.title: Unlike packets
questions.prompt: One pack has 6 erasers for $3. Another has 10 for $4. How many cents less does one eraser cost in the cheaper pack?
questions.hint: Put both prices in cents per eraser.

questions.title: Which original price?
questions.prompt: After a 25% discount, a helmet costs $54. What was its original price in dollars?
questions.hint: The sale price is what percentage of the original?

questions.title: Buy three or buy four
questions.prompt: A shop sells identical notebooks for $6 each. Deal A gives 25% off the full price of any four. Deal B gives $4 off every group of three, with other notebooks at full price. For 12 notebooks, how many dollars cheaper is the better deal?
questions.hint: Apply each deal to the same number of notebooks.

lessons.headline: Recover the step from two landmarks
lessons.intro: Two terms in a constant-step sequence reveal the difference even if neither is first. Divide the change in their values by the number of gaps between their positions.
lessons.bridge: In the film’s term-number puzzle, count the gaps before multiplying by the common difference. The same gap count lets you recover a missing difference.
lessons.recap: Use term-number differences to count jumps. With the step recovered, move in either direction and check both given landmarks.

example.prompt: A plant is 18 cm tall at the end of week 2 and 30 cm at the end of week 5. It grows by the same amount each week. How much per week?
steps: The rise is 12 cm over 5 − 2 = 3 gaps.
The weekly growth is 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm.

questions.title: The hidden difference
questions.prompt: Term 4 is 19 and term 9 is 44 in an arithmetic sequence. What is the common difference?
questions.hint: Divide the value change by the index change.

questions.title: The first report
questions.prompt: A tank drains at a constant rate. At hour 3 it holds 64 L and at hour 7 it holds 44 L. How many litres did it hold at hour 0?
questions.hint: Find the loss per hour first.

questions.title: Between the signs
questions.prompt: A road has kilometre signs at equal distances. Sign 6 is at kilometre 34 and sign 14 at kilometre 74. At what kilometre is sign 11?
questions.hint: Find the step, then move from the nearer known sign.

questions.title: Two production lines
questions.prompt: On day 2 line A makes 28 parts and on day 6 it makes 44. Line B makes 40 on day 2 and 48 on day 6. Each continues at its own constant daily increase. On which day do their outputs match?
questions.hint: Measure how fast A closes the day-2 gap.

lessons.headline: Use the most restrictive comparison
lessons.intro: One clue may eliminate several possibilities at once. Combine clues about the same person, time or number before listing the rest.
lessons.bridge: When the film rules out a position near the end of the schedule, pause and ask which other people or films lose an option as a result.
lessons.recap: Use the largest or smallest allowed value to test an ordering before making a long list.

example.prompt: Three numbers are 2, 5 and 8. Mira’s number is above 2 but below Sol’s. Which number belongs to Mira?
steps: It cannot be 2. If it were 8, Sol could not have a larger number.
The only remaining possibility is 5.

questions.title: The timetable comparison
questions.prompt: Four departure times are 9, 11, 13 and 16 hours. The express leaves after 11 but before the last departure. At what hour does it leave?
questions.hint: Look for a time satisfying both strict bounds.

questions.title: The weight order
questions.prompt: Four boxes labelled Nia, Oli, Pia and Quin have different weights. Nia is heavier than Pia. Oli is lighter than Quin but heavier than Nia. Which box is second lightest?
questions.hint: Join the comparisons into one chain from lightest to heaviest.

questions.title: Recover a locker code
questions.prompt: A code uses each of 5, 7, 8, 10 once. The third entry is the smallest, the second is the largest, and the first is larger than the last. What is the first entry?
questions.hint: Reserve the two forced entries before comparing the rest.

questions.title: Two seats apart
questions.prompt: Four children sit in seats 1 to 4: Liv, Mo, Nia and Oli. Liv is exactly two seat numbers before Mo. Oli is in seat 1. Which seat number belongs to Nia?
questions.hint: Write every possible pair for the two numbered seats.

lessons.headline: Restrict a search to one remainder class
lessons.intro: A remainder condition selects evenly spaced candidates. Keep that spacing when you apply a second condition, so you do not test every number in an interval.
lessons.bridge: In the film's final number-line puzzle, find the first number that obeys the remainder clue and watch how the allowable numbers are spaced.
lessons.recap: Find the first eligible number, the step and the last eligible number. After a second rule, the step may be larger than before.

example.prompt: List the numbers from 20 to 35 that leave remainder 1 on division by 6.
steps: The first is 25, one more than 24.
The next is 31. Adding another 6 gives 37, beyond the interval.

questions.title: The next label
questions.prompt: A shelf uses numbers leaving remainder 4 on division by 9. What is the first such number above 40?
questions.hint: Start from 40 itself.

questions.title: Inclusive end
questions.prompt: How many numbers from 18 to 58 inclusive leave remainder 2 on division by 4?
questions.hint: Find the endpoints of the matching progression.

questions.title: A second filter
questions.prompt: Which number between 30 and 50 is divisible by 5 and leaves remainder 3 when divided by 7?
questions.hint: Write the multiples of 5 in the interval.

questions.title: Striped fence
questions.prompt: Posts numbered 1 to 90 are painted blue when their number leaves remainder 1 on division by 4. A blue post gets a star only if its number is also divisible by 3. How many stars are painted?
questions.hint: Find the first shared number and the repeat interval.

lessons.headline: Give the unknown a clear meaning
lessons.intro: An unknown might represent one item, a fixed fee or an entire group. State its meaning first so every term in your equation has the same units.
lessons.bridge: The film chooses an unknown for the ticket problem. Ask what the other ticket count becomes once the total number sold is known.
lessons.recap: Substitute the value into the original sentence. It should answer the exact quantity asked for, with its unit.

example.prompt: A ticket plus a $3 booking fee costs $11. How much is the ticket?
steps: Let the unknown be the ticket price. Ticket price plus 3 equals 11.
Subtract 3 to get an $8 ticket.

questions.title: Price per wheel
questions.prompt: Three identical wheels and a $4 axle cost $25. How many dollars does one wheel cost?
questions.hint: Remove the known item before sharing.

questions.title: Not the base fee
questions.prompt: A hire costs $6 plus $4 per hour. A customer pays $26. How many hours did they hire the equipment?
questions.hint: Name the unknown as hours.

questions.title: Two crate sizes
questions.prompt: A large crate holds 5 more books than a small crate. Two small crates and one large crate hold 41 books. How many books fit in the large crate?
questions.hint: Replace the large crate by a small crate plus five.

questions.title: When two tickets match
questions.prompt: One climbing pass costs $20 plus $3 per visit. Another costs $5 plus $6 per visit. After how many visits have the two cost the same in total?
questions.hint: Compare the opening gap with the change per visit.

lessons.headline: Find the cases that break the rule
lessons.intro: When separated objects are hard to count directly, count all arrangements and remove the forbidden ones. Define touching to mean immediately beside each other.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film subtract arrangements where either named pair touches. Draw the arrangements where both pairs touch and decide how many times they were subtracted.
lessons.recap: Subtract an unwanted arrangement only once. With two forbidden pairs, inspect orders that break both rules.

example.prompt: In the six orders of A, B, C, how many keep A and B apart?
steps: Four orders have A and B together: the pair has two internal orders and two positions beside C.
The other 6 − 4 = 2 orders are ACB and BCA.

questions.title: Letters apart
questions.prompt: How many orders of four different letters J, K, L and M keep J and K apart?
questions.hint: Subtract the orders containing a JK or KJ block.

questions.title: Between two friends
questions.prompt: In a row of four different children, Iris must stand somewhere between Jo and Kit. How many of the 24 orders are allowed?
questions.hint: Ignore the fourth child and compare the relative order of the other three.

questions.title: Two forbidden neighbours
questions.prompt: How many orders of A, B, C and D keep A away from B and also away from C?
questions.hint: Look at A's remaining possible neighbour.

questions.title: Two twin pairs
questions.prompt: Five different photographs A, B, C, D and E form a row. A and B cannot touch, and C and D cannot touch. How many rows meet both rules?
questions.hint: Two forbidden blocks may appear in the same row.

lessons.headline: Count groups that move together
lessons.intro: A symmetry rule can force several cells to have one shared colour. Look for the smallest group whose members must agree.
lessons.bridge: When the coloured square must satisfy two reflections, watch why cells have to be chosen in whole groups.
lessons.recap: After applying a symmetry, collect positions into whole groups before counting colour choices.

example.prompt: A row of five cells is symmetric about its middle. How many cells can be coloured independently?
steps: Positions 1 and 5 form a pair, as do 2 and 4.
The centre forms its own group. One free choice per group makes 3 independent choices.

questions.title: Colours opposite each other
questions.prompt: Six fixed windows sit at equally spaced points around a circular door. Each window is blue or gold. A half-turn must preserve the colours, and the top window is gold. How many colouring patterns are possible?
questions.hint: Pair each window with the window directly opposite it.

questions.title: Two flags in the mirror
questions.prompt: Five flags hang in a straight line. Exactly two are blue and three are white. How many arrangements read the same from both ends?
questions.hint: If the centre were blue, could the other blue flags come in matching pairs?

questions.title: Tile meeting point
questions.prompt: Congruent wedge-shaped tiles each contribute an angle of 90° at the same interior point. How many of these angles exactly fill one turn?
questions.hint: A full turn has 360°.

questions.title: Paired lamps
questions.prompt: An array has 4 rows of 6 lamps. Under a half-turn, paired lamps must always agree. What is the smallest number of independent switches needed if every allowed pattern must be possible?
questions.hint: Count pairs and then check for a lamp that maps to itself.

lessons.headline: Compare rates on unequal intervals
lessons.intro: A larger rise can take a longer time. To compare steepness, divide each change by the horizontal interval. A flat section means the recorded quantity did not change.
lessons.bridge: At the chart with unequal time intervals, watch the film divide each rise by its own elapsed time. The tallest rise need not give the greatest rate.
lessons.recap: For each interval, form the change in the vertical quantity per one unit horizontally. Keep the units the same when comparing.

example.prompt: A cyclist's distance readings are 0 km at 0 min, 4 km at 10 min and 9 km at 30 min. Which interval is faster?
steps: The first covers 4 ÷ 10 = 0.4 km/min. The second covers 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25 km/min.
The first interval is faster despite covering less distance.

figure.alt: Points on a distance–time chart are (0 minutes, 0 km), (10 minutes, 4 km) and (30 minutes, 9 km).

questions.title: Hourly rate
questions.prompt: A reading rises from 14 to 35 between hours 2 and 5. What is the average increase per hour?
questions.hint: Use elapsed time, not the ending hour.

questions.title: Two intervals
questions.prompt: At minutes 0, 3 and 5 a tank reads 5, 17 and 27 litres. What is the greater of the two interval rates in litres per minute?
questions.hint: The intervals have different lengths.

questions.title: Stop on the track
questions.prompt: A runner's distances at minutes 0, 2, 5 and 8 are 0, 400, 400 and 1000 metres. What is the runner's average speed over the entire eight minutes in metres per minute?
questions.hint: The flat interval still takes time.

questions.title: Recover a timestamp
questions.prompt: A pump meter reads 10 L at minute 0 and 34 L at an unknown minute. From then to minute 11 it gains 15 L at exactly 3 L/min. What was its average rate before the unknown minute in L/min?
questions.hint: Work backwards from the final interval.

lessons.headline: Build the whole from what survived
lessons.intro: When a final amount is known, work backwards through the fractions that remained. Knowing that two thirds stayed is enough to reconstruct the earlier amount.
lessons.bridge: In the film's final pile, the gift is added between two fractional changes. Start at the end and decide when the gift must be taken back.
lessons.recap: Check your reconstructed starting amount by acting out the story forwards, using the current amount at every step.

example.prompt: After a third of a bag of marbles is removed, 10 marbles remain. How many were in the bag?
steps: The 10 marbles represent two equal thirds. Each third holds 5.
All three thirds hold 15 marbles.

lessons.videoTitle: Parts and wholes, including remaining fractions

questions.title: Before the refill
questions.prompt: A tank is emptied by one fifth of the water it contains. There are 32 litres left. How many litres were there first?
questions.hint: The remaining water fills four equal fifths.

questions.title: Not one half of the start
questions.prompt: A club spends a third of its money on paint, then half of what remains on tools. What fraction of the original money remains?
questions.hint: Write the two fractions that stay unspent.

questions.title: A fixed gift as well
questions.prompt: Amir gives away one quarter of his stickers and then 5 more. He has 16 left. How many did he start with?
questions.hint: Undo the fixed gift before undoing the fraction.

questions.title: Open the middle crate
questions.prompt: Three crates share 84 apples. The first contains a quarter of all the apples. The last contains a third of what remains after taking the first crate. How many apples are in the middle crate?
questions.hint: The middle crate holds the rest after the other two are counted.

lessons.headline: Separate positions from dimensions
lessons.intro: Knowing a rectangle’s width and height does not usually determine its location. Slide its lower-left corner across the grid and count where the far edge still fits.
lessons.bridge: The film lets the sides of a frame move around a marked cell. Watch which edge positions continue to fit as the frame slides.
lessons.recap: For a fixed size, count legal starts separately in each direction and multiply.

example.prompt: A block of length 2 slides along a row of 5 cells. In how many positions does it fit?
steps: Its starting cell can be 1, 2, 3 or 4.
That gives 4 positions. Starting at cell 5 would go beyond the right edge.

questions.title: Turn the notice
questions.prompt: An oblong notice covers a 3-by-2 rectangle of cells. A board is 5 cells wide and 3 high. How many placements are possible when the notice may also stand 2 wide and 3 high?
questions.hint: Count the two orientations separately.

questions.title: Hidden grid distance
questions.prompt: A robot moves one unit horizontally or vertically at a time. It starts at (1,1) and finishes at (7,3). What is its shortest possible distance?
questions.hint: Add the changes in the two coordinates.

questions.title: Leave a side margin
questions.prompt: On a board 7 columns wide and 5 rows high, a 2-by-2 sign must touch the upper or lower edge but leave at least one unused column on both sides. How many placements meet these conditions?
questions.hint: Remove the two outer columns from the available width.

questions.title: Clear the repair square
questions.prompt: A display panel is 6 columns wide and 5 rows high. A rigid filter covers exactly 3 consecutive columns and 2 consecutive rows. It may not rotate. Cell (3,3), numbered from the lower left starting at 1, is under repair. How many filter placements avoid that cell?
questions.hint: Count unrestricted positions, then count placements covering the repair.

lessons.headline: Pair factors from opposite ends
lessons.intro: Every divisor of a positive integer has a partner. Search for the smaller member of each pair up to the square root. A square root that is a whole number pairs with itself.
lessons.bridge: In the film, try to test 37 for a factor before the prime check finishes. Then see why counting the divisors of 60 needs a different list.
lessons.recap: A rectangle and its rotation correspond to the same unordered factor pair. A square uses the same factor twice but only one positive divisor.

example.prompt: How many factor pairs of 24 are there, counting swapped order as the same pair?
steps: Try possible smaller factors 1 through 4.
The pairs are 1×24, 2×12, 3×8 and 4×6. There are 4 pairs.

questions.title: The prime shelf
questions.prompt: How many prime numbers lie strictly between 10 and 20?
questions.hint: Test small prime factors of each candidate.

questions.title: Rectangles of thirty
questions.prompt: Thirty identical square tiles make a rectangle with no gaps. How many shapes are possible if rotations count as the same?
questions.hint: List the smaller side up to the square root.

questions.title: A middle factor
questions.prompt: How many positive divisors does 36 have?
questions.hint: Find its factor pairs and look for the repeated middle.

questions.title: Exactly three dividers
questions.prompt: What is the smallest whole number greater than 20 with exactly three positive divisors?
questions.hint: A number with three positive divisors must be a square. What must its root be?

lessons.headline: Put an entire journey on one clock
lessons.intro: Speed compares distance with moving time or elapsed time, depending on the question. For a whole journey, match its whole distance to the whole time being counted.
lessons.bridge: The film times an outward ride, a stop and a return. Decide which parts belong in the total time when the average refers to the whole outing.
lessons.recap: Sum kilometres and sum hours before taking a journey average. Keep track of whether stops count.

example.prompt: A walker covers 4 km in an hour and rests for half an hour. What is the average speed from start to finish?
steps: The total time is 1.5 hours, including the rest.
Average speed is 4 ÷ 1.5 = 8/3 km/h.

questions.title: The canal path
questions.prompt: A boat covers 18 km in 45 minutes. What is its speed in km/h?
questions.hint: Write 45 minutes as hours.

questions.title: Rest on the ridge
questions.prompt: A walker covers 12 km in 2 hours of walking and rests for another hour. What is the average speed over the whole outing in km/h?
questions.hint: Include the stop in the denominator.

questions.title: Two equal times
questions.prompt: A rider cycles for 30 minutes at 10 km/h and 30 minutes at 18 km/h. What is her average speed in km/h?
questions.hint: Find the distance in each half hour.

questions.title: Out and back
questions.prompt: A boat travels 12 km out at 8 km/h and the same distance back at 12 km/h. What is its average speed over both legs, in km/h? Give an exact fraction or decimal.
questions.hint: The slower leg takes longer.

lessons.headline: Build the list from a fixed end
lessons.intro: A route or code can have several parts. Fix the first part and list every legal finish before changing it. Choices with the same total can still be different outcomes.
lessons.bridge: The film lists two numbered counters as A and B. Notice when reversing their readings creates a new outcome and use that decision for ordered routes afterwards.
lessons.recap: Pin down the part that identifies a branch. Test whether changing the order changes the object you are counting.

example.prompt: You may walk 1 or 2 steps at a time. Which ordered sequences reach step 3?
steps: Starting with 1 gives 1–1–1 and 1–2.
Starting with 2 gives 2–1. Every route has one of these first moves, so there are 3.

questions.title: Two-letter signs
questions.prompt: Make a two-letter sign from A, B and C using different letters. How many signs are possible if the left and right positions matter?
questions.hint: Fix the left letter.

questions.title: Staircase journeys
questions.prompt: How many ordered lists of 1s and 2s have sum 5 and contain exactly one 2?
questions.hint: How many 1s are needed beside the 2?

questions.title: Code with a middle
questions.prompt: A three-letter code uses A, B and C, with repetition allowed. The middle letter must differ from both neighbours and the code must contain exactly one A. How many codes are possible?
questions.hint: Separate codes with A in the middle from those with A at an end.

questions.title: A box of weights
questions.prompt: A box has one weight each of 1, 3, 4 and 6 g. How many different positive totals can you make on one pan of an empty scale by adding some of the weights, using each at most once?
questions.hint: List totals without 6, then add 6 to every total, including zero.

lessons.headline: Remove or add back?
lessons.intro: When one region sits inside another, subtraction measures what is left. When two regions overlap, look carefully at which part has been counted twice.
lessons.bridge: In the shaded board, find the region that belongs to both rectangles. Follow what happens to that area when the film calculates the unshaded space.
lessons.recap: Sketch the overlap and label its area before deciding whether to subtract it or add it back.

example.prompt: Of 15 unit tiles, 8 carry blue paint, 6 carry yellow paint and 2 carry both. How many have neither?
steps: The painted union contains 8 + 6 − 2 = 12 tiles.
The 3 remaining tiles have neither colour.

questions.title: The untouched part of a card
questions.prompt: A card has area 84 cm². A printed design covers 55 cm² and a transparent sticker covers 60 cm². Both lie wholly on the card and 45 cm² lies under both. How much of the card, in square centimetres, lies under neither?
questions.hint: Subtract the shared part once when counting the covered area.

questions.title: Two pools of light
questions.prompt: Two lamps each light 20 m² of a stage. An area of 7 m² receives light from both of them. How many square metres receive light from exactly one lamp?
questions.hint: Start with one lamp and remove its overlap. Then do the same for the other.

questions.title: Which part has two coats?
questions.prompt: A 10 cm wide, 8 cm high rectangle gets a coat of paint everywhere. Its leftmost 3 cm strip gets one extra coat, and its top 2 cm strip also gets one extra coat. How many square centimetres finish with exactly two coats?
questions.hint: Cells in both strips have three coats.

questions.title: Untouched seats
questions.prompt: An auditorium has 9 rows of 13 seats. Every seat in the first 3 rows or in the leftmost 3 columns is reserved. How many seats remain available?
questions.hint: Describe the unreserved rows and columns at the same time.

lessons.headline: Match the middle quantity
lessons.intro: Two ratios can describe three quantities. Scale the ratios until the quantity they share has the same value in both.
lessons.bridge: In the map example, match centimetres to centimetres before changing to metres. Watch how keeping one shared quantity consistent links the two descriptions.
lessons.recap: A shared letter stands for the same actual amount in both ratios. Check both original pairs after finding the three amounts.

example.prompt: A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 1:4. If A is 4, what is C?
steps: In the first ratio A doubles from 2 to 4, so B doubles to 6.
In the second ratio C is four times B, giving C = 24.

questions.title: Three ribbons
