questions.prompt: Red to blue length is 3:4 and blue to gold is 2:5. Red measures 9 cm. How many centimetres of gold are there?
questions.hint: Find the blue length first.

questions.title: Find the outer pair
questions.prompt: A:B = 4:5 and B:C = 10:3. If C is 9, what is A?
questions.hint: Find B from the second ratio.

questions.title: Combine the teams
questions.prompt: The sizes of teams A and B are in the ratio 3:2. Teams B and C are in the ratio 4:5. All three teams together have 60 players. How many are on team C?
questions.hint: Write A:B with four parts for B.

questions.title: Scaling a model twice
questions.prompt: The length of a new model is 3/2 of an old model's length. The old model is 2/5 of the length of the real object. The new model measures 18 cm. How long is the real object in centimetres?
questions.hint: Link the two comparisons using the old model.

lessons.headline: Check both parts of a claim
lessons.intro: The word “and” matters. A sentence containing two claims can be false even when one part is correct. You need both parts only when you assert the whole sentence is true.
lessons.bridge: As the film reaches the final speaker’s claim about two others, pause and test the whole sentence under each remaining assignment of types.
lessons.recap: Write down the values of the small claims before deciding whether the whole sentence is true.

example.prompt: A box is blue and empty. Is “The box is blue and contains a key” true?
steps: Its first part is true. Its second part is false.
An “and” sentence requires both, so this sentence is false.

questions.title: Two claims in sequence
questions.prompt: Every person either always tells the truth or always lies. Ira says Jia is truthful. Jia says Kir is a liar. If Kir is truthful, how many of these three lie?
questions.hint: Start with the person whose type is given.

questions.title: The second witness
questions.prompt: Every person either always tells the truth or always lies. Hiro says, “Ira and I are both truthful.” Ira says, “Hiro lies.” How many of the pair are truthful?
questions.hint: Try making the first speaker truthful, then test the second statement.

questions.title: One honest label
questions.prompt: A spare key is in exactly one box: red, blue or gold. The labels read “in red”, “outside blue”, and “outside red”, in that order. Exactly one label is true. Which box holds the key? Answer red, blue or gold.
questions.hint: The first and third labels cannot agree.

questions.title: A message from the keeper
questions.prompt: Every person either always tells the truth or always lies. Mo says “The gate is open.” Nia says “The gate is closed and Mo is truthful.” Exactly one of the two is truthful. Is the gate open? Answer yes or no.
questions.hint: Test the gate in each of its two states.

lessons.headline: Find the edges a net must share
lessons.intro: When a cuboid folds, opposite faces have equal dimensions. A net or a wrapping problem may use only some of those faces, so list them individually.
lessons.bridge: Look at the base and the four walls of the film’s open box. Which of those five panels change when the base dimensions change?
lessons.recap: Match opposite faces by their dimensions. Include the lid, base or walls only as the physical object requires.

example.prompt: A closed box has sides 2, 3 and 4 cm. How much area is on the two largest faces?
steps: The largest face measures 3 × 4 = 12 cm².
Its opposite matches it, so the pair contributes 24 cm².

lessons.videoTitle: Nets, surface area, volume and 3D views

questions.title: The missing lid
questions.prompt: A box with a 5 by 7 cm base is 4 cm high. What area of card makes its four walls and base, ignoring tabs?
questions.hint: Draw the base once and the walls in opposite pairs.

questions.title: A cube inside a band
questions.prompt: A cube of side 5 cm has its top and bottom left uncovered. How many square centimetres of its surface are covered by paper if all four side faces are wrapped exactly once?
questions.hint: How many whole square faces does the band cover?

questions.title: Match the adjacent face
questions.prompt: A closed rectangular carton has a base 3 cm wide and 8 cm long. A side panel sharing an 8 cm base edge has area 40 cm². What is the area of the side panel sharing a 3 cm base edge, in square centimetres?
questions.hint: The two upright panels have a common height.

questions.title: Slice into equal blocks
questions.prompt: A cuboid 10 cm by 21 cm by 4 cm is packed exactly with blocks 2 cm by 3 cm by 4 cm, each oriented in the stated order. How many blocks fit?
questions.hint: Count blocks along each direction, then multiply.

lessons.headline: Read a palindrome as a number
lessons.intro: The mirrored letters in ABBA describe a numerical structure. The outside pair contributes 1001A and the inside pair contributes 110B, so some factors can be found without division.
lessons.bridge: The film opens up 2772 using its mirrored places. Ask how the two outer digits and the two inner digits contribute differently to its value.
lessons.recap: Separate the digit pairs by place value. When every pair has a common factor, that factor also divides their sum.

example.prompt: Why does the four-digit palindrome 1221 divide evenly by 11?
steps: The two outer ones contribute 1001 = 11 × 91. The two inner twos contribute 220 = 11 × 20.
Both parts are multiples of 11. Their sum is 11 × 111.

questions.title: The inner pair
questions.prompt: A mirror display reads 6336. The two outside digits contribute 6 × 1001. How many groups of 110 do the two inner digits contribute?
questions.hint: Write the value of each inner 3 in its own place.

questions.title: Recover the inside digit
questions.prompt: A four-digit palindrome starts with 6 and has digit sum 26. What is the repeated inner digit?
questions.hint: The two outside digits already supply 12.

questions.title: A step between mirrors
questions.prompt: What is the difference between the four-digit palindromes 7337 and 7227?
questions.hint: Only the middle pair changes.

questions.title: How many share the divisor?
questions.prompt: How many four-digit palindromes are divisible by 22 and have different first and second digits?
questions.hint: Separate the factors 2 and 11. What does each force?

lessons.headline: Match the time unit to the rate
lessons.intro: A rate of items per minute can describe an hour or a few seconds. Convert either the rate or the time so that the units meet.
lessons.bridge: When the film changes a trail length into one unit, check which unit it chooses. Carry that habit into the sensor example before comparing an interval with the total time.
lessons.recap: Write the unit beside the rate and beside the time. The time units should cancel when multiplied.

example.prompt: A belt moves 90 cm per minute. How far does it move in 20 seconds?
steps: Twenty seconds is one third of a minute.
The belt moves one third of 90 cm, or 30 cm.

questions.title: The conveyor
questions.prompt: A belt moves 240 metres in 4 minutes. How many metres does it move in one second?
questions.hint: Convert the full time to seconds.

questions.title: Seconds of sewing
questions.prompt: A machine makes 150 stitches per minute. How many stitches does it make in 18 seconds at a steady rate?
questions.hint: Eighteen seconds is what fraction of a minute?

questions.title: Across the pool
questions.prompt: A robot moves at 30 cm per second. How many seconds does it take to travel 12 metres?
questions.hint: Write the distance in centimetres.

questions.title: The changing line
questions.prompt: A label printer produces 36 labels per minute for 90 seconds, then 48 per minute for 30 seconds. How many labels are produced?
questions.hint: Convert each time separately.

lessons.headline: Separate a turn from an angle inside
lessons.intro: As you walk around a polygon, the turn at a corner and the angle inside that corner usually have different sizes. Mark the original direction of travel before measuring the turn.
lessons.bridge: In the film, extending a side creates an exterior turn. Mark the interior angle next to it before following the bisectors.
lessons.recap: Keep straight-line, interior and exterior angles labelled separately on your sketch.

example.prompt: A walker turns 90° at each corner of a square. How much has she turned after three corners in the same direction?
steps: Each quarter-turn adds 90° to her change of direction.
Three quarter-turns total 270°. One more completes a full turn.

questions.title: Turn at every post
questions.prompt: A path follows all the sides of a regular 9-gon. What is the angle inside the polygon at each post, in degrees?
questions.hint: A complete walk turns through 360°.

questions.title: Parallel edges
questions.prompt: Two horizontal parallel lines are cut by one slanted line. At the first crossing a marked acute angle is 54°. What is the size, in degrees, of an obtuse angle at the second crossing?
questions.hint: Move the acute angle to the other crossing before finding its neighbour.

questions.title: Diagonals from one corner
questions.prompt: Every possible diagonal from one fixed vertex of a convex 7-gon is drawn. What is the sum of the interior angles of the whole polygon in degrees?
questions.hint: Count the triangles that fill it.

questions.title: Reconstruct the dance floor
questions.prompt: A convex regular dance floor has the same number of sides as vertices. Each interior angle exceeds its corresponding exterior turn by 100°. How many sides does the floor have?
questions.hint: The interior angle and its turn also sum to 180°.

lessons.headline: Separate frequency from value
lessons.intro: When the same reading appears several times, a frequency table stores its value once and says how often to use it. Add the frequencies to find the number of observations.
lessons.bridge: Watch how the film attaches a count to a mean when it reconstructs totals. A frequency does the same job for repeated copies of a single reading.
lessons.recap: Read a frequency as the number of copies. Check your total both across the rows and against the number of observations.

example.prompt: Two pupils score 3 and three pupils score 8. What is the mean?
steps: The five pupils score 2 × 3 + 3 × 8 = 30 points.
Divide 30 by 5 to get 6. The two distinct score labels are not the count of pupils.

lessons.videoTitle: Averages, weighted means and simple distributions

questions.title: Pet survey
questions.prompt: Three homes have one pet, four homes have two and one home has five. What is the mean number of pets per home?
questions.hint: Count all homes, then all pets.

questions.title: Zero is a reading
questions.prompt: Four sessions had zero visitors, two had three visitors and two had five. What was the mean number per session?
questions.hint: Include the quiet sessions in the denominator.

questions.title: A lost frequency
questions.prompt: A survey has two 1s, some 4s and one 10. It contains six readings. What is its mean?
questions.hint: Recover the missing frequency from the total number of readings.

questions.title: Two possible scores
questions.prompt: Each of 20 players scored either 2, 5 or 8 points. Their mean is 5. Six players scored 2. How many players scored 5?
questions.hint: A low score and a high score balance equally around 5.

lessons.headline: Subtract equal parts to expose a difference
lessons.intro: Two bundles can contain an identical part. Subtract their totals and that part disappears, leaving only the difference between the bundles.
lessons.bridge: Watch the bun-and-drink orders. Cross out the drinks common to both before you ask what the difference in price buys.
lessons.recap: Before subtracting, point to the objects that match exactly. The remaining objects must explain the entire difference in totals.

example.prompt: A sandwich and two juices cost $13. The same sandwich and one juice cost $9. What does a juice cost?
steps: Cross out one sandwich and one juice from both purchases.
The extra juice accounts for $13 − $9 = $4.

questions.title: One more badge
questions.prompt: A scarf and 3 badges cost $27. The same scarf and 2 badges cost $22. What is one badge's price in dollars?
questions.hint: Which item differs?

questions.title: Two extra jars
questions.prompt: A basket and 5 jars weigh 24 kg. The same basket and 3 jars weigh 16 kg. What does one jar weigh in kilograms?
questions.hint: The difference contains two jars.

questions.title: Recover the shared item
questions.prompt: Three pens and one notebook cost $17. Three pens and two notebooks cost $25. What does one pen cost in dollars?
questions.hint: Find the notebook from the difference first.

questions.title: A fee disappears
questions.prompt: A hall charges a fixed booking fee plus a constant price per chair. Hiring 18 chairs costs $126 and 12 costs $90. How many dollars would 15 chairs cost?
questions.hint: Compare the cost of six extra chairs.

lessons.headline: Change the unit you count
lessons.intro: A pair can overlap several groups. Count small objects inside each group and compare that total with how often each object appears across the whole system.
lessons.bridge: In the film’s tournament, count a missed meeting from each participant’s side. Watch where dividing by two turns player reports into actual missed meetings.
lessons.recap: Decide whether your unit is a person, a pair or a group membership. A pair inside two groups contributes twice to a count of memberships.

example.prompt: Four children form every possible three-person group. How many groups contain one particular pair?
steps: The third child can be either of the two outside the pair.
Each pair therefore belongs to exactly two of the groups.

questions.title: Round tables
questions.prompt: Six tables each seat five pupils. Every pupil works at three different tables during the day, and each table's five pupils are its full daily list. How many pupils are there?
questions.hint: Count pupil–table memberships.

questions.title: Triangles per edge
questions.prompt: Draw all edges joining four points, no three on a line. How many triangles contain one particular edge?
questions.hint: Choose a third point outside the edge.

questions.title: Repeated games
questions.prompt: Ten teams each play six games. Three pairs of teams meet twice; every other pair meets at most once. How many distinct pairs meet?
questions.hint: Count games first, then remove just the repeated meetings.

questions.title: The garden tags
questions.prompt: Every bed in a garden contains four different herbs. Each pair of the seven herbs occurs in exactly two beds. How many beds are there?
questions.hint: Count occurrences of an unordered pair in a bed.

lessons.headline: Account for removed cubes once
lessons.intro: Removing a hole from a solid is subtraction. If two cuts pass through the same cube, a second subtraction at that position would remove it twice.
lessons.bridge: When the six stacks appear, try counting the same arrangement by stacks and by layers. Then watch what changes when a hidden stack grows.
lessons.recap: Count the union of all removal positions. Check repeated positions before subtracting.

example.prompt: A block holds 12 cubes. One cut removes 3. Another passes through 4 positions, one already empty. What remains?
steps: The second cut removes only 3 new cubes.
The result is 12 − 3 − 3 = 6 cubes.

questions.title: A through tunnel
questions.prompt: A solid block is 8 cubes long, 6 wide and 2 high. A straight tunnel one cube wide and the full 2 cubes high is cut through its whole length. How many cubes remain?
questions.hint: Consider a cross-section perpendicular to the tunnel.

questions.title: The list from two inspectors
questions.prompt: Two inspectors mark defective cubes in an otherwise solid model. One marks 7 cubes, the other 6, and 3 cubes carry both marks. How many different cubes must be removed if either mark disqualifies a cube?
questions.hint: A double mark still refers to one physical cube.

questions.title: Read the intersection from the result
questions.prompt: A model initially has 50 cubes. A cutter is programmed to remove two sets of positions, one containing 9 cubes and the other 8. After both cuts, 37 cubes remain. How many positions belonged to both sets?
questions.hint: Compare the number actually removed with the sum of the two programmed removals.

questions.title: Two one-cube tunnels
questions.prompt: A cube of side 7 unit cubes is hollowed by two straight one-cube-wide tunnels through the entire block. They run along two different directions parallel to edges and meet in exactly one cube. How many cubes remain?
questions.hint: What would subtracting the tunnels separately do to the crossing?

lessons.headline: Split work into active intervals
lessons.intro: A worker may start, stop or change speed during a job. Within each interval use its own active rate. Only the completed work carries over to the next interval.
lessons.bridge: At the point where one pump stops in the film, pause. Which rate applies to work already finished and which rate applies only to the work that remains?
lessons.recap: Keep one running total of work. Start a new row whenever someone arrives or leaves.

example.prompt: One printer makes 4 sheets per minute for 3 minutes. A second joins it at 2 per minute. How many sheets do both make in the next minute?
steps: Before the join, 12 sheets are complete.
In the next minute the two together make 4 + 2 = 6 more sheets.

questions.title: Only the first stage
questions.prompt: A crew lays 14 tiles per hour for 3 hours, then stops. How many tiles have already been laid?
questions.hint: Multiply the hourly amount by hours worked.

questions.title: Lunch interruption
questions.prompt: Two people fold 5 and 7 boxes per minute. They fold together for 4 minutes. The faster person then stops and the other continues for 6 minutes. How many boxes are folded?
questions.hint: The second interval uses only the slower rate.

questions.title: Join at halfway
questions.prompt: A worker can paint a fence in 8 hours. When half the fence is painted, a second worker joins who could paint it alone in 24 hours. How many hours does the whole job take?
questions.hint: Find the time for the first half and the combined rate for the second.

questions.title: One machine removed
questions.prompt: Three identical machines can finish an order in 10 hours. All three work for 4 hours, then one machine breaks. How many hours from the start until completion?
questions.hint: Measure the order in machine-hours.

lessons.headline: Find the part that actually repeats
lessons.intro: A device can spend its first few moves entering a loop. Find two occurrences of the same full state. The interval between them repeats, while the opening path may never happen again.
lessons.bridge: In the numbered machine, mark the first repeated state. Look back to its earlier visit to decide which part of the list actually cycles.
lessons.recap: Measure a remainder from entry into the loop, not from the very first state. Count visits using the first actual visit to your target.

example.prompt: A machine follows 8 → 5 → 2 → 6 → 2 → 6 and keeps alternating between 2 and 6. Where does the loop start?
steps: At step 2 the state is 2, and it is 2 again at step 4.
States 2 and 6 form the loop. The opening 8 and 5 never recur.

questions.title: Find the period
questions.prompt: A device follows P → Q → R → S → Q and thereafter follows the same arrows. How many moves make one complete loop after the first Q?
questions.hint: Trace from Q to the next Q.

questions.title: Entry time
questions.prompt: A display at steps 0,1,2,3,4 is 9,8,3,4,5. From step 2 onwards it repeats 3,4,5. Which number shows at step 20?
questions.hint: Remove the steps before entry into the loop.

questions.title: Double and reduce
questions.prompt: Start with 1. At each move double the current value and take its remainder on division by 6. What is the value after 101 moves?
questions.hint: Write the opening values and locate the first repeated value.

questions.title: Visit count
questions.prompt: A machine visits states A,B,C,D,E,C,D,E,… with A at time 0 and a move each second. Counting both endpoints, how many times is it at D from time 0 to time 100?
questions.hint: Find the first D, then the spacing between visits.

lessons.headline: Reconstruct a shared boundary
lessons.intro: A drawing can hide the edge where two pieces touch. A difference between the separate and joined perimeters can tell you its length.
lessons.bridge: In the film’s board with a window, think backwards from the new total. Which contribution comes from the inner boundary alone?
lessons.recap: When working backwards, first find the boundary that disappeared. Check whether it was counted once or twice.

example.prompt: Two shapes have perimeters 12 cm and 14 cm. Joining along one straight segment makes an outline of 20 cm. How long is the join?
steps: Together they started with 26 cm of boundary. The join accounts for 6 cm that vanished.
Each shape contributed one copy, so the join measures 3 cm.

lessons.videoTitle: Perimeter, shared edges and boundary effects

questions.title: Four squares in a strip
questions.prompt: Four identical square patches are sewn into one straight strip. Their three complete shared edges have a combined length of 12 cm. How many centimetres of ribbon are needed around the outside of the strip?
questions.hint: Use the seams to find the side of one square.

questions.title: A bent cut
questions.prompt: A paper island has a perimeter of 27 cm. One cut, starting and ending on its boundary, separates it into two pieces. The cut has three straight sections of lengths 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. What is the sum of the two piece perimeters in centimetres?
questions.hint: Every part of the cut becomes an edge on each new piece.

questions.title: Fence between pens
questions.prompt: A rectangular 12 m by 8 m enclosure is split into three side-by-side pens by two straight internal fences of length 8 m. How many metres of fence are needed, counting each fence once?
questions.hint: Internal fencing is real material even though it is not outer perimeter.

questions.title: Read a footprint backwards
questions.prompt: A 12 m by 7 m cabin grows a rectangular alcove 3 m wide, joined along that full width. The new outside perimeter is 44 m. How far does the alcove stick out in metres?
questions.hint: The width it covers is replaced with an equal width at its far end.

lessons.headline: Use the pattern of colours
lessons.intro: When every connection joins opposite colours, a route must alternate. This fixes the colours of all positions before individual stops are selected.
lessons.bridge: Before the film considers the missing connection, write the red-blue pattern of a route with the given endpoints. Use it to rule out impossible orders.
lessons.recap: Write the forced colour sequence first. Then place each labelled stop subject to the available links.

example.prompt: A route starts at red and takes three moves, each to the opposite colour. Which colour does it end on?
steps: The successive colours are blue, red, blue.
Three is odd, so the finish is blue. Any odd number of such moves has the same effect.

questions.title: Opposite colours
questions.prompt: An array has 14 columns and 4 rows with alternating black and white cells. A token starts on black and each move crosses a shared edge. After an odd number of moves, how many cells have the only possible ending colour?
questions.hint: Each step flips the colour. The problem asks about colour, not distance.

questions.title: Possible starting colour
questions.prompt: Every track joins an orange station to a purple station. A route ends at purple after exactly five moves. Among its six station visits, including the start and finish, how many are orange?
questions.hint: Work back from the finish, changing colour each time.

questions.title: The common interchange
questions.prompt: Orange stations A and B are linked only to purple stations. A links to P,Q,R and B links to Q,R,S. How many different two-move routes go from A to B?
questions.hint: The middle station must be linked to both ends.

questions.title: The guided tour
questions.prompt: A museum has three red rooms A,B,C and three blue rooms P,Q,R. Every red room has a doorway to every blue room. A tour begins at A, finishes at C after four moves, and never repeats a room. The middle room must have a name from A,B,C. How many tours use room Q somewhere?
questions.hint: Write the colour pattern first. Which red room has to be in the middle?

lessons.headline: Make several groups finish together
lessons.intro: If an amount is one short in two different packing schemes, adding one completes both. Work with that adjusted total, then undo the adjustment before answering.
lessons.bridge: On the film's ruler, locate the first tick that satisfies all the remainder clues. What step repeats every clue together?
lessons.recap: The common multiple belongs to the adjusted amount. Test the original number against the stated remainders and range.

example.prompt: A positive number below 20 is one less than a multiple of both 3 and 4. What is it?
steps: After adding one, the number must be a common multiple of 3 and 4.
The only suitable common multiple is 12, so the original is 11.

questions.title: One shy
questions.prompt: What is the smallest positive number that is one less than a multiple of 5 and also one less than a multiple of 8?
questions.hint: What must happen after adding one?

questions.title: Two missing
questions.prompt: A bag needs 2 more beads to be exactly divisible into groups of 6 or into groups of 9. It contains between 40 and 60 beads. How many beads are there?
questions.hint: Try the multiples of 18 after adding 2.

questions.title: Different-looking remainders
questions.prompt: A number leaves remainder 3 on division by 4 and remainder 6 on division by 7. What is the least such number greater than 30?
questions.hint: Both remainders are how far below a completed group?

questions.title: The count of attendance records
questions.prompt: Between 1 and 150 inclusive, how many numbers leave remainder 4 on division by 6 and remainder 6 on division by 8?
questions.hint: Add the same small number to both remainders to complete each group.

lessons.headline: Separate the fixed and changing costs
lessons.intro: A fixed fee is paid once. A price per unit is paid repeatedly. Keep them separate when you compare two orders or recover an unknown quantity.
lessons.bridge: In the film's opening number rule, identify the part that is added once and the part that changes with the input. A setup fee works the same way.
lessons.recap: Try zero items in your rule. The amount left should be exactly the fixed fee whenever the booking is made.

example.prompt: A printing shop charges $4 to set up and $2 for each poster. What do 3 posters cost?
steps: Three posters add 3 × $2 = $6.
Add the single setup fee to get $10.

questions.title: Opening charge
questions.prompt: A taxi charges $7 to start and $3 per kilometre. How much in dollars does a 6 km trip cost?
questions.hint: Count the opening fee once.

questions.title: Work out the fee
questions.prompt: A service charges a flat fee and $5 per visit. Four visits cost $31 altogether. What is the flat fee in dollars?
questions.hint: Remove the variable part.

questions.title: Two orders
questions.prompt: A bakery charges the same setup fee for each cake order. Six cupcakes plus setup cost $25. Nine cupcakes plus setup cost $34. What is the setup fee in dollars?
questions.hint: Use the difference to get the cost of one cupcake.

questions.title: A waived charge
questions.prompt: A club charges $9 plus $3 per class. A promotion waives the $9 charge but increases the price to $4 per class. What is the fewest whole number of classes for which the usual plan is strictly cheaper?
questions.hint: Find the break-even point, then check the next whole count.

lessons.headline: Peel the clean core away
lessons.intro: Counting cubes with at least one painted face is often easier by finding the cubes with no paint. Keep track of the number of affected ends in each dimension.
lessons.bridge: Watch the unpainted top of the cuboid. Sketch what is left after removing only layers touched by the painted faces.
lessons.recap: Subtract the entirely clean core from the original volume when the question asks for any paint.

example.prompt: A 4-by-4-by-3 block has its top and bottom painted. How many cubes stay clean?
steps: The painted layers have height 1 each, leaving a single interior layer.
All 4 × 4 = 16 cubes in that layer stay clean.

lessons.videoTitle: Painted faces, boundary and hidden cubes

questions.title: Cover all but the base
questions.prompt: A solid 3-by-3-by-3 block has its top and four upright faces painted, leaving the bottom unpainted. How many cubes have no paint?
questions.hint: A clean cube must be in the central column and below the top.

questions.title: An edge with two untouched ends
questions.prompt: A bar is one unit cube wide, one cube high and nine cubes long. Only its two square end faces are painted. How many cubes have at least one painted face?
questions.hint: Check how many cubes one square end can reach.

questions.title: A cubic sleeve
questions.prompt: A hollow open-ended tube has an outside square cross-section 5 by 5 cubes, a centred square hole 3 by 3 cubes, and length 4 cubes. Its four long outside faces are painted, while its bore and ends get no paint. How many cubes in the tube receive paint?
questions.hint: Inspect one cross-section. Are there any material cells that do not touch an outside side?

questions.title: Divide before painting
questions.prompt: A solid cube has 6 unit cubes on each edge. One workshop paints it whole. Another first cuts an identical cube into eight 3-by-3-by-3 cubes, separates them, then paints every surface of each smaller cube. How many more unit cubes get paint in the second workshop?
questions.hint: Compare the number left completely clean by the two procedures.

lessons.headline: Keep occurrences separate from labels
lessons.intro: A question may ask for labels containing a digit, labels containing it exactly twice, or the total ink needed for that digit. Write which object you are counting before choosing a method.
lessons.bridge: For the film's multiples of nine, try marking the hundreds, tens and units occurrences of the target digit separately. Can a single number belong in two column counts?
lessons.recap: For a label used twice in a column tally, ask whether that double count is required by the question.

example.prompt: The labels are 4, 14, 40, 44. How many labels contain a 4, and how many printed fours are there?
steps: All four labels contain the digit 4.
The first three contribute one each and 44 contributes two. There are 5 printed fours.

lessons.videoTitle: Digit sums and counting digits in ranges

questions.title: Labels with a seven
questions.prompt: From 1 to 70 inclusive, how many numbers contain at least one 7?
questions.hint: Count those ending in 7 and then the part in the seventies.

questions.title: Two appearances
questions.prompt: Among the labels 100 through 299, how many contain exactly two copies of 2?
questions.hint: Separate the 100s from the 200s.

questions.title: Copies on odd pages
questions.prompt: On odd-numbered pages from 101 through 199 inclusive, how many copies of the digit 1 are printed?
questions.hint: Count each of the three columns separately.

questions.title: Lost ink total
questions.prompt: A machine printed every label from 10 to 99. It recorded that 18 labels contained a digit 4. How many individual 4s did it actually print?
questions.hint: Which of those labels needs two copies of the digit?

lessons.headline: Weight a fraction by the number behind it
lessons.intro: A group's fraction alone does not show how much it contributes. A small group with a high fraction can supply fewer objects than a large group with a lower fraction.
lessons.bridge: When the marked cards move from separate groups into a single total, ask what each group has actually contributed. Keep those counts for the film's unknown-group puzzle.
lessons.recap: Record group size, group fraction and actual count in separate columns. Add counts before dividing by the combined group size.

example.prompt: One bus has 10 people and half have hats. A second has 40 and a quarter have hats. Which bus has more people with hats?
steps: The first bus has 5 people with hats. The second has 10.
The lower fraction on the second bus applies to four times as many people.

questions.title: Two pools
questions.prompt: In one pool 3/5 of 20 swimmers are children. In another 1/4 of 44 are children. How many children are swimming?
questions.hint: Find the two counts separately.

questions.title: Can we average the percentages?
questions.prompt: A class of 10 has 80% present. A class of 30 has 60% present. What percentage of the combined classes is present? Enter a number.
questions.hint: How many students are present out of the combined 40?

questions.title: Unknown second group
questions.prompt: One crate contains 20 pens, of which half are blue. A second crate has 30 pens. Two fifths of all 50 pens are blue. How many blue pens are in the second crate?
questions.hint: Find the total number of blue pens, then take away the first crate's contribution.

questions.title: How many voted?
questions.prompt: At a club all 12 juniors vote and half favour a change. All seniors vote too, and three quarters of them favour it. Altogether two thirds of all voters favour it. How many seniors voted?
questions.hint: Try recording the number in favour for each four seniors.

lessons.headline: Change the multiplier, keep track of the terms
lessons.intro: A multiplication sequence can grow by a factor other than two. Separate the first amount, the multiplier and the number of multiplications. A sum contains all the successive terms.
lessons.bridge: When the film doubles an entire sum, watch its middle terms cancel. Identify the starting amount left at one end and the new term at the other.
lessons.recap: Use the multiplier once for each gap. For a sum, write enough terms to see what cancels when you multiply the entire sum by the growth factor.

example.prompt: A film clip is forwarded to 2 new people in round 1. Each round reaches three times as many new people as before. How many new people are reached in round 3?
steps: Round 2 reaches 2 × 3 = 6 and round 3 reaches 6 × 3 = 18.
The answer for round 3 alone is 18. The total through round 3 would be 26.

lessons.videoTitle: Doubling, geometric growth and finite sums

questions.title: Third growth stage
questions.prompt: A branching model has 4 tips at stage 0. Each stage triples the number. How many tips are at stage 3?
questions.hint: Stage 0 precedes three changes.

questions.title: Halfway down
questions.prompt: A strip starts 96 cm long. After each cut the retained piece is exactly half its previous length. How long in cm is it after four cuts?
questions.hint: Follow four changes from the initial strip.

questions.title: Total over four rows
questions.prompt: Four rows contain 2, 6, 18 and 54 beads. How many beads are present in all four rows?
questions.hint: Pair the terms or add the first three before the last.

questions.title: A branching budget
questions.prompt: A club plants 1 shrub in its first round and three times as many new shrubs in each later round. How many more shrubs must it buy to finish five rounds if it already owns 100?
questions.hint: Count the total for rounds 1 through 5.

lessons.headline: Count an outline by its size
lessons.intro: If a frame must be square, its width and height are linked. Count positions of each possible size separately before adding their totals.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film use the grid lines as choices of sides. When you later require a square, consider which two of those choices become linked.
lessons.recap: Choose a size first when dimensions must match. Within that size, count positions of one representative corner.

example.prompt: How many squares fit along the lines of a 2-by-2 grid?
steps: Four are unit squares, each at a different position.
The outside lines form one more square of side 2. The total is 5.

questions.title: Frames with a chosen top edge
questions.prompt: On a 4-column by 3-row board a square outline must have its top side on the board's top edge and must cover more than one cell. How many such squares lie on grid lines?
questions.hint: Consider side lengths 2 and 3 separately.

questions.title: Equal perimeter, different shapes
questions.prompt: A 4-by-4 grid of cells can hold rectangles of perimeter 8 unit edges. How many different placements are there, including both orientations of an oblong?
questions.hint: Which whole-number side pairs add to 4?

questions.title: Four central posts
questions.prompt: A board has 5 columns and 5 rows of unit cells. How many axis-aligned grid squares of any size have their centre at the centre of the board?
questions.hint: Think about whether an even side length can keep the centre at the middle of a cell.

questions.title: Adjoining display windows
questions.prompt: Two identical 2-by-2 square windows are drawn on a board 6 columns wide and 4 rows high. They must meet along a complete side, without overlap. How many unordered pairs of positions are there?
questions.hint: Find the outer rectangle formed by the pair.

lessons.headline: Match a repeated component
lessons.intro: Two equations may hide one unknown in equal amounts. Align the repeated parts and subtract, or combine totals to recover the amount you need directly.
lessons.bridge: Watch what adding the notebook-and-ruler purchases produces. The film asks for a combined price, so check whether both prices really need to be found separately.
lessons.recap: Write the two conditions side by side. If the answer is a combination of prices, see whether you can obtain it without finding every price.

example.prompt: A notebook and a ruler cost $11. A notebook and two rulers cost $14. How much is the notebook?
steps: The extra ruler costs $3.
Subtract its $3 price from $11, leaving $8 for the notebook.

questions.title: A second lamp
questions.prompt: A desk and a lamp cost $42. A desk and two lamps cost $58. What does the desk cost in dollars?
questions.hint: Find the extra lamp first.

questions.title: A combined price
questions.prompt: Two bells and one whistle cost $16. One bell and two whistles cost $14. How many dollars does one bell and one whistle cost together?
questions.hint: Add both purchases.

questions.title: Double an order
questions.prompt: Two pens and a folder cost $11. Three pens and two folders cost $19. How many dollars does the folder cost?
questions.hint: Double the first order to match the folders.

questions.title: A new hamper
questions.prompt: Three pears and one melon cost $10. One pear and two melons cost $10. For the same unit prices, what is the cost in dollars of four pears and three melons?
questions.hint: Look at the two given orders together.

lessons.headline: Look for the turning point
lessons.intro: A change that improves one shape may worsen another. Compare adjacent legal choices to see where an area stops increasing.
lessons.bridge: In the wall-side pen, compare the best two nearby whole-number depths. Which one uses the most area under the same fencing limit?
lessons.recap: Identify the best legal pair, then explain why moving farther away cannot improve it.

example.prompt: Change a 2 by 6 rectangle to a 3 by 5 rectangle. How do its perimeter and area change?
steps: Both adjacent-side sums are 8, so both perimeters are 16.
The areas are 12 and 15. A less extreme pair gains 3 square units.

lessons.videoTitle: Optimising areas and lengths under constraints

questions.title: Two positive scores
questions.prompt: Two positive whole-number scores add to 15. A bonus awards their product. What is the largest bonus possible?
questions.hint: What happens if two scores differing by 3 become one closer?

questions.title: Even lengths only
questions.prompt: A rectangular stage has a perimeter of 36 m. Both side lengths must be positive even whole numbers of metres. What is its greatest possible area in square metres?
questions.hint: The adjacent sides add to 18. Test the closest allowed pair, not just the closest whole-number pair.

questions.title: Use a packet of border tiles
questions.prompt: A rectangle uses at most 32 cm of ribbon around its outside. Whole-centimetre side lengths are required. What is the greatest area in square centimetres?
questions.hint: Check whether leaving any usable ribbon can improve area.

questions.title: The display must be wider
questions.prompt: A designer lays exactly 49 unit tiles in a rectangle. The longer side must be at least 8 units. What is the smallest possible perimeter?
questions.hint: List factor pairs and discard the square before comparing sums.

lessons.headline: Split numbers to compare products
lessons.intro: Sometimes a comparison needs only the differing pieces, even if the products are large. Centre the factors near a common number and record the extra strips and corner.
lessons.bridge: The film compares products near 1,000. Look for equal large parts that can be discarded before comparing the small corrections.
lessons.recap: Make sure the two offsets really are opposite before using the difference-of-squares shortcut. Otherwise keep the unmatched strip.

example.prompt: Which is larger, 20 × 20 or 19 × 21?
steps: The second is (20 − 1)(20 + 1) = 20² − 1.
The square is larger by 1. The large common part never needed to be computed.

questions.title: An extra strip
questions.prompt: A rectangular mosaic has 48 rows and 52 columns. The designer adds one column, keeping the number of rows fixed. How many more tiles are needed?
questions.hint: Think of the narrow strip being attached to one side.

questions.title: Unequal offsets
questions.prompt: How much larger is 102 × 99 than 100 × 100?
questions.hint: The offsets are +2 and −1, so one long strip survives.

questions.title: A changed field
questions.prompt: A 40 m by 40 m square is changed to a 36 m by 44 m rectangle. How many square metres of area are lost?
questions.hint: Compare (40 − 4)(40 + 4) with 40².

questions.title: Invisible centre
questions.prompt: Two whole numbers differ by 6. Their midpoint is 200. How much smaller is their product than the square of their midpoint?
questions.hint: The full difference is twice the offset from the midpoint.

lessons.headline: A transfer changes two parts
lessons.intro: Moving items between groups preserves the combined total. Set the final ratio against that fixed total to find each group's target.
lessons.bridge: In the film's counter box, track both piles during the transfer. Point to the part of the picture that represents a total that has not changed.
lessons.recap: Check both groups after the transfer. Their total should match the start, and their final amounts should give the stated ratio.

example.prompt: Two baskets hold 5 and 15 balls. How many must move from the larger to the smaller basket to make them equal?
steps: There are 20 balls altogether, so each final basket must contain 10.
Move 5 balls. One basket gains 5 while the other loses 5.

questions.title: Boxes of badges
questions.prompt: Two boxes contain 12 and 28 badges. How many must move from the larger to the smaller to make the smaller contain 16?
questions.hint: Find the change in just the receiving box.

questions.title: A two-to-three split
questions.prompt: A pair of tubs holds 9 and 31 pegs. How many must move from the second to the first to make the first-to-second ratio 2:3?
questions.hint: Find two fifths of the combined total.

questions.title: Four go the other way
questions.prompt: Two starting piles have a ratio of 1:3. Moving 4 stones from the larger pile to the smaller makes their sizes 1:2. How many stones are in both piles together?
questions.hint: The smaller pile changes from one quarter to one third of the same total.

questions.title: Borrowed players
questions.prompt: Two squads have 45 players altogether. Before a match the smaller lends 3 players to the larger, after which the sizes are in the ratio 1:4. What was the original difference between the squad sizes?
questions.hint: Reconstruct the two final groups, then undo the loan.

lessons.headline: A transfer has a double effect on the lead
lessons.intro: When the leader gives an item to the other side, one total falls as the other rises. Follow the difference as well as the individual totals.
lessons.bridge: When the three teams in the film share points, watch two score bars at once. A point passed from one team changes both ends of their gap.
lessons.recap: Distinguish a transfer between the two sides from a new item entering from outside. Only a transfer changes both sides at once.

example.prompt: Blue leads Gold by 10 counters. Blue gives Gold 3 counters. What is Blue's new lead?
steps: Blue loses 3 and Gold gains 3.
The lead shrinks by 6, leaving 4.

lessons.videoTitle: Winner margins, shared totals and linear rules

questions.title: Moving one ball
questions.prompt: A holds 21 balls and B holds 13. A hands B one ball. What is A's new lead?
questions.hint: Update both numbers.

questions.title: Catch the leader
questions.prompt: An orange team leads a purple team by 18 chips. How many chips must orange hand to purple to make the teams level?
questions.hint: How much does a one-chip transfer close the gap?

questions.title: A prize from outside
questions.prompt: A leads B by 6. B wins 4 new tokens from a referee. A then gives B one token. What is A's final lead?
questions.hint: The prize affects one player; the transfer affects two.

questions.title: Back past level
questions.prompt: The larger pile leads by 10 stones. After one transfer between piles, the pile that was smaller now leads by 6. How many stones moved?
questions.hint: Track the change from a lead of 10 to a deficit of 6.

lessons.headline: Use colour as a test
lessons.intro: On a checkerboard, every domino occupies one light and one dark square. Compare the colour counts before spending time trying placements.
lessons.bridge: As the film tiles a two-row strip, check the square count first and then watch the placement forced by the first open cell.
lessons.recap: Balanced colour counts are necessary for a domino tiling. When claiming it works, also supply actual legal placements.

example.prompt: Remove the middle cell from a row coloured black, white, black. Can one domino cover the remaining cells?
steps: The two surviving cells are both black.
A domino requires one of each colour, so it cannot cover them.

questions.title: Can this tray take another piece?
questions.prompt: A tray's remaining free cells comprise six black and four white cells in a checkerboard pattern. What is the greatest number of ordinary dominoes its colour counts alone allow?
questions.hint: Which colour runs out first?

questions.title: Balanced but separated
questions.prompt: A board consists of two separate strips of three cells each, with a gap between the strips. One strip is coloured black-white-black and the other white-black-white. What is the maximum number of dominoes that can be placed without crossing the gap?
questions.hint: Check the colour counts separately on each connected strip.

questions.title: Which square can be removed?
questions.prompt: One cell is removed from a 3-by-3 checkerboard. In how many of the nine positions can it be removed so that dominoes cover the remaining eight cells?
questions.hint: Start with the more numerous colour, then find a covering for each type of position of that colour.

questions.title: Two missing floorboards
questions.prompt: A 2-row, 5-column floor loses its bottom cells in columns 2 and 5. Each remaining piece must cover two edge-neighbouring cells. How many complete domino coverings exist?
questions.hint: Both colours remain in equal numbers. Now start at the bottom-left cell and the top-right cell, each of which has just one neighbour.

lessons.headline: Choose between a shared factor and a shared multiple
lessons.intro: Equal groups with no leftovers require a size or count that divides the available quantities. Events that repeat together require a time divisible by the intervals.
lessons.bridge: At the marker-packing example, decide why the pack count must divide two totals. Compare that with the earlier restart time, which both intervals must divide into.
lessons.recap: Use the story to decide the direction of divisibility. Pack counts divide quantities; recurring intervals divide elapsed times.

example.prompt: A teacher has 12 red cards and 18 blue cards. What is the greatest number of identical packs she can make using them all?
steps: The pack count must divide both 12 and 18.
The greatest common divisor is 6. Each pack then has two red and three blue cards.

questions.title: Longest equal strips
questions.prompt: Two strips measure 28 cm and 42 cm. What is the greatest whole-centimetre length into which both can be cut with no waste?
questions.hint: List common divisors.

questions.title: Ringing together
questions.prompt: One bell rings every 8 minutes and another every 14. Both ring now. How many minutes until they next ring together?
questions.hint: What positive time will both intervals divide?

questions.title: Contents per kit
questions.prompt: A camp packs 45 maps and 60 pencils into the largest possible number of identical kits with none left. How many items in total are in each kit?
questions.hint: Find the kit count first.

questions.title: A rectangle of squares
questions.prompt: A 42 cm by 30 cm poster is covered exactly with the largest identical square stickers whose sides are whole centimetres. How many stickers cover the poster?
questions.hint: A sticker side must divide both dimensions.

lessons.headline: Meetings repeat on a loop
lessons.intro: On a circular track runners may meet several times. Between consecutive meetings the relative distance travelled changes by one full circumference.
lessons.bridge: Follow the two runners on the film's circular track. After the head start, notice when gaining a complete lap matters and when only part of a lap is needed.
lessons.recap: Check whether you are counting separate meetings, elapsed intervals, or the initial meeting at time zero.

example.prompt: Two runners move in the same direction at 9 and 6 m/s on a 60 m loop. How long between successive meetings?
steps: The faster runner gains 3 m each second.
Gaining one 60 m lap takes 20 seconds.

lessons.videoTitle: Relative speeds, timed movement and meetings

questions.title: Passing the start
questions.prompt: A cyclist goes round a 350 m circuit at 7 m/s. How many seconds does one lap take?
questions.hint: Use distance divided by speed.

questions.title: First overtake
questions.prompt: Starting together, two skaters travel in the same direction on a 240 m track at 9 and 5 m/s. After how many seconds does the faster first lap the slower?
questions.hint: The faster skater must gain one lap.

questions.title: The fourth meeting
questions.prompt: Two couriers move in opposite directions along a 150 m loop at 4 and 6 m/s. Starting together, after how many seconds do they meet for the fourth time after departure?
questions.hint: Do not count their shared start.

questions.title: An offset start
questions.prompt: Two runners go clockwise on a 200 m track at 8 and 5 m/s. The slower runner starts 50 m ahead. How many seconds pass before the slower runner is caught for the second time? Give an exact fraction.
questions.hint: Separate the initial gap from the next complete lap gained.

lessons.headline: Count by choosing the unused objects
lessons.intro: Choosing a large group can be easier if you record who stays out. This gives exactly one record per group, even when the resulting groups will later receive a captain or a task.
lessons.bridge: In the film's team puzzle, decide when a selection of artists is already fully specified. Ask whether choosing those left out could describe the same selection.
lessons.recap: Look for a smaller selection that uniquely identifies the larger one. Add roles only when they are part of the outcome.

example.prompt: Choose four of six different cards. How many hands are there?
steps: Each hand leaves exactly two cards on the table.
The two left out can be chosen in 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15 ways.

questions.title: One chair empty
questions.prompt: Eight musicians have places in a group of seven. How many different seven-person groups are possible?
questions.hint: Identify the musician outside the group.

questions.title: Labelled boats
questions.prompt: Four paddlers split into two pairs for a red boat and a blue boat. Seats inside each boat are interchangeable. How many allocations work?
questions.hint: Choose the red crew first.

questions.title: Museum pass
questions.prompt: A pass includes four of seven exhibits, exactly one of which must be chosen from the two space exhibits. How many passes are possible?
questions.hint: How many of the other exhibits must be chosen?

questions.title: Lab kits
questions.prompt: Six different samples go into three labelled kits, two per kit. Each sample is used once. How many ways are there to pack the kits?
questions.hint: Fix the contents of the first kit, then the second.

lessons.headline: Link two small triangles
lessons.intro: A shared corner or a straight edge can carry information from one part of a figure into another. Find the angle that connects the two totals.
lessons.bridge: Watch how the exterior angle in the film links the original triangle to the triangle formed by the two bisectors.
lessons.recap: Mark the shared angle or line. Use a triangle sum on one side and check which rule applies on the other.

example.prompt: Two adjacent angles share a straight side and add to 180°. One belongs to a triangle whose other angles are 40° and 60°. What is the adjacent angle?
steps: The triangle’s missing angle is 180 − 40 − 60 = 80°.
Its straight-line partner is 180 − 80 = 100°.

questions.title: The crossing in a brace
questions.prompt: Two straight rods cross. Above their intersection they form two sides of a triangle whose other two angles are 52° and 61°. Below the intersection a second triangle uses the vertically opposite angle. One of its other angles is 34°. How large is its remaining angle in degrees?
questions.hint: Find the angle at the intersection in the upper triangle first.

questions.title: The shared line
questions.prompt: A straight line passes through points P, Q and R in that order. In triangle QRS, angle QRS is 32° and angle QSR is 39°. What is angle SQR in degrees?
questions.hint: Name the vertex in the middle of the three-letter angle.

questions.title: Which side of the straight line?
questions.prompt: D lies strictly between B and C on side BC of triangle ABC. The segment AD bisects angle A. Angle BAD is 29° and angle ABC is 47°. What is angle ADC in degrees?
questions.hint: The angle at D in triangle ABD and the requested angle lie on a straight line.

questions.title: The surveyor’s unequal split
questions.prompt: In triangle ABC, angles B and C are 52° and 68°. D lies on BC, and angle BAD is twice angle DAC. What is angle ADC in degrees?
questions.hint: Find the whole angle A, split it into three equal parts, then choose the small triangle using C.

lessons.headline: Undo a replacement or removal
lessons.intro: Replacing a reading keeps the number of entries fixed. Removing a reading changes both total and count. Work with the before and after totals to see exactly what changed.
lessons.bridge: During the overlapping-readings puzzle, watch the film recover the group totals before removing a duplicate. Track the number of observations as carefully as their values.
lessons.recap: Write a before line and an after line for both count and total. A large change to one item can make only a small change to the mean.

example.prompt: Five lengths average 12 cm. A length of 8 cm is replaced by one of 18 cm. What is the new mean?
steps: The replacement adds 10 cm to the total and the count stays five.
The mean rises by 10 ÷ 5 = 2 cm, to 14 cm.

lessons.videoTitle: Averages, weighted means and simple distributions

questions.title: Correct a digit
questions.prompt: Ten scores average 31. A recorded 16 should have been 26. What is the corrected mean?
questions.hint: Only the difference should be added.

questions.title: Drop the shortest
questions.prompt: Six sticks average 9 cm. Remove a 4 cm stick. What is the mean length in cm of the remaining sticks?
questions.hint: The denominator becomes five.

questions.title: Which score vanished?
questions.prompt: A dataset of 12 scores has mean 18. Removing one score raises the mean of the others to 19. Which score was removed?
questions.hint: Compare the two totals.

questions.title: Swap between crews
questions.prompt: A crew of four has mean age 14. Another crew of six has mean age 19. They exchange one member each. Both crews now have the same mean. How many years older was the member moving into the crew of four than the one leaving it?
questions.hint: The combined mean stays fixed during the swap.

lessons.headline: Keep all surviving arrangements
lessons.intro: Some puzzles have more than one valid arrangement. Cross out a candidate only when you can name the clue it breaks. Count every surviving arrangement if the question asks how many.
lessons.bridge: During the painting arrangement, note the difference between a position that works temporarily and an order that satisfies every clue at once.
lessons.recap: A single working arrangement shows possibility. A complete count needs every surviving arrangement exactly once.

example.prompt: A, B and C fill three slots. A must be first. How many complete orders fit?
steps: After A is fixed, B and C may appear in either order.
ABC and ACB are the two possibilities, so the answer is 2.

questions.title: A short screening schedule
questions.prompt: Four distinct films named Pia, Quin, Rae and Tia fill four successive slots. Quin immediately follows Pia. Rae is later than Quin. How many complete schedules are possible?
questions.hint: Treat the consecutive pair as one item when listing orders.

questions.title: The timetable window
questions.prompt: Three talks Rae, Tia and Uma start at different whole hours from 8 through 11 inclusive. Tia is two hours after Rae; Uma is strictly between them. How many schedules are possible?
questions.hint: List possible start times of the first talk only.

questions.title: Who stands in the middle?
questions.prompt: Mo, Nia and Oli stand in three places. Mo is next to both other people and Oli stands to the left of Mo. Who is on the right?
questions.hint: Only the middle place has two neighbours.

questions.title: Place the end pieces
questions.prompt: Five distinct cards in a row read Tia, Uma, Vik, Wes and Yara in some order. Vik must be exactly in the middle. Uma immediately follows Tia. Yara is before Tia. Which position from the left must Uma occupy?
questions.hint: Can the consecutive pair straddle the occupied middle?

lessons.headline: Split the walk at a checkpoint
lessons.intro: A checkpoint divides a route into a journey to the checkpoint and a journey onward. An option before it can be paired with any option after it if there are no further restrictions.
lessons.bridge: At the film’s closed crossings, imagine counting the routes that would have passed through each one. Look for routes that would be counted in both groups.
lessons.recap: Add routes arriving by alternatives. Multiply counts on consecutive, independently chosen sections of the same route.

example.prompt: Two routes reach a fountain and there are four ways from it to the gate. How many journeys go through the fountain?
steps: For each route to the fountain, choose one of the four continuations.
The choices make 2 × 4 = 8 journeys.

questions.title: A short stop on the boardwalk
questions.prompt: A boardwalk runs only east and north along a unit grid. Starting at (0,0), a visitor must stop at (2,1) and end at (2,3). How many different walks can she take?
questions.hint: Look for the section after the stop where only one sequence of moves is possible.

questions.title: Order the two errands
questions.prompt: A rider starts at (0,0) and finishes at (4,3), using only unit steps east or north. Both (1,1) and (3,2) must be visited. How many routes are possible?
questions.hint: Decide which stop must come first and count choices on each of the three legs.

questions.title: One broken bridge
questions.prompt: A walker starts at (0,0), finishes at (5,4) and uses only unit steps right or up. Only the horizontal edge joining (1,1) to (2,1) is closed. How many routes remain?
questions.hint: The ends of the bridge can still be visited using other edges.

questions.title: An authorised river crossing
questions.prompt: A robot travels from (0,0) to (4,2) in unit east or north moves. Its step from x = 1 to x = 2 must be taken at height y = 0 or y = 2. How many full routes use an authorised crossing?
questions.hint: A route crosses from x = 1 to x = 2 exactly once. Count each of the two bridge heights separately.

lessons.headline: Track the carry as a second clue
lessons.intro: Column addition has two outputs. The last digit goes into the answer and a possible carry enters the next column. A letter that appears in both columns must satisfy both jobs.
lessons.bridge: The film adds a number ending in five to itself. Pause at the units column. The written units digit and the carry do two different jobs.
lessons.recap: Confirm the completed addition with ordinary numbers. Check leading digits and every “different digits” rule.

example.prompt: Two copies of the digit 8 are added. What is written in the units column and what carries?
steps: Eight plus eight equals 16.
Write 6 in the units and carry 1 to the tens. Those two numbers cannot be interchanged.

questions.title: A single carry
questions.prompt: In the units column A + A ends in 4 and carries 1. What digit is A?
questions.hint: Include the carry in the full sum.

questions.title: Which carry?
questions.prompt: A two-digit number ending in 8 is doubled. What digit appears in the tens column of the result when the original tens digit is 4?
questions.hint: Do not lose the carry from doubling 8.

questions.title: Two letters, one total
questions.prompt: In the addition 3A + 3A = 7B, the letters are different digits and B = 2. What is A? Here 3A and 7B are two-digit numbers.
questions.hint: Use the tens digit to decide whether a carry occurred.

questions.title: Leading digit forced
questions.prompt: AB is a two-digit number and BA its two-digit reversal, with A and B different. AB + BA = 121. What is the smallest possible AB?
questions.hint: The total equals 11 times the digit sum. Minimise the leading digit next.

lessons.headline: Infer a worker from two teams
lessons.intro: Sometimes a job tells you the time for teams but keeps an individual's rate hidden. Write the amount each team completes in the same time and compare.
lessons.bridge: In the film's batch of boxes, compare two individual rates with their combined rate. Hold on to that relationship when the practice gives you only the teams' rates.
lessons.recap: When comparing team rates, cancel only the shared workers. Test a recovered rate against every team mentioned.

example.prompt: Lee and Jo pack 15 boxes per minute together. Lee packs 6. How many does Jo pack per minute?
steps: The team's 15 boxes include Lee's six.
Jo contributes the other 9 each minute.

questions.title: Remove one worker
questions.prompt: A and B sort 19 books per minute together. B sorts 8 per minute. How many does A sort per minute?
questions.hint: Subtract B's share of one minute's work.

questions.title: Compare two teams
questions.prompt: A and B make 16 badges per minute. A and C make 21. How many more badges per minute does C make than B?
questions.hint: What contribution cancels?

questions.title: Three pairs
questions.prompt: A and B make 11 tags per minute, A and C make 13, and B and C make 16. How many tags per minute do all three make together?
questions.hint: Count how often each person occurs across the three teams.

questions.title: Minutes for the third worker
questions.prompt: Two teams A+B and A+C can each finish a job alone in 6 hours, while B+C can finish it in 4 hours. How many hours does A alone take to finish it?
questions.hint: The first two team rates show B and C have equal rates.

lessons.headline: Follow the position, not the label
lessons.intro: A shuffle moves a token even if the names of its positions stay fixed. Follow one token through the rule until its position returns. Different tokens may have different cycle lengths.
lessons.bridge: When the film combines two turning dials, record their positions together. See why one dial returning alone does not reset the whole display.
lessons.recap: Distinguish the travelling object from the fixed labels. When the question asks about the full arrangement, combine the cycles of all the objects involved.

example.prompt: Three boxes are labelled 1, 2 and 3. On every move their contents shift 1 → 2, 2 → 3 and 3 → 1. A bead starts in box 2. Where is it after 5 moves?
steps: Tracing the bead gives boxes 2,3,1,2 at moves 0 to 3.
Two moves beyond a complete three-move cycle take the bead from 2 to 1.

questions.title: Three-position shuffle
questions.prompt: A shuffle moves contents A → C, C → B and B → A. A coin starts in A. In which position is it after 10 shuffles? Answer A, B or C.
questions.hint: Trace one cycle from A.

questions.title: Reconstruct the start
questions.prompt: Boxes 1 through 5 form a loop. A token advances two boxes per move and is in box 4 after seven moves. Which box did it start in?
questions.hint: Undo the total advance modulo five.

questions.title: Two disjoint shuffles
questions.prompt: One shuffle cycles the contents of positions A,B,C in that order and swaps D and E. All five tokens are different. After how many positive shuffles is the complete arrangement first restored?
questions.hint: One cycle length applies to A–C and another to D,E.

questions.title: A coloured exception
questions.prompt: Eight seats form a ring. Starting at seat 1 the colours around the ring are red, blue, red, green, red, blue, red, green. All counters move one seat clockwise together. What is the least positive number of moves that restores the colour pattern?
questions.hint: Equal colours may exchange seats without changing the pattern.

lessons.headline: Find the crossover between two plans
lessons.intro: Two cost tables may have different starting charges and different costs per visit. Track both when comparing the plans. Whole-number visits can put the change of advantage between two rows.
lessons.bridge: For the two visit plans, pause at the point where the costs match. Check the next whole visit to establish which plan actually becomes cheaper.
lessons.recap: If the question asks for the first cheaper visit, check the row on each side of equality. A tie has no cheaper plan.

example.prompt: Plan A costs 4 dollars plus 3 per visit. Plan B costs 10 plus 1 per visit. At how many visits do their costs match?
steps: B starts 6 dollars higher but A gains 2 dollars on B each visit.
After three visits both cost 13 dollars. The next visit makes B cheaper.

figure.alt: Cost table for zero through four visits. Plan A costs $4, $7, $10, $13, $16. Plan B costs $10, $11, $12, $13, $14.

questions.title: First row
questions.prompt: A pass costs 8 dollars plus 2 per trip. What is shown in the cost row for five trips, in dollars?
questions.hint: Include the charge at zero trips.

questions.title: Equality or cheaper?
questions.prompt: A charges 3 dollars per game. B charges 9 dollars plus 2 per game. At what whole number of games is B first strictly cheaper?
questions.hint: Find the tie, then test the next row.

questions.title: Read the rule
questions.prompt: Two tables use a constant price per visit plus a possible starting fee. At 2 and 5 visits X costs 14 and 26 dollars; Y costs 20 and 26. What is the cost difference at 9 visits, in dollars?
questions.hint: Find the cost increase per visit in each table.

questions.title: A capped fare
questions.prompt: A ferry charges 5 dollars per trip, capped at 28 dollars for the week. Another pass costs 10 dollars plus 2 a trip with no cap. At what whole number of trips does the capped ferry first become strictly cheaper again after it has been more expensive?
questions.hint: Start by checking when the cap is reached.

lessons.headline: Reassemble overlapping descriptions
lessons.intro: A part may be named as a fraction of the original whole or as a fraction of something already selected. Sketch one bar and label each bracket with its own whole.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film's two classes take chalk. Keep a finger on the collection a fraction refers to before deciding whether to multiply it by the original number or the remainder.
lessons.recap: Read your calculation aloud with the word “of”. Each fraction should name the collection that comes immediately after it.

example.prompt: Three quarters of 20 cards have pictures. One fifth of the picture cards show a tree. How many show a tree?
steps: There are 15 picture cards.
One fifth of those 15 gives 3 tree cards.

lessons.videoTitle: Parts and wholes, including remaining fractions

questions.title: In the top drawer
questions.prompt: Two thirds of 45 tickets are in a drawer. Of those in the drawer, one fifth are red. How many red tickets are in the drawer?
questions.hint: Select the drawer tickets before selecting red ones.

questions.title: Outside the marked part
questions.prompt: Three fifths of a garden is planted. Half the planted area is beans. What fraction of the whole garden is planted with something other than beans?
questions.hint: Only planted land can qualify.

questions.title: Find the missing tray
questions.prompt: Of all the pastries, 3/8 are on a large tray. A small tray holds one fifth of the remainder. The other 30 pastries are in boxes. How many pastries are there altogether?
questions.hint: Find the fraction packed in boxes.

questions.title: Matching leftovers
questions.prompt: A first tank starts with 36 litres and loses a quarter. A second tank loses two fifths of its starting amount and ends with the same amount as the first. How many litres did the second start with?
questions.hint: Find the shared final amount.

lessons.headline: Undo repeated rules without guessing
lessons.intro: When a machine repeats a rule, undo one complete round before undoing another. A short reverse table keeps track of which values sit between rounds.
lessons.bridge: The final machine in the film combines several moves. Trace its arrows backwards one at a time, just as you will trace repeated scoring rounds.
lessons.recap: Write the intermediate value after each undoing. It should reproduce the next value in one forward step.

example.prompt: A score doubles and then gains 1 each round. It ends on 15 after two rounds. What was its starting value?
steps: Undo the most recent round: (15 − 1) ÷ 2 = 7.
Undo the first round: (7 − 1) ÷ 2 = 3.

questions.title: Before the second doubling
questions.prompt: A score doubles each round. After three rounds it is 56. What was the starting score?
questions.hint: Divide by 2 once for each round.

questions.title: Fee on each day
questions.prompt: A savings jar doubles its contents and then loses $2 each day. After one day it holds $20. What was the opening amount in dollars?
questions.hint: Return the fee before halving.

questions.title: Undo three turns
questions.prompt: Each turn a game doubles a score and adds 3. After three turns the score is 61. What was the initial score?
questions.hint: Apply the inverse rule three times.

questions.title: Two possible orders
questions.prompt: A machine uses doubling and adding 5 exactly once each, in an unknown order. A positive whole-number input produces 27. What was the input?
questions.hint: Try reversing the two orders and test whole-number inputs.

lessons.headline: Choose the first point of difference
lessons.intro: For a complicated list, let the first unusual event decide the case. Every allowed outcome then has one clear home even when a later position also looks unusual.
lessons.bridge: In the exhibit puzzle, follow where a particular exhibit sits. Notice how its position is a feature that each complete arrangement can have only once.
lessons.recap: When a condition can be satisfied several times, classify by its first occurrence to avoid counting the same outcome in several cases.

example.prompt: A three-letter code uses X or Y and contains Y. How many codes have their first Y in position two?
steps: The first letter must be X and the second must be Y.
The last letter is free, giving XYX and XYY.

questions.title: First tail
questions.prompt: Four coin tosses give H or T. How many strings have their first T on toss three?
questions.hint: Write the fixed prefix.

questions.title: Two turning points
questions.prompt: A four-symbol signal uses 0 or 1. How many signals change value exactly twice between neighbouring positions?
questions.hint: Choose the starting value and the two boundaries where it changes.

questions.title: First missed target
questions.prompt: A six-shot record uses H for hit and M for miss. How many records have exactly two misses with the first miss among the first two shots?
questions.hint: Count by whether the first miss is shot one or shot two.

questions.title: Break in the fence
questions.prompt: Six fence panels in a line are each black or white. Exactly three are black. How many patterns have the first black panel immediately followed by a white panel?
questions.hint: Fix where the first black lies and choose the two later black panels.

lessons.headline: Several columns share one ink supply
lessons.intro: A complete set of fixed-width codes treats all positions alike because a leading zero is printed. Ordinary page numbers drop those zeros. Decide which labels the printer actually makes.
lessons.bridge: Watch how the film counts fours without writing hundreds of labels. Why can complete blocks be handled together while the unfinished block needs its own check?
lessons.recap: Use symmetry only when the label rules treat places the same way. Account explicitly for any suppressed leading zeros.

example.prompt: A timer prints 00 to 09. How often does it print 0?
steps: Every tens position prints 0, contributing ten copies.
The units position also prints 0 in 00, so the answer is 11.

lessons.videoTitle: Digit sums and counting digits in ranges

questions.title: Fixed-width zero
questions.prompt: A machine prints the codes 00 through 99. How many zeros does it print?
questions.hint: Count one column over a complete hundred codes.

questions.title: Pages instead of codes
questions.prompt: A booklet prints the ordinary page numbers 1 through 99. How many printed zeros appear?
questions.hint: There are no leading zeros.

questions.title: Page one hundred and fifty
questions.prompt: How many copies of zero are needed to print the ordinary labels 1 through 150?
questions.hint: Count units zeros and tens zeros.

questions.title: A covered drum
questions.prompt: A three-drum display cycles once through every code from 000 through 999. The middle drum is covered. Across all the visible two-digit readings, how many copies of 7 appear?
questions.hint: How many full codes have a 7 in a fixed visible place?

lessons.headline: Use a boundary to shorten the list
lessons.intro: Sometimes a condition makes most rows impossible. Put the variables in order and use the total to bound the first one before doing any detailed counting.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film fill its labelled boxes. For a fixed first box, try the smallest and largest possible completions before listing the middle choices.
lessons.recap: Try the smallest or largest possible completion. If even that misses the target, discard the entire row.

example.prompt: Three different positive numbers sum to 9. How large could the smallest be?
steps: If the smallest were 3, the least possible total would be 3 + 4 + 5 = 12.
A smallest value of 2 works, since 2 + 3 + 4 = 9. The largest possible smallest value is 2.

questions.title: Strictly increasing
questions.prompt: Three positive integers are in strictly increasing order and sum to 11. What is the largest possible first integer?
questions.hint: Check the three smallest possible numbers for each starting value.

questions.title: Triangle check
questions.prompt: How many different triangles with whole-number sides have perimeter 10? A different ordering of the same sides is the same triangle.
questions.hint: Order the sides and check that the two shorter sides together exceed the longest.

questions.title: Ticket values
questions.prompt: A ticket bundle costs exactly 29 dollars. Its tickets cost 3 or 5 dollars each. How many different pairs of ticket counts are possible? Either count may be zero.
questions.hint: Try the number of 5-dollar tickets from 0 to 5.

questions.title: Weather readings
questions.prompt: Four different whole temperatures from 0 to 8 degrees have a mean of 3 degrees. How many unordered sets could they form?
questions.hint: First convert the mean into the total. Group by the lowest temperature.

lessons.headline: Use what the clue tells you
lessons.intro: A clue removes some outcomes before you calculate. Keep only the outcomes compatible with that clue. Then compare the successful outcomes with this smaller set.
lessons.bridge: At the two spinners, watch how the outcome table gives a place to each ordered pair. Imagine crossing out cells incompatible with an extra clue.
lessons.recap: State the remaining sample space after the clue. Make sure the clue describes an event, not a different experiment.

example.prompt: A fair die has shown an odd number. What is the probability it showed 5?
steps: Only 1, 3 and 5 remain possible. They were equally likely before the clue.
One of those three results is 5, giving probability 1/3.

questions.title: Above three
questions.prompt: A fair die is known to show a number above 3. What is the probability it shows an even number? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: List the possible results after this information.

questions.title: At least one tail
questions.prompt: Two fair coins were tossed. You are told at least one showed tails. What is the probability both showed tails? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Only HH is excluded.

questions.title: Known sum
questions.prompt: Two fair six-sided dice have a total of 8. What is the probability that at least one die shows 3? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Use ordered pairs satisfying the total.

questions.title: The inspected pair
questions.prompt: Two different badges are selected uniformly from badges numbered 1 to 7. The inspector reports that their sum is even. What is the probability both badges are odd? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: An even sum requires matching parities.

lessons.headline: Find a quantity that keeps its parity
lessons.intro: Some moves change a number but preserve whether it is odd or even. Trace that property through one legal move before trying long move sequences.
lessons.bridge: Notice every move the film's counter can make from thirteen. What information about its position survives even when you forget the exact number?
