lessons.recap: State the starting parity, the effect of each allowed move and the target parity. Matching parity alone does not construct a route.

example.prompt: A counter starts at 5 and may add 4 or subtract 2. Can it ever reach 12?
steps: Both moves change its position by an even amount.
Every reachable position is odd, while 12 is even. Reaching 12 is impossible.

questions.title: A mixed sum
questions.prompt: Is the sum of 17 and 26 odd or even? Enter odd or even.
questions.hint: Look only at the parity of each addend.

questions.title: Jump by two sizes
questions.prompt: An integer starts at 14. Each move adds 6 or subtracts 4. Can it reach 21? Enter yes or no.
questions.hint: What do both changes have in common?

questions.title: Odd cards paired
questions.prompt: A bag contains 9 odd-numbered cards and 8 even-numbered cards. Cards are put into disjoint pairs so that every paired sum is even. What is the fewest number of cards left unpaired?
questions.hint: An even sum needs like parities.

questions.title: Turning two coins
questions.prompt: Thirteen coins begin tails up. A move turns exactly two distinct coins over. What is the greatest number of heads that can be showing after any number of moves?
questions.hint: How can a move change the count of heads?

lessons.headline: Two totals can describe changing ages
lessons.intro: Time adds the same number of years to each person. Differences stay fixed while sums grow by the number of people times the years elapsed.
lessons.bridge: In the film's opening sum-and-gap puzzle, use the difference to find a pair that fits the total. In an age problem, that same difference survives the passing of time.
lessons.recap: Put a time label beside each age. Check ratios at the date named in the question.

example.prompt: Two sisters are 12 and 8. What will their age difference be in five years?
steps: Both gain five years, becoming 17 and 13.
Their difference is still 4 years.

questions.title: A constant gap
questions.prompt: A child is 11 and a sibling is 6. How much older in years will the older child be in 8 years?
questions.hint: Both ages change equally.

questions.title: Today's two ages
questions.prompt: Two cousins' ages total 34 and differ by 8. How old is the younger cousin?
questions.hint: Remove the age difference, then split.

questions.title: Years from now
questions.prompt: A parent is 38 and a child is 8. In how many years will the parent be three times the child's age?
questions.hint: Add the same unknown number of years to both ages.

questions.title: Recover a past pair
questions.prompt: The present ages of two people total 54. Six years ago the older person was twice the younger person's age. What is the older person's present age?
questions.hint: What was the total six years ago?

lessons.headline: Put the boundaries into the count
lessons.intro: A regular list may start inside an interval. Count all multiples through the upper endpoint, then remove those lying before the lower endpoint. The same subtraction works on overlaps.
lessons.bridge: In the film’s final intervals of integers, look at which endpoint is included. Also locate the first common multiple in each pair of excluded lists.
lessons.recap: At a lower endpoint L, remove through L − 1. Recheck the endpoints when an overlapping list is involved.

example.prompt: How many multiples of 4 lie from 9 to 24 inclusive?
steps: There are 6 multiples up to 24. Two lie below 9: 4 and 8.
So 6 − 2 = 4 multiples lie in the interval.

questions.title: On the shelf
questions.prompt: From 21 to 51 inclusive, how many labels are multiples of 7?
questions.hint: Find the first and the last multiple.

questions.title: Clean labels
questions.prompt: From 30 to 50 inclusive, how many labels are divisible by neither 3 nor 4?
questions.hint: There are 21 labels including both ends.

questions.title: One detour
questions.prompt: A calendar marks every fifth day for inspection and every eighth day for cleaning. Between days 31 and 80 inclusive, how many days have exactly one mark?
questions.hint: Check both common multiples inside the interval.

questions.title: Numbered badges
questions.prompt: From the two-digit integers, discard every multiple of 6 and every number ending in 6. How many badges remain?
questions.hint: List the two-digit multiples of 6 that end in 6.

lessons.headline: Locate a palindrome by its prefix
lessons.intro: The leading half of a palindrome fixes the other half. To find a neighbour or a range, compare the first possible reflected prefix with the actual boundary.
lessons.bridge: The film studies the mirrored number 3663 before counting longer palindromes. Look for the independent choices hidden inside the mirrored notation.
lessons.recap: For a strict boundary, even an exact match must be skipped. Reflect the next or previous prefix as needed.

example.prompt: What is the least four-digit palindrome greater than 4388?
steps: Reflecting 43 gives 4334, which is too small.
The next prefix 44 gives 4444. No prefix between 43 and 44 exists.

questions.title: Mirror the prefix
questions.prompt: What four-digit palindrome begins with 37?
questions.hint: Reflect both leading digits.

questions.title: Strictly after the mirror
questions.prompt: What is the smallest four-digit palindrome strictly greater than 5665?
questions.hint: The boundary is already a palindrome.

questions.title: Count between gates
questions.prompt: How many four-digit palindromes lie strictly between 2112 and 2662?
questions.hint: Use the first two digits as an ordered index.

questions.title: A different distance at the turn
questions.prompt: What is the gap in value between the greatest four-digit palindrome below 3000 and the least four-digit palindrome above 3000?
questions.hint: Check the two prefixes around the boundary.

lessons.headline: Read an operating cycle
lessons.intro: A timer might include active time and idle time. Sketch one complete cycle, label when output happens, then place the stopping time exactly.
lessons.bridge: Watch both flashing signals in the film and locate the end of one full repeat. A machine that alternates between working and resting also has a cycle you can mark.
lessons.recap: For a partial final cycle, count what occurs before the stated finishing instant. A scheduled rest contributes time but no output.

example.prompt: A nozzle sprays for 2 seconds, then rests for 3 seconds. How many seconds does it spray in the first 10 seconds if it starts by spraying?
steps: A complete cycle lasts 5 seconds.
Two full cycles contain 2 + 2 = 4 seconds of spraying.

questions.title: On duty
questions.prompt: A lamp stays lit 4 seconds and dark 2 seconds repeatedly. Starting as it turns on, how many seconds is it lit in the next 30 seconds?
questions.hint: Count complete cycles.

questions.title: Three bursts
questions.prompt: A cutter makes 6 pieces in a 10-second burst and then rests 5 seconds. It starts cutting immediately. How many seconds pass from the first start until the third burst ends?
questions.hint: How many rests are needed before three bursts finish?

questions.title: Last short run
questions.prompt: A pump runs for 3 minutes at 5 litres per minute, then rests for 2 minutes. Starting at the beginning of a run, how many litres does it deliver in 12 minutes?
questions.hint: Separate complete cycles and the start of the next.

questions.title: Which signal first?
questions.prompt: One signal flashes every 9 seconds starting at time 0. A second flashes every 12 seconds starting at time 3. At what positive time in seconds do they first flash together?
questions.hint: List multiples of 9 and compare with 3, 15, 27, …

lessons.headline: Remember how a route ended
lessons.intro: A new restriction may make the landing alone insufficient. Keep different counts for routes with different possible next moves, such as routes ending in a long move and routes ending in a short move.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film’s blocked rung remove a possible previous landing. Then ask what extra information a path count would need if an entire kind of move were restricted.
lessons.recap: Store exactly the piece of history that changes the legal next choices. Keep your ending categories disjoint before adding them.

example.prompt: Build three-letter strings from A and B without consecutive Bs. How many are possible?
steps: Strings ending in A come from any legal two-letter string: AA, AB or BA. That gives 3.
Strings ending in B come from AA or BA, the two legal strings ending in A. Together there are 5.

questions.title: Two lights in a row
questions.prompt: Four lamps are on or off. How many settings have no neighbouring lamps on?
questions.hint: Split settings by the last lamp.

questions.title: One more restriction
questions.prompt: A word of length 4 uses X and Y, cannot contain YY, and must end in Y. How many words are possible?
questions.hint: The penultimate letter is forced.

questions.title: No successive doubles
questions.prompt: A frog reaches 6 by forward hops of length 1 or 2. Two length-2 hops may not be consecutive. How many hop sequences work?
questions.hint: Count by the number of length-2 hops, separating them with 1s.

questions.title: Beacon strings
questions.prompt: Five beacons in a row can be red, blue or white. Blue and red are both bright. No two bright beacons may be adjacent. How many signals are possible?
questions.hint: Let the final beacon be white, or let it be bright with a forced white before it.

lessons.headline: Make each case stand for one outcome
lessons.intro: If a problem asks about unordered pairs or shapes, swapping their labels may leave the same outcome. Choose a fixed convention before counting.
lessons.bridge: Follow the film’s rectangle search with the smaller side listed first. Notice how that convention keeps the same rectangle from appearing twice.
lessons.recap: Give each possibility one representative, prove that you considered them all and check the original conditions.

example.prompt: Two positive numbers add to 7. Counting reversed pairs once, how many pairs are there?
steps: Use the smaller number first. It can be 1, 2 or 3.
The resulting pairs are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4). The larger partner is fixed each time.

lessons.videoTitle: Proving all cases and unique solutions

questions.title: Pairs from six counters
questions.prompt: Six counters are numbered 1 through 6. Choose two different counters whose numbers add to a multiple of 3. How many unordered pairs work?
questions.hint: Organise the pairs by remainders when divided by 3.

questions.title: An odd counterexample
questions.prompt: A sign claims that every integer from 1 through 14 is the sum of two even integers. How many integers in that interval disprove the claim?
questions.hint: What parity must every sum of two even numbers have?

questions.title: Find every remainder case
questions.prompt: How many positive integers below 22 leave remainder 2 on division by 3?
questions.hint: Write the first and last valid integers, then step by three.

questions.title: Choose the archive shelves
questions.prompt: A librarian selects three different shelves numbered 1 through 7. Their numbers must total 12, and their product must be divisible by 4. How many different sets of shelves can she select?
questions.hint: List the possible increasing triples summing to 12 before checking products.

lessons.headline: Distinguish crossing a seam from touching it
lessons.intro: A seam splits a board into two sections. If tiles may not cross it, those sections can be tiled independently. If a tile must cross, look at what placement the crossing forces.
lessons.bridge: As the film marks upright dominoes, sketch where a horizontal pair can cross a line between columns. What would forbid that crossing?
lessons.recap: For a “must cross” condition, subtract seam-respecting tilings from all tilings or fix the crossing pieces directly.

example.prompt: Two pieces of strip have 2 possible tilings and 3 possible tilings. How many tilings respect the seam?
steps: Any tiling of the first strip can be paired with any tiling of the other.
That gives 2 × 3 = 6 combined tilings.

lessons.videoTitle: Tiling a strip with forced domino pairs

questions.title: A pencil line between columns
questions.prompt: A domino tiling fills a 2-by-6 board. One horizontal domino crosses the vertical line after column 3 in the top row. How many dominoes in total must cross this line?
questions.hint: The cells on the left of the line must be covered either in pairs entirely on the left or by crossing pieces.

questions.title: A second unsplit line
questions.prompt: A 2-by-5 board is tiled with dominoes. No piece may cross either vertical line after columns 1 and 3. How many complete tilings respect both lines?
questions.hint: What are the widths of the independent strips?

questions.title: The odd room
questions.prompt: A domino-tiled floor is 3 cells high and 4 cells wide. A vertical line separates its leftmost column from the other three columns. How many different values can the number of dominoes crossing this line take?
questions.hint: The three cells in the leftmost column must be accounted for. Try both possible odd crossing counts.

questions.title: Only one join may disappear
questions.prompt: Two lines on a 2-by-6 board lie after columns 2 and 3. A line disappears if at least one domino crosses it. How many tilings make exactly one of these two lines disappear?
questions.hint: Can crossing blocks cover both adjacent lines at once?

lessons.headline: Find the first positive shared return
lessons.intro: A return problem asks when cycles return together. Write the time of their shared start as zero and look for the least positive common multiple. A later question might ask for a different shared return.
lessons.bridge: Mark the coinciding restarts in the film's first example. Decide whether zero is a valid answer when the question asks for the next shared restart.
lessons.recap: Distinguish the start, the first return and the number of shared instants in a closed interval.

example.prompt: Two lights flash together now and repeat every 4 and 6 seconds. When is the second shared flash after now?
steps: The least common multiple is 12, so they meet every 12 seconds.
The first positive shared flash is at 12 and the second at 24 seconds.

questions.title: Third return
questions.prompt: Two drums strike every 6 and 9 seconds, starting together. At what time in seconds is their third shared strike after the start?
questions.hint: Find one shared interval.

questions.title: Three clocks
questions.prompt: Three devices tick every 4, 6 and 10 seconds and tick together now. How many seconds until all three next tick together?
questions.hint: Find a common multiple of all three intervals.

questions.title: Within two minutes
questions.prompt: Lights flash together at time zero, then individually every 8 and 12 seconds. How many simultaneous flashes occur from 0 through 120 seconds inclusive?
questions.hint: Does time zero count here?

questions.title: Shifted calendar
questions.prompt: Two stalls are both open on day 5. From then one opens every 6 days and one every 8. What is the number of the first day after day 50 on which both open?
questions.hint: Measure time from day 5, not from day zero.

lessons.headline: Count a shared boundary
lessons.intro: Adding perimeters treats a common edge as part of both pieces. At the outer boundary it occurs just once. Identify which edges are counted once and which twice.
lessons.bridge: The handshake example counts one meeting from both ends. Watch for the same double report in the tournament before applying the idea to two tiles sharing an edge.
lessons.recap: Convert piece counts into boundary counts by subtracting two reports for each shared full edge. Holes also have boundary edges.

example.prompt: Two unit squares touch along a full edge. How many unit edges lie on the outside?
steps: Adding both perimeters gives 8 edge reports.
Their common edge is reported twice and lies inside. Subtract 2 to get 6 outside edges.

questions.title: Tile chain
questions.prompt: Five unit squares make a straight strip. How many unit edges are on its outside?
questions.hint: There are four shared full edges.

questions.title: Hidden joins
questions.prompt: Eight unit squares make a connected shape with a boundary of 14 unit edges, including any edges around holes. How many full edges are shared by two squares?
questions.hint: Compare the boundary with eight separate perimeters.

questions.title: Three-dimensional joins
questions.prompt: A solid is built from six unit cubes. Exactly six pairs of cube faces are glued together. How many unit faces are exposed?
questions.hint: Each join hides two faces.

questions.title: Tiled ring
questions.prompt: A 5 by 5 square of unit tiles loses its centre tile. How many full edges are now shared by pairs of remaining tiles?
questions.hint: Either remove joins from the whole square or count from the exposed boundary.

lessons.headline: Recover an unseen stack
lessons.intro: A plan can reveal most heights but leave one hidden. The total number of cubes gives an equation for the missing stack, even when its outline is hard to draw.
lessons.bridge: In the film, a vertical removal and a tunnel share a cube. Watch how counting that location once recovers the correct number left.
lessons.recap: Use the total to recover missing heights, then test that the completed plan satisfies the visible views.

example.prompt: A model contains 11 cubes. Its four solid stacks are 2, 3, 1 and an unknown height. Find that height.
steps: The three visible heights use 6 cubes.
The fourth stack holds 11 − 6 = 5.

questions.title: Read the missing column from the shadow
questions.prompt: Three nonempty stacks lie along a sightline. The first two are 2 and 3 cubes high. Viewed along the line, the silhouette is 5 cubes high. What must be the height of the third stack?
questions.hint: At least one stack must reach the top of the silhouette.

questions.title: Move without changing the total
questions.prompt: Two towers together use 16 cubes. Moving two cubes from the first to the second makes the towers equal. How many cubes did the taller tower contain before the move?
questions.hint: Reverse the transfer from the equal final heights.

questions.title: Subtract two level counts
questions.prompt: A model consists of vertical stacks of unit cubes. Its second layer contains 7 cubes and its third layer contains 4. How many stacks have height exactly 2?
questions.hint: Compare the stacks reaching level 2 with the subset reaching level 3.

questions.title: The missing delivery column
questions.prompt: Four nonempty stacks A, B, C and D contain 18 boxes altogether. A and B together contain 9. B and C together contain 8. D has one box more than C. How many boxes are in B?
questions.hint: Use the total to find C + D, then separate their two heights.

lessons.headline: Choose the tightest position first
lessons.intro: A restriction on size, parity or order may determine one digit more tightly than the others. Split into its cases first, then fill the remaining places.
lessons.bridge: In the film's even-number puzzle, group the possibilities by their last digit. Test what happens to the first-place choices in the group that ends in zero.
lessons.recap: Ensure your cases are mutually exclusive. A number ends in exactly one digit, making its last digit a reliable way to split cases.

example.prompt: Using different cards 0, 3 and 4, how many three-digit even numbers can you make?
steps: For a last digit 0, both 340 and 430 work.
For a last digit 4, only 304 works. The total is 3.

questions.title: An even last place
questions.prompt: Make a two-digit number from different digits 1, 2, 3 or 5. How many are even?
questions.hint: Fix the final digit.

questions.title: Inside an interval
questions.prompt: A three-digit number uses different cards from 0, 1, 3 or 5. How many such numbers lie strictly between 200 and 500?
questions.hint: Which hundreds digit is possible?

questions.title: Increasing digits
questions.prompt: Form a three-digit number using three different cards from 0, 1, 2, 5 or 7. How many have digits strictly increasing from left to right?
questions.hint: Can a number written in increasing order use zero?

questions.title: Divisible suffixes
questions.prompt: Use three different cards from 0, 1, 2 or 4 to make an ordinary three-digit number divisible by 4. How many numbers are possible?
questions.hint: List allowable final pairs, including a zero in the tens place.

lessons.headline: Pair terms equally far from the ends
lessons.intro: When each term changes by the same amount, moving one term inwards from each end preserves their sum. Pairing lets you total a long sequence without adding every entry.
lessons.bridge: In the row-of-seats problem, compare an outside pair with the next pair moving inwards. Watch how the unchanged pair sum shortens the total.
lessons.recap: Count the terms before pairing. In an odd-length list the middle term is half the outside pair’s sum.

steps: The outside pair sums to 22 and the next pair also sums to 22.
There is a middle term of 11 left over. The total is 55.

questions.title: Festival benches
questions.prompt: Benches seat 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 and 18 people. What is their total capacity?
questions.hint: Pair the seats on the shortest and longest benches.

questions.title: Odd length
questions.prompt: What is the sum of every odd integer from 11 through 29 inclusive?
questions.hint: Count terms, not the difference between the endpoints.

questions.title: Inside the interval
questions.prompt: A lamp flashes at seconds 4, 11, 18 and every 7 seconds afterwards. Add the flash times from second 20 through second 60 inclusive. What is the sum?
questions.hint: Find the first and last flash actually inside the interval.

questions.title: One row missing
questions.prompt: A staircase of 12 rows starts with 5 tiles and adds 3 per row. All rows except one contain 238 tiles altogether. Which row was removed?
questions.hint: Find the complete total to recover the missing row length.

lessons.headline: Mark a bound on each position
lessons.intro: “Exactly two places after” and “somewhere after” give different legal intervals. Write the place numbers so that gaps cannot disappear when you reason.
lessons.bridge: Watch where the film tests a two-place gap in an ordered list. Which potential start causes the other end to run out of room?
lessons.recap: Write each possible start of a gap or block, and rule out positions that would fall beyond the ends.

example.prompt: Four boxes occupy positions 1 to 4. The blue one is exactly two positions after the gold one. Which positions are possible for gold?
steps: The partner for each possible gold position is two higher.
Only starts 1 and 2 work. Starts 3 and 4 would put blue beyond the shelf.

questions.title: The timetable window
questions.prompt: Three talks Vik, Wes and Yara start at different whole hours from 9 through 12 inclusive. Wes is two hours after Vik; Yara is strictly between them. How many schedules are possible?
questions.hint: List possible start times of the first talk only.

questions.title: Two seats apart
questions.prompt: Four children sit in seats 1 to 4: Rae, Tia, Uma and Vik. Rae is exactly two seat numbers before Tia. Vik is in seat 1. Which seat number belongs to Uma?
questions.hint: Write every possible pair for the two numbered seats.

questions.title: A short screening schedule
questions.prompt: Four distinct films named Tia, Uma, Vik and Wes fill four successive slots. Uma immediately follows Tia. Vik is later than Uma. How many complete schedules are possible?
questions.hint: Treat the consecutive pair as one item when listing orders.

questions.title: Three linked bookings
questions.prompt: Six different attractions fill slots 1 to 6. Jetty is exactly two slot numbers after Fern. Mine immediately follows Jetty. Kiln is before Fern, and Oak is before Pier. How many schedules meet all four clues?
questions.hint: Determine the possible positions of Fern before placing Oak and Pier.

lessons.headline: Intersect two quick divisibility tests
lessons.intro: Some numbers can be tested from their final digits, while others can be tested from their digit sum. Apply the shorter test first and keep only candidates that satisfy the other.
lessons.bridge: The film's last-digit puzzle combines two divisibility clues. Track the candidates still possible after the first clue, then cross-check the second.
lessons.recap: After using a fast rule, verify the finished numbers against every divisor. Check whether the task needs one solution or a count.

example.prompt: Which digits can complete 31A so it is divisible by both 2 and 3?
steps: The final digit must be even. For divisibility by 3, the digit sum 4 + A must be divisible by 3.
Both 2 and 8 satisfy the clues, giving 312 and 318. The clues can allow more than one choice.

questions.title: A missing last digit
questions.prompt: How many digit choices make 51A divisible by 3?
questions.hint: The known digits sum to 6.

questions.title: Only the ending matters
questions.prompt: Which one of 735, 736 and 738 is divisible by 4? Enter the number.
questions.hint: Check only the final two digits.

questions.title: Find the largest candidate
questions.prompt: What is the largest three-digit number 7A2 divisible by both 3 and 4?
questions.hint: List the possible middle digits from the last-two-digit test.

questions.title: A delivery window
questions.prompt: Parcels can be packed in rows of 4 or 9 with none left over. The count is a three-digit number beginning with 2 and ending in 2. What is the count?
questions.hint: Use divisibility by 9 to restrict the middle digit before checking the last pair.

lessons.headline: Compare two rules on the same input
lessons.intro: When two payment or scoring rules apply to the same number of items, represent that number only once. A smaller starting fee can be overtaken by a larger charge per item.
lessons.bridge: The film writes expressions for two ticket categories using one unknown. Watch which expressions describe the same input, a useful step when two pricing rules must agree.
lessons.recap: Once you find equality, test one count on either side to see which rule wins there.

example.prompt: Rule A scores 3 per turn plus a bonus of 6. Rule B scores 5 per turn. After how many turns are they level?
steps: Rule B gains 2 more per turn. Rule A begins with a 6-point advantage.
It takes 3 turns to use up that advantage. Both rules then give 15 points.

questions.title: Which fee grows?
questions.prompt: A game starts players at 12 points and adds 5 per win. How many points follow 4 wins?
questions.hint: Count the starting score only once.

questions.title: Same fare
questions.prompt: One boat fare is $8 plus $2 per stop. Another is $2 plus $3 per stop. At how many stops do the fares match?
questions.hint: Compare the fixed charges and then the rates.

questions.title: First strict lead
questions.prompt: A runner begins 14 points ahead. On each round she scores 4 and her rival scores 7. What is the first round after which her rival leads?
questions.hint: Find when the three-point gains first exceed 14.

questions.title: Same cost, different counts
questions.prompt: Nia hires a boat for $12 plus $4 per hour. Tom hires another for $6 plus $5 per hour and uses it for one hour longer. Their bills are equal. How many hours did Nia use her boat?
questions.hint: If Nia uses h hours, Tom uses h + 1.

lessons.headline: Separate identical pieces using gaps
lessons.intro: Identical pieces have no individual labels. Arrange the distinct objects first and use their gaps to place repeated pieces. A gap at either end is usually legal unless the problem says otherwise.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film turn two neighbours into a block. Draw the gaps around the other objects as a second way to handle things that must stay apart.
lessons.recap: Count the gaps actually available, then decide whether the things going into them are distinguishable.

example.prompt: Arrange three identical dots and two different letters A and B so no dots touch. How many rows are possible?
steps: The two letters make three gaps. All three gaps must get one dot.
Only the order of the letters can change. There are 2 rows.

questions.title: Ribbon pattern
questions.prompt: Place two identical stars among four identical circles in a line. No stars touch. How many patterns are possible?
questions.hint: Four circles create five gaps.

questions.title: Inside only
questions.prompt: Four different books stand in a fixed order. Insert two identical dividers in different gaps. A divider cannot go at an end. How many choices are there?
questions.hint: Count the inner gaps only.

questions.title: An alternation
questions.prompt: Line up four different red counters and three different blue counters so neighbouring colours alternate. How many orders are possible?
questions.hint: Which colour must occupy both ends?

questions.title: Festival queue
questions.prompt: Four different adults and three different children form a queue. The children must stay apart, and at least one end must be occupied by a child. How many queues are possible?
questions.hint: From all separated-child patterns, remove those with both ends occupied by adults.

lessons.headline: Apply transformations in order
lessons.intro: After a turn, translation or reflection, the second move starts from the newly reached position. Mark the intermediate image as carefully as the final one.
lessons.bridge: Follow the point reflected across the film’s vertical mirror. On the square board, apply one reflection and then the other to the same cell.
lessons.recap: Record each image in order and verify that a reflection or turn preserved the distances it should.

example.prompt: A counter starts at 3, reflects across 0, then moves 2 places right. Where does it finish?
steps: Reflecting gives −3.
Moving right by 2 now takes the counter to −1.

questions.title: Move then reflect
questions.prompt: A counter starts at x = 5 on a number line. Move it 6 units right and then reflect it across 0. What is its final coordinate?
questions.hint: Write the intermediate position before changing sign.

questions.title: First image, second image
questions.prompt: A dot starts at (3,−2). Reflect it in the line y=x, then translate four units right and one unit up. What is the x-coordinate of its final position?
questions.hint: Reflection in y=x interchanges the two coordinates. Apply the shift to that new point.

questions.title: Two parallel mirrors
questions.prompt: On a number line a dot at 0 is reflected first across 5 and then across 7. What is its final coordinate?
questions.hint: Find the image after each reflection. It can lie on either side of the next mirror.

questions.title: Recover the starting pin
questions.prompt: A pin is turned a quarter-turn anticlockwise about the origin. It is then translated four units right and one unit up, finishing at (2,6). What is the sum of its two original coordinates?
questions.hint: Undo the translation before undoing the turn.

lessons.headline: Compare shares of different wholes
lessons.intro: The same number of objects can be a different fraction in each box. When two fractions describe equal amounts, use that equal amount to link the wholes.
lessons.bridge: The film redraws a pile after a fraction has gone. Notice that a surviving group can describe one fraction of its old whole and a different fraction of its new one.
lessons.recap: Name the amount the two expressions share. Then restore each whole separately, and use any total or difference to fix the scale.

example.prompt: Half of one bag is 6 shells. A third of another bag is also 6 shells. How many shells are in the two bags together?
steps: The first bag holds 12. The second holds 18.
The two bags therefore hold 30 shells altogether.

lessons.videoTitle: Parts and wholes, including remaining fractions

questions.title: An equal slice
questions.prompt: A quarter of jar A is 8 sweets. A third of jar B is also 8 sweets. How many more sweets are in A than in B?
questions.hint: Find both whole jars.

questions.title: Which whole is larger?
questions.prompt: Two fifths of one rope has the same length as three fifths of a 40 cm rope. What is the length of the first rope in centimetres?
questions.hint: What length do both fractions describe?

questions.title: Pages in two books
questions.prompt: One third of the pages of book A equals one quarter of the pages of book B. The books have 210 pages together. How many pages are in book B?
questions.hint: Call the equal number of pages one share.

questions.title: Ribbons after cutting
questions.prompt: A blue and a gold ribbon measure 90 cm together. After one third of the blue and one sixth of the gold are cut off, the two remaining lengths match. How long was the blue ribbon at first, in centimetres?
questions.hint: Write the equality for the fractions that remain.

lessons.headline: Carry a symbol’s value between lines
lessons.intro: The same symbol has the same value wherever it appears. Two equations can together reveal a value that neither equation gives alone.
lessons.bridge: When the film uses a cell in two different magic lines, follow the same value through both equations. This is the same test for a repeated symbol.
lessons.recap: Subtract equations with matching parts, and check recovered values in both original lines.

example.prompt: A star plus a circle is 9. Two stars plus a circle total 13. What is a star worth?
steps: Compare the two expressions. The second contains one extra star and nothing else changes.
That extra star accounts for 13 − 9 = 4.

lessons.videoTitle: Magic grids, symbolic rules and consistency

questions.title: Translate an icon key
questions.prompt: A triangle followed by a square represents the sum of their values. A pair of triangles totals 10, and a triangle with a square totals 14. What value does the square represent?
questions.hint: Use the repeated triangle to decode one symbol first.

questions.title: A missing output
questions.prompt: An operator takes an ordered pair (x,y) to 2x + y. The output for (8, y) equals the output for (10, 11). What is y?
questions.hint: Equal outputs can balance different inputs.

questions.title: Two symbols, two rows
questions.prompt: The row “star, star, moon” totals 27. The row “star, moon, moon” totals 30. What does one star plus one moon total?
questions.hint: Add the two line totals before solving for separate symbols.

questions.title: Repair the recorder
questions.prompt: The cells in a 3-by-3 magic square each show a different number from 6 through 14. A corner contains 7. What must be printed in the diagonally opposite corner?
questions.hint: First recover the line sum and the centre from all nine entries.

lessons.headline: Choose the unwanted frames carefully
lessons.intro: With two marked regions, a frame can include both. To exclude the second mark, remove frames that satisfy its condition and the first mark’s condition together.
lessons.bridge: Watch how the film counts frames that cover both A and B. That unwanted group is precisely what must come out of the first count.
lessons.recap: When subtracting bad frames, keep every condition imposed by the original count.

example.prompt: A strip has three cells. How many intervals of full cells contain the first cell but exclude the last?
steps: The intervals containing the first cell may stop after cells 1, 2 or 3.
Only the third choice also contains the last cell. Two remain.

questions.title: One blocked end
questions.prompt: Six unit cells form a row of lockers. A label covers a contiguous strip of at least two cells and cannot cover either end locker. How many placements are possible?
questions.hint: Discard the two ends before counting strips by length.

questions.title: Straight along the west wall
questions.prompt: A rectangular plot covers whole cells on a 4-column by 3-row garden. It must touch the west edge but may not touch the south edge. How many such plots are possible?
questions.hint: Fix the west boundary. Which rows can the plot use?

questions.title: Just one corner flag
questions.prompt: A 4-by-3 board has a flag in each corner cell. How many rectangular pieces along cell lines contain exactly one flag?
questions.hint: Count pieces that contain the top-left flag alone. Can a piece counted there also belong to another corner’s case?

questions.title: Machining around two faults
questions.prompt: A metal sheet has 4 columns and 3 rows of square cells. A rectangular part may use only intact cells. Faults occur in column 2, row 2 and in column 4, row 3. How many different grid rectangles avoid both faults?
questions.hint: Subtract rectangles covering each fault, then restore rectangles that covered both.

lessons.headline: Choose prime copies to build a divisor
lessons.intro: A factorisation tells you exactly which prime copies a divisor may contain. Choosing no copy is a real choice, and choosing every copy gives the number itself.
lessons.bridge: When the film counts the divisors of 60, look for a choice with no copy of a prime. Losing that choice would miss some factors.
lessons.recap: The exponent is one less than the number of available choices. Restrict the choices first if the divisor must be even or meet another condition.

example.prompt: How many positive divisors does 12 have?
steps: Write 12 = 2² × 3. A divisor can use zero, one or two copies of 2 and zero or one copy of 3.
There are 3 × 2 = 6 choices, giving 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.

questions.title: The omitted factor cards
questions.prompt: A club needs a card for every positive divisor of 32. The cards for 1 and 32 are already made. How many more different cards does the club need?
questions.hint: A divisor of 32 can only use factors of 2.

questions.title: A restricted carton size
questions.prompt: A carton size must divide 72 exactly and must itself be divisible by 6 but not by 9. How many different positive whole-number carton sizes qualify?
questions.hint: In the prime factorisation of a qualifying size, how many copies of 3 must appear?

questions.title: Keep odd divisors
questions.prompt: How many odd positive divisors does 180 have?
questions.hint: Which prime must be absent from every odd divisor?

questions.title: Square choices
questions.prompt: How many positive divisors of 144 are perfect squares?
questions.hint: A square uses even exponents for every prime.

lessons.headline: Compare travel plans against a deadline
lessons.intro: A fixed journey or deadline makes one missing speed or time recoverable. Subtract the completed leg from the total before finding the remaining rate.
lessons.bridge: During the film's out-and-back ride, put the stop on the same clock as both legs. A deadline leaves only the time after everything already done has been subtracted.
lessons.recap: Calculate the remaining distance and the remaining time separately. A speed for the last leg must use both remaining quantities.

example.prompt: A courier must travel 30 km in 2 hours. She covers 12 km in the first hour. How fast must she go for the last hour?
steps: She has 18 km left and one hour left.
The needed speed is 18 km/h.

questions.title: Time left
questions.prompt: A ride must end 90 minutes after it starts. The first section takes 38 minutes and a stop takes 12. How many minutes remain?
questions.hint: Remove both elapsed intervals.

questions.title: The final six kilometres
questions.prompt: A runner must cover 15 km in 90 minutes. She covers the first 9 km in 60 minutes. What speed in km/h does she need on the last leg?
questions.hint: Write the unused time in hours.

questions.title: Two limits
questions.prompt: A van has 2 hours to cover 100 km. It covers the first 40 km at 40 km/h. At 80 km/h on the rest, how many minutes can it spend stopped and still arrive on time?
questions.hint: Find the moving time for each leg.

questions.title: The amended schedule
questions.prompt: An 80 km trip was planned at 40 km/h throughout. After 20 km at that speed, a stop takes 15 minutes. At what speed in km/h must the final 60 km be driven to meet the original arrival time?
questions.hint: Subtract both the driven time and the stop from the original time budget.

lessons.headline: Make a list that reveals collisions
lessons.intro: A choice and its result are two different things. If several choices produce the same result, keep a separate list of the results. Sorted rows make collisions easier to see.
lessons.bridge: In the two-counter puzzle, the film treats the counters as labelled. Decide which different readings share the same sum, and why a question about sums would need a different list.
lessons.recap: Count a repeated result once. Keep repeated choices when the question asks for ways, and merge them when it asks for different outcomes.

example.prompt: Choose two numbers from 1, 2, 3, 4, allowing repeats. How many different products are possible?
steps: In rows by the smaller factor, the products are 1,2,3,4 then 4,6,8 then 9,12 then 16.
Only 4 appears twice. The ten factor pairs give nine different products.

questions.title: Two wheels
questions.prompt: One wheel shows 1, 3, 5 and another shows 1, 2, 3. How many different sums can the two wheels show?
questions.hint: List one row per first-wheel result.

questions.title: Matching areas
questions.prompt: A rectangle has sides chosen from 2, 3, 4, 6 cm. The sides may be equal. How many different areas can occur?
questions.hint: Try factors in nondecreasing order.

questions.title: Reading a ruler
questions.prompt: A ruler has marks at 0, 1, 4, 6 and 10 cm. How many different positive distances occur between two marks?
questions.hint: List differences by the smaller mark.

questions.title: Mixing paints
questions.prompt: Three pots contain 1, 2 and 4 litres. You may pour all or none of each into a bowl. What is the smallest whole-number amount of paint you could add as a fourth full pot so that every whole total from 0 to 15 litres becomes possible?
questions.hint: Find what the first three pots can make and consider the total needed to reach 15.

lessons.headline: Lengths and areas scale differently
lessons.intro: A drawing enlarged with the same scale factor in both directions keeps its shape. An area changes in both directions, so its scale factor is the square of the length scale factor.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film scale the length of a drawn wall. Think about whether that scale factor should act once or twice if the next question asks about a rectangular area.
lessons.recap: Identify what the measurement counts. Length follows one scale factor, while a covering of square units follows two.

example.prompt: A 2 cm by 3 cm rectangle is enlarged by a factor of 2. What is its new area?
steps: The sides become 4 cm and 6 cm.
Its area becomes 24 cm², four times the original 6 cm².

lessons.videoTitle: Ratios on a bead strand, a scale drawing and two trays

questions.title: A wider sign
questions.prompt: A logo 8 cm wide is enlarged by a factor of 3/2. How wide is it in centimetres?
questions.hint: Scale the width once.

questions.title: Border and paint
questions.prompt: A rectangle with perimeter 18 cm is enlarged by a length factor of 3. What is the new perimeter in centimetres?
questions.hint: How does each side change?

questions.title: Square metres of lawn
questions.prompt: A model plot has sides 3 cm and 7 cm. Each centimetre represents 2 m. What is the real plot's area in square metres?
questions.hint: Convert both sides before multiplying.

questions.title: Reverse the enlargement
questions.prompt: Two similar rectangular posters have areas 32 and 72 square centimetres. A side of the smaller poster measures 4 cm. What is the matching side on the larger poster, in centimetres?
questions.hint: Reduce the area ratio and look for square numbers.

lessons.headline: Give every change its own sign
lessons.intro: In a sequence of gains, losses and transfers, update one chosen difference consistently. State which side is subtracted and let a negative value mean the lead has changed hands.
lessons.bridge: When the film adjusts the three teams' scores, follow one team's lead over another through each transfer. Keep the direction of subtraction fixed.
lessons.recap: Check a signed difference by making up one possible pair of opening scores and replaying the changes.

example.prompt: The first team leads by 4. The second scores 7 with no change to the first. Who leads now?
steps: The first team's lead changes from 4 to 4 − 7 = −3.
A negative lead for the first means the second now leads by 3.

lessons.videoTitle: Winner margins, shared totals and linear rules

questions.title: A lost point
questions.prompt: Team A leads B by 5. A loses 2 points to a penalty with no change to B. By how many points does A lead now?
questions.hint: Only the first score changes.

questions.title: Unequal bonuses
questions.prompt: A leads B by 4. A gains 3 points and B gains 9 points. By how many points is the new leader ahead?
questions.hint: Compare the two bonuses.

questions.title: Two changes combined
questions.prompt: A and B start equal. A gains 12 tokens from a referee and then passes 4 tokens to B. By how many tokens does A lead?
questions.hint: A transfer changes both accounts.

questions.title: Token audit
questions.prompt: Two clubs share 100 tokens and A initially leads B by 12. A then loses 4 tokens to a referee. How many must A pass to B next for B to lead by 6?
questions.hint: Compute the gap just before the transfer.

lessons.headline: Follow a chain of descriptions
lessons.intro: When one speaker describes another as truthful, their types match. When the description says the other is a liar, the types differ. A chain of clues can force a result before any name gets a definite type.
lessons.bridge: As Iris, Kai, Lia and Mo make their claims, track which pairs match or differ. Then test whether Mo’s entire claim is true.
lessons.recap: Carry equality or difference along the chain, then find a claim that fixes which type actually occurs.

example.prompt: Sue calls Tom a liar. Tom calls Uri a liar. Must Sue and Uri have the same type?
steps: Sue and Tom differ. Tom and Uri also differ.
Two type changes lead back to the starting type, so Sue and Uri match.

questions.title: A true observation
questions.prompt: Every person either always tells the truth or always lies. Jia calls Kir a liar. We know Jia always lies. Is Kir truthful? Answer yes or no.
questions.hint: Evaluate what the sentence would say if it were true.

questions.title: A claim about two people
questions.prompt: Every person either always tells the truth or always lies. Oli says, “Pia is a liar and Quin is truthful.” We know Pia is truthful. Can Oli be truthful? Answer yes or no.
questions.hint: What is required for a sentence containing “and” to be true?

questions.title: Who called whom truthful?
questions.prompt: Every person either always tells the truth or always lies. Nia calls Oli truthful. Oli calls Pia truthful. Pia says Nia and Oli are the same type. How many are truthful?
questions.hint: The first two descriptions link what types can agree.

questions.title: The five notices
questions.prompt: A key is in one of eight boxes numbered 1 to 8. Five notices say (A) the number is less than 5, (B) it is prime, (C) it is a square, (D) exactly one of A and B is true, and (E) it is even. Exactly four notices are true. Which box holds the key?
questions.hint: How many of A, B and D can be true together?

lessons.headline: Follow the faces made by a cut
lessons.intro: Cutting and separating a solid can create fresh faces even when the volume stays fixed. The shape of the cutting plane determines how much surface appears.
lessons.bridge: The open box in the film counts only material that actually forms a face. Keep that idea for a cut, where a face inside the solid can become exposed.
lessons.recap: Draw the cross-section first. Count one copy of its area for every new face that becomes exposed.

example.prompt: A brick with a 2 by 3 cm cross-section is sliced once straight across that section and pulled apart. How much new surface appears?
steps: Each of the two pieces gains one exposed face of area 6 cm².
Together the pieces gain 12 cm² of surface.

lessons.videoTitle: Nets, surface area, volume and 3D views

questions.title: Which face appears twice?
questions.prompt: A block is 8 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high. A single cut perpendicular to its length splits it into two separate pieces. What is the area of just one new face in square centimetres?
questions.hint: Which two dimensions lie across a cut perpendicular to the longest direction?

questions.title: Find the area of the cut
questions.prompt: A rectangular block is sawn once into two pieces and the pieces are pulled apart. Their combined surface area is 30 cm² greater than that of the original block. What is the area of the cross-section in square centimetres?
questions.hint: Each side of the cut produces a matching new face.

questions.title: Slices of cheese
questions.prompt: A rectangular cheese block has a constant 4 cm by 5 cm cross-section. Three parallel cuts across that section produce four separate slices. By how many square centimetres does total surface area increase?
questions.hint: Count fresh faces per cut, not per finished piece.

questions.title: Opening the hollow block
questions.prompt: A 5 × 5 × 5 cube has a completely enclosed 3 × 3 × 3 hollow centre, leaving a wall one cube thick all round. Remove the middle unit cube from one outer face. How many unit square faces can an ant now reach from outside? It can crawl along the inside as well as the outside.
questions.hint: Count the old outer and inner surfaces, then look at the four sides of the new opening.

lessons.headline: A mirror doubles some digit contributions
lessons.intro: For a five-digit palindrome ABCBA the digit sum is 2A + 2B + C. Use the digit-sum condition while choosing the free digits, remembering that A cannot be zero.
lessons.bridge: Look at the five-digit palindrome in the film's final question. Before testing divisibility by nine, decide which digits must be counted twice.
lessons.recap: After finding a centre digit, check that it is an integer from 0 to 9. For divisibility by nine, both 0 and 9 may qualify.

example.prompt: A palindrome is 31C13. If its digit sum is 12, what is C?
steps: The matched outer digits contribute 6 and the matched ones contribute 2.
The centre must supply 12 − 8 = 4.

questions.title: Check the sum
questions.prompt: What is the digit sum of 63536?
questions.hint: Group paired digits around the centre.

questions.title: Centre of a multiple
questions.prompt: A palindrome is 42C24. It is divisible by 9. What is its centre digit?
questions.hint: The outside pairs already contribute 12.

questions.title: How many mirrors?
questions.prompt: How many three-digit palindromes have digit sum 12?
questions.hint: For ABA, set B = 12 − 2A and enforce digit bounds.

questions.title: Two possible centres
questions.prompt: How many five-digit palindromes start with 18 and are divisible by 9?
questions.hint: Check the digit sum with both extreme centre digits.

lessons.headline: Count departures and arrivals separately
lessons.intro: A service timetable is a sequence of events. Departure and arrival occur on different clocks linked by travel time. Anchor the first time before counting intervals.
lessons.bridge: In the film, note the time of the sensor's first flash before listing later ones. A departure timetable likewise needs both the first event and the interval.
lessons.recap: Move an arrival deadline backwards by the travel time. Then count only departures that actually satisfy it.

example.prompt: A ferry leaves at 8:00 and every 12 minutes thereafter. The trip lasts 5 minutes. When does the third ferry arrive?
steps: The third departs two intervals after 8:00, at 8:24.
Five more minutes brings it to 8:29.

questions.title: The fifth bus
questions.prompt: Buses first leave at noon and then every 7 minutes. How many minutes after noon does the fifth bus depart?
questions.hint: The first departure is at minute zero.

questions.title: Last usable departure
questions.prompt: A boat leaves at 1:00 and every 8 minutes. The trip takes 13 minutes. How many minutes after 1:00 is the latest departure that arrives by 2:00?
questions.hint: Find the latest allowable departure time before choosing a scheduled one.

questions.title: The waiting time
questions.prompt: A shuttle leaves at 9:00 then every 11 minutes. A passenger arrives at 9:35. How many minutes must she wait for the next shuttle?
questions.hint: Locate the multiples of 11 surrounding minute 35.

questions.title: Count passengers ashore
questions.prompt: A boat leaves a dock every 6 minutes starting at 10:00. Each boat carries 8 passengers and takes 11 minutes to cross. How many passengers have reached the far bank by 10:40 inclusive?
questions.hint: Count boats whose departure time allows the entire crossing.

lessons.headline: Follow halved angles
lessons.intro: An angle bisector divides an angle into two equal turns. When more than one bisector appears, label the halves before adding them.
lessons.bridge: Follow the two halves at B and C into the smaller triangle in the film. Add them before trying to use the 180° sum.
lessons.recap: When a diagram contains bisectors, work with the two halves as a sum and then finish the triangle they bound.

example.prompt: Angles B and C of a triangle total 110°. Their bisectors make a smaller triangle with the original side BC. What do its angles at B and C add to?
steps: Those two angles are half of B and half of C.
Their sum is half of 110°, or 55°.

questions.title: Halfway between two bearings
questions.prompt: Two rays from O point at 34° and 78°, measured anticlockwise from the same horizontal ray. At what direction in degrees does the bisector of the smaller angle point?
questions.hint: Find the gap, halve it, then measure from the first ray.

questions.title: Restore the whole apex
questions.prompt: The internal bisector AD of angle A in triangle ABC meets side BC at D. Angle ABC is 64° and angle ADB is 86°. What is the whole angle A in degrees?
questions.hint: Triangle ABD contains only one half of angle A.

questions.title: Two halves in an open fan
questions.prompt: An open fan spans an angle AOC of 140°. A spoke OB lies somewhere strictly inside the fan. Draw the internal bisectors of AOB and BOC. What is the angle in degrees between these two bisectors?
questions.hint: Call the smaller sectors x and 140−x. Which halves are between the two bisectors?

questions.title: Two bisectors inside a courtyard
questions.prompt: A convex four-sided courtyard has corners A, B, C, D in order. Its angles at C and D are 102° and 118°. The internal bisectors of A and B meet inside the courtyard at P. How many degrees are in angle APB?
questions.hint: Find the total of angles A and B before taking halves.

lessons.headline: Compare totals over overlapping windows
lessons.intro: Two averages may refer to groups that share some readings. Convert means into totals, then cancel readings that occur in both groups.
lessons.bridge: In the film's overlapping groups, circle the reading that belongs to both groups. Follow how subtracting the overall total recovers it.
lessons.recap: Mark shared observations before adding or subtracting group totals. A sum of overlapping totals counts the overlap twice.

example.prompt: The first three days total 21 visits. The next three-day window, covering days 2–4, totals 25. How many more visits were there on day 4 than day 1?
steps: Days 2 and 3 occur in both totals.
The increase 25 − 21 = 4 comes entirely from replacing day 1 by day 4.

lessons.videoTitle: Averages, weighted means and simple distributions

questions.title: Rolling mean
questions.prompt: Days 1–4 average 12 visits. Days 2–5 average 15. How many more visits occurred on day 5 than day 1?
questions.hint: Multiply both means by four.

questions.title: Shared reading
questions.prompt: The first three entries in a five-number list average 8. The last three average 12. All five together total 47. What is the middle entry?
questions.hint: Which entry appears twice if you add the two group totals?

questions.title: Two shared readings
questions.prompt: Seven daily counts total 80. Days 1–4 average 12 and days 3–7 average 10. What is the combined count for days 3 and 4?
questions.hint: Compare the sum of window totals with the overall total.

questions.title: Recovered finish
questions.prompt: Four consecutive three-day average counts for days 1–3, 2–4, 3–5 and 4–6 are 10, 12, 11 and 15. Day 3 recorded 9. How many were recorded on day 6?
questions.hint: The last two windows differ only in days 3 and 6.

lessons.headline: Index one full cycle
lessons.intro: The last digit of a product depends only on the last digits of its factors. Repeated multiplication may settle into a short cycle. Label the first term carefully before reducing a large exponent.
lessons.bridge: In the film's powers of three, label the exponent above each last digit. Find the first repeated digit together with its position before tackling the sum of many powers.
lessons.recap: When an index divides exactly by the cycle length, it usually selects the final entry of a cycle indexed from 1. Check against a small exponent.

example.prompt: What is the last digit of 2 to the sixth power?
steps: Starting at exponent 1 the last digits are 2, 4, 8, 6, then repeat.
Exponent 6 is in the second position of the next cycle, so the last digit is 4.

questions.title: Powers of nine
questions.prompt: What is the last digit of 9 to the seventeenth power?
questions.hint: Write the last digit of the first few powers.

questions.title: Find the next index
questions.prompt: A display shows the units digit of 7 raised to successive positive integer powers. What is the first exponent strictly greater than 20 for which the display shows 1?
questions.hint: Find which position in a cycle shows 1 and check the strict lower bound.

questions.title: Combine two powers
questions.prompt: What is the last digit of 2²³ + 3¹⁴?
questions.hint: Reduce each exponent in its own last-digit cycle.

questions.title: The lamp changes hourly
questions.prompt: A dial shows the last digit of 7ⁿ at hour n, starting at hour 1. Over hours 1 through 50 inclusive, how many times does it show 9?
questions.hint: Locate 9 in one four-hour cycle.

lessons.headline: Scale before subtracting
lessons.intro: Equal parts cancel only if their counts match. You can multiply an entire purchase or balance to make one kind of item occur equally many times.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film scale a pen-and-marker purchase to match another one. Check that the price as well as every item count is multiplied before subtracting.
lessons.recap: Whenever you scale an equation or a bundle, scale its total as well as every item count.

example.prompt: One pen and one folder cost $6. Two pens and three folders cost $15. What does a folder cost?
steps: Double the first purchase: two pens and two folders cost $12.
The extra folder in the second purchase costs $3.

questions.title: Match the apples
questions.prompt: One apple and a pear cost $7. Two apples and three pears cost $17. What does a pear cost in dollars?
questions.hint: Double the first purchase.

questions.title: Find the other price
questions.prompt: A badge and two clips cost $11. Three badges and four clips cost $29. How many dollars does a clip cost?
questions.hint: Make four clips appear in two orders.

questions.title: Different multipliers
questions.prompt: Two pears and three plums cost $16. Three pears and two plums cost $14. How many dollars does a plum cost?
questions.hint: Make six pears appear in both lists.

questions.title: Weight of a pair
questions.prompt: Two bolts and a washer weigh 13 g. One bolt and three washers weigh 14 g. How much do one bolt and one washer weigh together, in grams?
questions.hint: Double the second bundle to match two bolts.

lessons.headline: Recover a missing group size
lessons.intro: A table of memberships can be read by rows or by columns. Even when you cannot name the memberships individually, the two totals must agree.
lessons.bridge: For the room bookings, watch a single booking from the viewpoint of the room and the viewpoint of its helper. Both views have to produce the same total.
lessons.recap: Equate two counts of the same events. If your totals do not agree, check for repeated visits or memberships before drawing a conclusion.

example.prompt: Five patrols each record four visits. The visits are shared equally among ten sites. How many visits does each site receive?
steps: The patrols record 5 × 4 = 20 visits.
Divide the same 20 visits among ten sites to get 2 per site.

questions.title: Photo appearances
questions.prompt: Eight team photographs each show six children. Each child appears in four photographs. How many children appear?
questions.hint: Count appearances rather than photographs.

questions.title: Specific captain
questions.prompt: Six pupils form every possible team of three. How many teams include Zara, one of the six?
questions.hint: Count the two other members.

questions.title: Sum of labels
questions.prompt: Form every unordered pair from 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Add the two labels in every pair, then add all those sums. What is the total?
questions.hint: How often is a particular label used?

questions.title: The seven-stop routes
questions.prompt: Every pair of seven stops is connected by exactly one of several routes. Each route visits three distinct stops and connects all three pairs among them. How many routes pass through one specified stop?
questions.hint: Count its six connections, grouping them by routes through it.

lessons.headline: Count the change across floors
lessons.intro: Changing a stack affects precisely the floors it reaches. Comparing two models is often quicker if you count only the added or removed cubes.
lessons.bridge: When the stack model changes in the film, track which hidden cubes could be added while leaving every displayed maximum the same.
lessons.recap: Track the deficit at each position. An unchanged position contributes zero to the change.

example.prompt: Stacks of heights 2, 4 and 1 are all raised to height 4. How many cubes are added?
steps: Their deficits from 4 are 2, 0 and 3.
The total added is 5. The new model has three stacks of 4.

questions.title: Lower only the tallest stacks
questions.prompt: Three stacks have heights 6, 4 and 2. Remove every cube above level 4. How many cubes are removed in total?
questions.hint: Only heights above the chosen ceiling contribute.

questions.title: One extra base row
questions.prompt: A solid rectangular stack is 5 cubes long, 3 wide and 4 high. A new row one cube wide is added along the entire five-cube length and built up to the original height. How many cubes are added?
questions.hint: Draw just the new material as a slab.

questions.title: A floor changes in two places
questions.prompt: A stepped model has 12 cubes on the lowest layer, 9 on the second and 3 on the third. Add 3 cubes to empty supported positions on the third layer, and remove 2 uncovered cubes from the second layer. What is the new total number of cubes?
questions.hint: Update the layer totals or find the net change in total.

questions.title: How different can two skyline models be?
questions.prompt: Both models use stacks of unit cubes on every square of a 3-row, 4-column floor. Each model has row maxima 4, 3, 2 and column maxima 2, 4, 3, 2, in those orders. What is the greatest possible difference between their cube counts?
questions.hint: For a maximum use the smaller of the two height limits at every cell. For a minimum, make tall stacks serve both views where possible.

lessons.headline: Use a pair when one entry cannot predict the next
lessons.intro: When a new output depends on the last two, a repeated single value says too little. A repeated ordered pair reproduces the same future, provided the rule never changes.
lessons.bridge: In the film’s machine, a state predicts the entire next move. Think about whether one term is enough information when the next output depends on two earlier terms.
lessons.recap: State what information determines the next output. Keep an ordered pair if the order matters, and compare like with like when finding the period.

example.prompt: Start with 0 and 1. Each new bit is the remainder when the sum of the previous two is divided by 2. What are the next four bits?
steps: From 0,1 we get 1; from 1,1 we get 0. The next pair is 1,0.
Continuing gives 1 and 1. The four new bits are 1,0,1,1.

questions.title: Next bit
questions.prompt: A list starts 1,1 and every new term is the sum of the previous two modulo 2. What is the fifth term?
questions.hint: Keep the last two bits as you advance.

questions.title: Possible memories
questions.prompt: A machine remembers an ordered pair of residues modulo 3. How many different ordered pairs could it remember?
questions.hint: Each position independently holds 0, 1 or 2.

questions.title: Odd Fibonacci steps
questions.prompt: The first two entries of a sequence are both 1. Each next entry is their usual preceding-two sum. How many of the first 40 entries are even?
questions.hint: Track parity pairs instead of the full values.

questions.title: A three-remainder clock
questions.prompt: Start x₁ = 0 and x₂ = 1. Each new entry is the remainder of the sum of the two preceding entries on division by 3. What is x₅₀?
questions.hint: Write entries until the ordered pair 0,1 returns.

lessons.headline: Read the boundary as evidence
lessons.intro: A drawing need not show every measurement. Separate the outer loop from holes and shared edges to infer a missing length.
lessons.bridge: The film draws a board with an inner hole and a corner cut. Watch which lengths can be recovered from the change in total boundary.
lessons.recap: Write one term for every boundary loop and use the geometry of each loop to recover unknown lengths.

example.prompt: A card has 24 cm around the outside. After a square window is cut inside, the combined boundary is 36 cm. What is the window side?
steps: The outside is still 24 cm. The window contributes 12 cm of boundary.
Divide its perimeter by four equal sides: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 cm.

lessons.videoTitle: Perimeter, shared edges and boundary effects

questions.title: Find the second opening
questions.prompt: A metal sheet has an outer boundary of 48 cm and two holes. All exposed boundaries together measure 74 cm. One hole is a square of side 3 cm. What is the perimeter of the other hole in centimetres?
questions.hint: Separate the outer boundary from both loops around the holes.

questions.title: The unmeasured side
questions.prompt: Three consecutive sides of a rectangular path total 28 m. The whole perimeter is 40 m. What is the length of the shorter side in metres?
questions.hint: First determine the missing fourth side. Then use opposite sides of a rectangle.

questions.title: Reconstruct the original array
questions.prompt: Twelve unit squares originally made a filled rectangle. One square was removed from a straight side, away from the corners. It shared three edges with the squares left behind. The new outline measures 18 units. How many units long was the longer side of the original rectangle?
questions.hint: Removing that square takes one outer edge away and exposes three others.

questions.title: Rebuild the hidden seams
questions.prompt: A mosaic piece consists of 10 unit squares. Its total exposed edge length is 18 units. Join two copies along exactly three pairs of complete unit edges, with no overlaps and no other edge contacts. In the finished mosaic, how many unordered pairs of squares share an edge?
questions.hint: Each new contact hides two edges. Count how many of the original 80 unit edges are hidden in the joined mosaic.

lessons.headline: Count the effect of one closed link
lessons.intro: A single closed link removes only routes that used that connection. To count them, work out at what point in the route using it would be possible.
lessons.bridge: At the missing connection in the red-blue route, identify the two stops that cannot be consecutive, then check both directions through that pair.
lessons.recap: When subtracting forbidden routes, keep endpoints, order and any no-repeat conditions in force.

example.prompt: A start S connects to U and V. Both U and V connect to finish F. Routes take exactly two steps. If the link U–F closes, how many routes remain?
steps: The two possible routes are S–U–F and S–V–F.
The closure removes the first route. The second still works, giving 1 route.

questions.title: Which closure cuts off the finish?
questions.prompt: Undirected paths link S to A and B, A to C, B to C, and C to F. If exactly one path is closed, how many of the five choices of closed path leave F unreachable from S?
questions.hint: Trace the two ways of arriving at C and look at how each continues.

questions.title: Closing a shortcut
questions.prompt: All roads in a village are two-way and have the same length. The roads are HA, HB, AT, BT, AB and HT. A walker takes a shortest route from H to T. After the direct road HT closes, how many shortest routes are available?
questions.hint: Find the new shortest length before counting its routes.

questions.title: The inspection lap
questions.prompt: The four rooms S, A, B and C have a doorway between every pair. Starting and finishing at S, a guide must visit A, B and C exactly once each. The doorway between A and B is now shut. How many ordered tours can the guide take?
questions.hint: Where must C lie in the three-room visiting order?

questions.title: Round trips lost to a closure
questions.prompt: Five two-way paths have these lengths in metres: AB 2, BC 3, CD 2, DA 7 and AC 8. Walk from A to C without visiting any junction twice, then return from C to A along a route sharing no edge with the outward one. Before AC closes, how many such ordered round trips of at most 16 metres use AC?
questions.hint: List the three simple ways from A to C, with their lengths. Which can share a round trip with AC?

figure.alt: Junctions A, B, C, D form a loop of lengths 2, 3, 2, 7 metres in that order. A diagonal from A to C is 8 metres.

lessons.headline: Model a change with one unknown
lessons.intro: Choose a quantity that makes every related amount easy to express. If the quantity changes, name its starting value and write each later value from it.
lessons.bridge: In the film's ticket sale, pause after choosing the first unknown. Form an expression for the remaining tickets and test what the two ticket counts must add to.
lessons.recap: Read the proposed answer back into the original story. Check any conditions on whole numbers and on what can be moved or spent.

example.prompt: A box holds an unknown number of counters. Another holds three less. Together they hold 17. How many are in the first box?
steps: If the first holds x then the other holds x − 3.
The total 2x − 3 is 17, so x is 10. The other box holds 7.

questions.title: One more row
questions.prompt: A display has 5 rows of the same size and 3 extra badges. There are 43 badges. How many badges fit in a row?
questions.hint: Remove the extras first.

questions.title: A length and its copy
questions.prompt: A red ribbon is 7 cm longer than half a blue ribbon. Together they measure 37 cm. What is the length of the blue ribbon in centimetres?
questions.hint: Express both lengths using the blue ribbon.

questions.title: Packages on two shelves
questions.prompt: The upper shelf has twice as many packets as the lower. Moving 5 from the upper to the lower makes their numbers equal. How many packets were there altogether?
questions.hint: Before moving, how large must the gap have been?

questions.title: A partly used voucher
questions.prompt: A voucher covers $2 of each of the first five tickets. Every ticket normally has one common price. Eight tickets with this voucher cost $46. What would six tickets cost without the voucher, in dollars?
questions.hint: Calculate the full value of the voucher used.

lessons.headline: Read the paint count backwards
lessons.intro: A count of painted pieces can tell you the size of the original block. Translate what a piece’s paint category says about its position.
lessons.bridge: In the painted-cuboid film, look for an edge count or a face-interior count you could undo if one large dimension were hidden.
lessons.recap: Reverse the classification before taking a square root or restoring edge layers.

example.prompt: On one face of a big cube, exactly 9 small cubes lie strictly inside the face border. How many cubes run along the outer edge?
steps: Nine interiors form a 3-by-3 square.
One border cube at each end adds two, giving an edge length of 5.

lessons.videoTitle: Painted faces, boundary and hidden cubes

questions.title: Reverse the clean core
questions.prompt: All six faces of a solid cube are painted. Exactly 27 of its unit cubes remain completely clean. How many unit cubes are along an outside edge?
questions.hint: Find the side of the clean cube before restoring the painted layers.

questions.title: Count the border before recovering its side
questions.prompt: The square top face of a cubical box is paved with unit squares. Exactly 24 squares lie along its four edges, counting each corner once. How many unit squares make up a full edge?
questions.hint: Four edge counts include four corner repeats.

questions.title: Find the depth from the blue side
questions.prompt: A solid block is 6 cubes wide and 4 cubes high. All faces are painted. Exactly 12 unit cubes lie strictly inside its top face, away from that face’s edges. How many cubes deep is the block?
questions.hint: Remove the two border positions from each horizontal dimension.

questions.title: What shape could the painted block have been?
questions.prompt: A solid rectangular block of unit cubes is painted on all six outside faces. Each outer dimension is at least 4, and one dimension is exactly 4. When the cubes are separated, 24 have no paint. What is the largest possible number with exactly two painted faces?
questions.hint: Remove the one-cube skin. List the factor pairs for the two unknown inner dimensions.

lessons.headline: Use a second rule before counting
lessons.intro: When labels must satisfy both a divisibility rule and a digit requirement, do not count those properties independently. One choice can already fix another.
lessons.bridge: In the film the hard count keeps only multiples of nine. Ask which digit choices force the missing digit before you start a long list.
lessons.recap: Check each candidate against both rules. Organising by position helps show that the list is complete.

example.prompt: Which two-digit multiple of 9 starts with 4?
steps: Its digit sum must be a multiple of 9.
Only 4 + 5 works, so the number is 45.

lessons.videoTitle: Digit sums and counting digits in ranges

questions.title: The missing digit
questions.prompt: A number is written 6A3, where A is a digit from 1 to 8. It is divisible by 3. How many choices are there for A?
questions.hint: The known digits already sum to 9.

questions.title: Multiples ending in five
questions.prompt: On the positive multiples of 5 up to 100 inclusive, how many copies of the digit 5 appear?
questions.hint: Count units fives and tens fives separately.

questions.title: Exactly two twos
questions.prompt: How many numbers from 200 through 399 inclusive contain exactly two copies of 2 and are divisible by 3?
questions.hint: Place the two twos, then use the digit sum to restrict the remaining digit.

questions.title: An unseen printing roll
questions.prompt: A roll contains every three-digit label with digit sum 3, once each. How many copies of the digit 1 appear on the roll?
questions.hint: Enumerate by the hundreds digit.

lessons.headline: Use a target fraction to balance groups
lessons.intro: A combined fraction can reveal how many objects came from each group. Compare the contribution from each group with what it would contribute at the target fraction.
lessons.bridge: For the film's two groups of marked items, compare what each group would contribute on its own. Which shared total gives a way to recover a missing group size?
lessons.recap: Check that the final fraction lies between the two starting fractions. Use actual counts to check the exact mix.

example.prompt: Half the 8 red cups are filled. All 4 blue cups are filled. What fraction of the 12 cups are filled?
steps: There are 4 filled red and 4 filled blue cups.
Eight of twelve are filled, giving 2/3.

questions.title: A mixed packet
questions.prompt: A packet contains 12 dark seeds, a quarter sprouted, and 8 pale seeds, half sprouted. How many seeds have sprouted?
questions.hint: Find the sprouted number in each group.

questions.title: Empty places
questions.prompt: At one table 3/4 of 16 places are occupied. At another 1/2 of 12 are occupied. What fraction of all the places is empty?
questions.hint: Subtract occupied places from the number of places.

questions.title: Blend the tins
questions.prompt: One paint is a quarter blue pigment, another is half blue pigment. Mix 8 litres of the first with some of the second to make a blend that is 3/8 blue pigment. How many litres of the second paint are needed? Assume volumes add.
questions.hint: The target fraction is halfway between the two starting fractions.

questions.title: Two seed trays
questions.prompt: Two trays hold 60 seeds altogether. Half of the first tray and three quarters of the second tray sprout. Altogether 38 seeds sprout. How many were in the second tray?
questions.hint: Suppose half sprouted in both trays. Which tray accounts for the excess?

lessons.headline: Use the missing end term
lessons.intro: When you shift a geometric series by multiplying it, nearly all the terms line up. The unmatched first and last terms let you recover a total or reverse a piece of missing information.
lessons.bridge: Follow the film’s daily budget until you see both the amount on the last day and the whole amount used. Which of those two numbers would need to be reversed?
lessons.recap: For doubling, the running total is the next term minus the first. With another multiplier, subtract the original sum from its shifted copy before solving.

example.prompt: The sum 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 has a missing next term. What is the difference between that next term and the sum?
steps: The sum is 60 and the next term is 64.
The difference is 4, exactly the starting term. This relationship holds for any finite doubling sum.

lessons.videoTitle: Doubling, geometric growth and finite sums

questions.title: Find what comes next
questions.prompt: A finite doubling sequence starts at 7 and its terms sum to 217. What would its next term be?
questions.hint: Add the first term back to the total.

questions.title: Missing middle
questions.prompt: Five positive numbers double successively. The first and last total 85. What is the middle number?
questions.hint: Express the endpoints in copies of the first number.

questions.title: Triple sum in reverse
questions.prompt: A tripling series starts at 2. Its terms sum to 242. What is the next term?
questions.hint: Subtract the original sum from three times that sum.

questions.title: A broken ledger
questions.prompt: A ledger should contain the first seven terms of a doubling sequence starting at 3. Exactly one entry was erased. The remaining entries total 333. Which term number was erased?
