questions.hint: Find the expected sum by using the eighth term.

lessons.headline: Add lines to reveal the shared entries
lessons.intro: Instead of solving each blank in isolation, add or compare whole lines. Count how many times each cell occurs before interpreting the total.
lessons.bridge: The magic-square film adds information from several lines through a shared cell. Keep track of how often the centre appears in those totals.
lessons.recap: When adding line totals, explicitly mark which cells were counted more than once.

example.prompt: Two lines each total 10 and share only the central value 3. What is the total of their distinct cells?
steps: Adding the lines gives 20, with the central 3 included twice.
Remove one extra copy of 3 to get 17.

lessons.videoTitle: Magic grids, symbolic rules and consistency

questions.title: Two overlapping totals
questions.prompt: A horizontal strip of three cells totals 25. A vertical strip of three cells totals 22. They meet in exactly one cell containing 7. What is the sum of the entries in the five distinct cells?
questions.hint: In the sum of the strips, where does the central 7 appear?

questions.title: The one uncounted cell
questions.prompt: A 3-by-3 grid contains numbers with total 52. A teacher covers the top two rows, whose entries total 32. Of the entries in the bottom row, the left and right together total 9. What is the bottom-middle entry?
questions.hint: Find the bottom-row total, then remove its two ends.

questions.title: Restore a diagonal total
questions.prompt: In a 3-by-3 magic square every row, column and main diagonal totals 21. The four edge-middle cells, excluding corners and centre, sum to 28. What is the sum of the four corner cells?
questions.hint: Add the middle row and middle column. Then use the total of all three rows.

questions.title: Recover the corner from a block total
questions.prompt: In a 4-row, 4-column ledger every row and every column totals 20. The nine entries in the upper-left 3-by-3 block add to 43. What is the bottom-right entry?
questions.hint: What total lies in the first three rows? Which three entries there are outside the given block?

lessons.headline: Read a crossing event once
lessons.intro: A diagonal can cross a vertical line and a horizontal line at the same lattice point. A route or beam that meets both there still enters just one fresh cell.
lessons.bridge: The film distinguishes grid cells from their boundary lines. As you follow the marked cells, also identify intersections where two boundary lines meet.
lessons.recap: Distinguish touching a boundary from crossing a tile interior, and count a simultaneous crossing once.

example.prompt: A diagonal joins opposite corners of a 2-by-2 tiled square. How many tile interiors does it cross?
steps: It runs through the middle intersection. Two other tiles meet it only at that corner.
Only the starting and finishing tiles contain part of the diagonal inside them, giving 2.

questions.title: A level laser
questions.prompt: A laser travels horizontally through the centres of all seven cells in a single row. It begins at the outside left edge and ends at the outside right edge. How many boundaries strictly inside the row does it cross?
questions.hint: Distinguish the seven cell interiors from the joins between them.

questions.title: Two readings at the same instant
questions.prompt: Along a straight journey through a tiled panel, a sensor reports vertical boundaries at one-quarter, one-half and three-quarters of the journey. It also reports a horizontal boundary at one-half. The path starts and finishes inside tiles and never follows an edge. How many tile interiors does it pass through?
questions.hint: A grid corner triggers both sensors at once.

questions.title: A beam across tiles
questions.prompt: A straight beam joins opposite corners of a 10-column by 5-row tiled rectangle. How many tile interiors does it cross?
questions.hint: Count grid-line crossings, counting a meeting of two lines only once.

questions.title: Two diagonal beams
questions.prompt: A window is 7 columns wide and 3 rows high, with all panes unit squares. Draw both diagonals of the whole rectangle. How many different panes have some interior point on at least one diagonal? Touching a corner alone does not count.
questions.hint: Count the rows reached in each column. Reflection across the vertical centre line gives the other half.

figure.alt: A seven-column, three-row window. The two diagonals join opposite corners and cross in the middle pane.

lessons.headline: Combine clues that overlap
lessons.intro: When totals overlap, an item may have been counted twice or missed altogether. Write the actual items below each total and compare the counts.
lessons.bridge: When the film weighs its three pairs of boxes, tally each box as it occurs. Notice why adding all the pair totals does not yet give the true overall total.
lessons.recap: Mark each quantity with a tally as you combine clues. Divide only when every quantity has the same tally.

example.prompt: A and B have 12 counters together. B and C have 15. A and C have 13. How many counters are there altogether?
steps: Adding 12, 15 and 13 counts each person's counters twice.
The sum of 40 represents two copies of the collection, so the actual total is 20.

questions.title: Three parcels
questions.prompt: Three parcels weighed in pairs give 13, 17 and 20 kg. What is their combined mass in kilograms?
questions.hint: How many weighings include each parcel?

questions.title: A missing group
questions.prompt: Three baskets contain 47 apples altogether. The first and third together contain 31. How many are in the second?
questions.hint: Which basket is absent from the pair?

questions.title: A pair inside another
questions.prompt: A + B = 19, B + C = 22, and A + B + C = 30. What is B?
questions.hint: Subtract a pair from the overall total to isolate one end.

questions.title: Four voices
questions.prompt: Four friends count their stamps. The totals when exactly one friend is omitted are 35, 38, 40 and 43. How many stamps does the friend with the most stamps own?
questions.hint: Each friend appears in three of the totals.

lessons.headline: Account for three lists
lessons.intro: With three lists, a common item appears three times in the first addition. Removing each pair overlap takes it away three times. One final addition restores it.
lessons.bridge: Track an integer belonging to three excluded lists in the film. Count its appearances after the single, pair and three-way terms.
lessons.recap: Draw one point inside all three sets and track its count through each operation. It must finish with the same weight as every other included point.

example.prompt: Seven different stickers are labelled A, B, C, AB, AC, BC, ABC. How many carry A or B?
steps: Four stickers carry A and four carry B. AB and ABC carry both.
This counts 4 + 4 − 2 = 6. The sticker carrying only C was excluded.

questions.title: Three clubs
questions.prompt: Three clubs have 8, 9 and 7 members. Each pair of clubs shares 2 members, and one member belongs to all three. How many different people belong to at least one?
questions.hint: The pair overlaps include the member in all three.

questions.title: Two clubs exactly
questions.prompt: Among three clubs the pairwise overlaps are 5, 4 and 6, each including the same 2 three-club members. How many people belong to exactly two clubs?
questions.hint: Remove all three-club members from each pair list.

questions.title: Three dividers
questions.prompt: How many numbers from 1 to 30 are divisible by 2, 3 or 5?
questions.hint: Use pair overlaps at multiples of 6, 10 and 15.

questions.title: Missing centre
questions.prompt: Three activities attract 32 different people in total. Their membership counts are 18, 15 and 13. Pairwise overlaps are 7, 5 and 4, each including everyone who attends all three. How many attend all three?
questions.hint: Write the union count with a blank for the three-way overlap.

lessons.headline: Estimate first, then recover the exact correction
lessons.intro: A near-round calculation can reveal an error before long arithmetic begins. The exact correction depends on how many times the substituted value was used.
lessons.bridge: In the film's rectangular model of multiplication, locate the strip removed from the large rectangle. Its width tells you how large the correction must be.
lessons.recap: Give the correction a direction and a unit. A rounding error per item must be multiplied by the number of items it affects.

example.prompt: A shop records 6 items at $20 instead of $19. How large is the error?
steps: The price is $1 too high per item.
Across 6 items the bill is $6 too high.

questions.title: One price too low
questions.prompt: Seven tickets were added at $30 each instead of $32. How many dollars too low is the bill?
questions.hint: Count the repeated $2 difference.

questions.title: Almost two hundred
questions.prompt: Calculate 202 × 35.
questions.hint: Separate 202 into 200 and 2.

questions.title: Missing correction
questions.prompt: A pupil uses 60 × 40 to estimate 58 × 43. By how much is the estimate below the exact product?
questions.hint: Expand the actual product around 60 and 40.

questions.title: Reconstruct the invoice
questions.prompt: A bill listed 12 identical lamps at $50 each, but the true price was $48. The correct bill also contains one cable. The final correct total equals the incorrect lamp-only subtotal. What is the cable's price in dollars?
questions.hint: The cable exactly cancels the overcharge on the lamps.

lessons.headline: Compare quantities through a shared unit
lessons.intro: A map, model or recipe can introduce a different unit for each column. Find one dependable relationship and use it in the direction that takes you to the requested quantity.
lessons.bridge: The film's plan uses 1:500. Trace the measurement from drawing centimetres to real centimetres, then to metres. Returning to the drawing would reverse those steps.
lessons.recap: Attach units to every side of the comparison. Interpreting 5 mm as 5 m would change the scale by a factor of a thousand.

example.prompt: On a model 5 mm represents 2 m. What real length is represented by 15 mm?
steps: Fifteen millimetres is three model units of 5 mm.
Three real units of 2 m make 6 m.

questions.title: The path key
questions.prompt: On a map 4 cm means 3 km. What distance in kilometres does 14 cm represent? Give an exact fraction or decimal.
questions.hint: How many lots of 4 cm fit into 14 cm?

questions.title: Measure the drawing
questions.prompt: A model uses the scale 1 cm to 80 cm. A real table is 2.4 m long. What is its model length in centimetres?
questions.hint: Change metres to centimetres first.

questions.title: Two map sections
questions.prompt: A traveller follows 6 cm of a map where 2 cm represents 5 km, then 4 cm of a second map where 1 cm represents 3 km. What is the total real distance in kilometres?
questions.hint: Convert each section using its own key.

questions.title: A photocopied map
questions.prompt: A map originally used 1 cm for 4 km. A copier enlarges every length to 125% of its former size. Two towns are 15 cm apart on the copy. How far apart are they in kilometres?
questions.hint: Find the distance on the original map before using its key.

lessons.headline: Follow a lead that changes each round
lessons.intro: A fixed starting advantage can shrink, grow or reverse. Write the lead after one round, then use the same change per round while the rules stay fixed.
lessons.bridge: In the film's three-team score exchange, find the difference before and after one transfer. For the later rounds, the same idea lets you track how much of a lead is used each time.
lessons.recap: Use a whole number of rounds if scores are awarded only at their ends. Distinguish reaching level from moving ahead.

example.prompt: A starts 12 ahead. Every round A gains 2 and B gains 5. How many rounds bring them level?
steps: B closes 3 points of gap per round.
Four rounds close all 12 points.

lessons.videoTitle: Winner margins, shared totals and linear rules

questions.title: Gap after three
questions.prompt: A starts 20 points ahead. Each round B gains 4 more points than A. By how many points does A lead after three rounds?
questions.hint: Calculate the accumulated gain.

questions.title: First round ahead
questions.prompt: A leads by 15. B gains 5 more points than A each round. In which round does B first finish strictly ahead?
questions.hint: Check the round that produces equality.

questions.title: Restore the opening score
questions.prompt: After 6 rounds, A leads B by 4 points. In each round B gained 3 more points than A. By how many points did A lead initially?
questions.hint: Undo six rounds of closing.

questions.title: A rule change
questions.prompt: Red starts 18 ahead. For four rounds Blue gains 2 more points per round than Red. For subsequent rounds Blue gains 3 more per round. In which round does Blue first finish ahead?
questions.hint: Find the gap when the rule changes.

lessons.headline: Count a chosen kind of domino
lessons.intro: Two tilings can cover the same board but use different numbers of upright pieces. Track how much width each kind of placement consumes before arranging them.
lessons.bridge: In the fixed-width domino board, count each paired sideways block as one choice of position but as two separate tiles.
lessons.recap: Convert individual horizontal dominoes to forced pairs before counting the order of the resulting blocks.

example.prompt: A 2-by-4 board is tiled. If exactly two dominoes stand upright, how many individual dominoes lie horizontally?
steps: Two upright dominoes fill two whole columns and use four cells.
The other four cells need two horizontal dominoes, forming one paired block.

questions.title: Read the top row
questions.prompt: A 2-by-5 board is completely tiled. In the top row, columns 1–2 share one horizontal domino, and columns 4–5 share another. How many vertical dominoes are in this tiling?
questions.hint: Find the only top cell not already occupied.

questions.title: Twice as many uprights?
questions.prompt: A 2-by-6 board is tiled using twice as many vertical dominoes as individual horizontal dominoes. In how many positions can the horizontal pieces occur?
questions.hint: First recover the numbers of pieces of each orientation.

questions.title: Count pieces across several designs
questions.prompt: An artist makes one copy of every domino tiling of a fixed 2-by-4 board. Across all copies, how many individual horizontal dominoes does she use?
questions.hint: Group designs by whether they have zero, one or two sideways pairs.

questions.title: A tiling that crosses a seam
questions.prompt: A 2-row, 9-column board has seams between columns 3 and 4 and between columns 6 and 7. How many domino tilings have at least one domino crossing at least one seam? The board is fixed and the dominoes are identical.
questions.hint: Count all tilings, then count the tilings that keep all three sections separate.

figure.alt: Two rows of nine cells. Two dashed seams after columns three and six divide the strip into three sections.

lessons.headline: Count overlaps of repeating lists
lessons.intro: If either of two events qualifies, adding the two counts includes their simultaneous events twice. A least common multiple identifies the shared times to remove once.
lessons.bridge: In the film, find the common part of the marker counts first. See why the two numbers left after dividing out their highest common factor cannot share another factor.
lessons.recap: For “either”, remove each overlap once. For “exactly one”, remove it from both individual counts.

example.prompt: Among numbers 1 to 12, how many are multiples of 3 or 4?
steps: There are four multiples of 3 and three of 4.
Twelve is counted twice, so the distinct count is 4 + 3 − 1 = 6.

questions.title: Common labels
questions.prompt: How many numbers from 1 to 100 inclusive are multiples of both 6 and 8?
questions.hint: Use their least common multiple.

questions.title: Either club day
questions.prompt: A club meets on every fourth day or sixth day, counting from day 1 and using days divisible by 4 or 6. On how many distinct days from 1 to 36 does it meet?
questions.hint: Find the counts and their overlap.

questions.title: Exactly one bell
questions.prompt: From minute 1 to minute 60 inclusive, a bell rings at multiples of 5 and a whistle sounds at multiples of 8. At how many minutes does exactly one signal sound?
questions.hint: The shared instant qualifies for neither of the two “only” counts.

questions.title: Unmarked posts
questions.prompt: Posts 1 to 120 receive red marks at multiples of 6 and blue marks at multiples of 10. How many posts receive neither colour?
questions.hint: Count the distinct marked posts first.

lessons.headline: Reverse a meeting story
lessons.intro: A meeting time can reveal a speed or a head start. Recover the total change in the gap first, then decide which speed sum or difference produced it.
lessons.bridge: In the film's head-start chase, identify the gap and the rate at which it closes. Read the same relationship backwards when a meeting time is given instead.
lessons.recap: Recreate both positions at the proposed meeting time. They must agree on the track or number line.

example.prompt: Two runners start 60 m apart and meet after 5 seconds running towards each other. One runs at 5 m/s. How fast is the other?
steps: Together they close 60 ÷ 5 = 12 m each second.
The other runner contributes 12 − 5 = 7 m/s.

lessons.videoTitle: Relative speeds, timed movement and meetings

questions.title: Known closing time
questions.prompt: Two robots move towards each other from 70 m apart. They meet after 10 seconds. One travels at 3 m/s. What is the other's speed in m/s?
questions.hint: Find the speed of the closing gap.

questions.title: Unknown head start
questions.prompt: A 6 m/s runner catches a 4 m/s runner 18 seconds after the faster runner begins. How many metres ahead was the slower runner at that moment?
questions.hint: Find the gain during those 18 seconds.

questions.title: Turn back time
questions.prompt: Two friends start together and walk in opposite directions at 3 and 2 m/s. After 8 seconds the faster turns and chases the slower at 7 m/s. How many further seconds until they meet?
questions.hint: Find their separation at the turn.

questions.title: Two measured meetings
questions.prompt: Two cyclists on a 240 m track meet every 12 seconds when travelling in opposite directions and every 40 seconds in the same direction. What is the faster speed in m/s?
questions.hint: Find the speed sum and the speed difference.

lessons.headline: Distinguish the team from the assignment
lessons.intro: A single chosen group can carry out several different assignments. Track which swaps an observer could detect. If a swap changes neither the group nor anyone's role, that swap should not generate another count.
lessons.bridge: The film counts groups of artists, builders and coders without assigning a leading role. Watch which swaps it treats as the same team, then decide how a named job would change that.
lessons.recap: Name a reference person or object to remove symmetry. Then check how real labels or roles restore distinctions.

example.prompt: Four friends split into two unnamed pairs. How many splits are possible?
steps: Choose the partner of one particular friend in 3 ways.
The other two friends form the second pair automatically. Naming the pairs would count each split twice.

questions.title: The reading pairs
questions.prompt: Six readers split into three unnamed pairs. For a particular reader there are five possible partners. How many complete pairings are possible?
questions.hint: Once the first pair is set, pick the partner of one particular remaining reader.

questions.title: Two committees
questions.prompt: Six pupils split into two unnamed groups of three. How many splits are possible?
questions.hint: Choose the two companions of one fixed pupil.

questions.title: Reserve positions
questions.prompt: Choose a captain, a deputy and two interchangeable reserves from seven players. How many assignments are there?
questions.hint: Fill the distinct jobs first.

questions.title: Three relay heats
questions.prompt: Nine runners split into three unnamed heats of three. One runner in each heat carries its timing chip. How many complete assignments are possible?
questions.hint: First form the heats by fixing a runner each time. Then choose the chip carriers.

lessons.headline: Recover what a fold preserves
lessons.intro: A crease acts like a mirror. Corresponding lines make equal angles with the crease. A straight angle or a triangle total often supplies the missing equation.
lessons.bridge: When the film halves angles at B and C, mark the two equal parts at each vertex. Carry the same habit into the later fold puzzle.
lessons.recap: Mark equal angles from a fold or symmetry first. Then choose a line or triangle linking those marks.

example.prompt: A fold sends one ray onto another, making a 70° gap between the original ray and its image. How far is either ray from the crease inside that gap?
steps: The fold makes the crease the mirror line between the rays.
It bisects 70°, so the turn from either ray to that crease is 35°.

questions.title: A reflected ray
questions.prompt: A ray makes an angle of 19° with a crease. Reflect the ray across the crease. What is the smaller angle in degrees between the original and reflected rays?
questions.hint: Measure from the original ray to the crease and on to the reflected ray.

questions.title: Fold a perpendicular edge
questions.prompt: A sheet has one horizontal edge and one vertical edge. A crease makes a 65° angle with the right-pointing horizontal edge and a 25° angle with the upward vertical edge. After folding the upward vertical edge across that crease, how many degrees separate its old and new directions?
questions.hint: Use the angle with the edge that actually moves.

questions.title: Locate the second crease
questions.prompt: An arrow points east, direction 0°. Fold it across a crease at direction 20°, then across another crease between 0° and 90°. The arrow finishes at direction 100°. All directions are measured anticlockwise from east. What is the direction of the second crease in degrees?
questions.hint: A crease bisects the old and new arrow directions.

questions.title: Two mirror lines at one point
questions.prompt: Measure directions anticlockwise from a horizontal ray at O. A light ray has direction 18°. Reflect its direction in a line through O at 32°, then reflect the new direction in a line through O at 60°. What is the smaller angle in degrees between the original and final directions?
questions.hint: After one reflection, the ray is as far from the mirror line on the other side.

lessons.headline: Use bounds to test an average
lessons.intro: A known mean fixes a total. If readings are whole numbers or must be distinct, a value you are testing may force too much or too little total for the rest.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film reconstruct a total from a mean and a count. Keep that total fixed when you later try to make a single reading as large as possible.
lessons.recap: Prove both a bound and an example attaining it. Distinctness and whole-number conditions can change the smallest possible leftovers.

example.prompt: Three different positive whole numbers average 4. What is the largest possible single number?
steps: The total is 12. To maximise one number, minimise the other two as 1 and 2.
The largest is 9, and 1,2,9 shows it can really occur.

lessons.videoTitle: Averages, weighted means and simple distributions

questions.title: Largest possible score
questions.prompt: Four different positive whole scores average 6. What is the largest score that could occur?
questions.hint: Reserve the three smallest different positive numbers for the other scores.

questions.title: How many tens?
questions.prompt: Five whole numbers from 0 to 10 average 7. What is the greatest number of entries that can equal 10?
questions.hint: Count how many tens fit into the total, then complete the list.

questions.title: The second highest
questions.prompt: Five different positive integers average 6. What is the largest possible second-highest value?
questions.hint: The top value must exceed the one you are testing.

questions.title: Can the average be right?
questions.prompt: Six different whole scores from 0 to 10 average exactly 6. Among possible lists, what is the greatest number of scores strictly above 6?
questions.hint: Try five high scores, then construct a list with four.

lessons.headline: Combine facts before making cases
lessons.intro: A fact that seems weak alone can force an entry once another clue narrows its options. Carry each new restriction through the remaining rows or positions.
lessons.bridge: Follow each change of position in the painting puzzle. Which later clue can be used only after the earlier block has been placed?
lessons.recap: Use each forced value to eliminate other choices. Verify the final assignment against the original clues.

example.prompt: Four parcels have masses 1, 2, 3 and 4 kg. A is heavier than B; B is heavier than C; C weighs 2 kg. What does B weigh?
steps: Only 3 and 4 are above 2. B still needs an even heavier parcel A.
B is therefore 3 kg, leaving 4 kg for A.

questions.title: The weight order
questions.prompt: Four boxes labelled Yara, Zed, Ana and Bea have different weights. Yara is heavier than Ana. Zed is lighter than Bea but heavier than Yara. Which box is second lightest?
questions.hint: Join the comparisons into one chain from lightest to heaviest.

questions.title: Bags with shared totals
questions.prompt: Three parcels have distinct whole-kilogram masses. The red and blue parcels together weigh 11 kg. Blue and gold weigh 9 kg. Red and gold weigh 12 kg. How heavy is the blue parcel in kilograms?
questions.hint: Compare the total of all three pair readings with the pair that omits blue.

questions.title: Badge and desk clues
questions.prompt: Four desks have numbers 1 to 4. Iris, Jo, Kit and Lee use different desks. Iris sits to the right of Jo, Kit sits immediately to the right of Lee, and Jo sits at desk 3. Which desk number belongs to Lee?
questions.hint: Remove desk 3 first. Where can the consecutive pair go without using it?

questions.title: The five speakers
questions.prompt: Talks A, B, C, D and E fill five consecutive time slots. C is before A. D is immediately after A. E is exactly two slots after B, and E is not last. Which numbered slot contains C?
questions.hint: Only two pairs of slots can hold B and E. Test whether the other three talks fit.

lessons.headline: Block a point or a single edge?
lessons.intro: A closed intersection removes every route entering it. A closed edge removes only journeys using one particular step, so its endpoints can still be available.
lessons.bridge: When the film closes a grid point, compare the change to erasing just one incoming edge. Look at the other routes still arriving at that point.
lessons.recap: Represent the restriction precisely and compare your result with the unrestricted route count.

example.prompt: On a unit grid square, go right or up from the lower-left to upper-right corner. Close only the bottom edge. How many routes survive?
steps: Right then up uses the closed edge. Up then right avoids it.
One of the two routes survives. The upper-right endpoint is still open.

questions.title: A point can still be reached
questions.prompt: A robot takes unit east and north steps from (0,0) to (2,2). Only the edge from (0,1) to (1,1) is closed. How many routes still visit (1,1)?
questions.hint: Find the remaining way into the centre and count its possible continuations.

questions.title: The disabled gate
questions.prompt: A cart takes east or north unit steps from (0,0) to (3,2). The gate along (1,0) → (2,0) is shut. A delivery must pass through (2,1). How many routes can deliver?
questions.hint: Count routes to the delivery point that avoid the gate, then add all possible continuations.

questions.title: Two barriers on the same diagonal
questions.prompt: A bug moves from (0,0) to (4,3) along east or north unit edges. The intersections (1,2) and (3,0) are closed. How many routes avoid both?
questions.hint: Both blocked points have coordinate sum 3. Could the same route encounter both?

questions.title: Visit exactly one checkpoint
questions.prompt: A path from (0,0) to (5,4) uses unit steps right or up. How many paths visit exactly one of the checkpoints P=(2,1) and Q=(3,3)?
questions.hint: Count paths through P, through Q, and through both. A path visiting both should contribute zero.

figure.alt: A five-by-four grid with start at (0,0), P at (2,1), Q at (3,3) and finish at (5,4).

lessons.headline: Filter digit assignments column by column
lessons.intro: Column equations often restrict the possible digits before you know any whole number. Write down carries and borrows, then apply conditions such as “different digits” or “smallest”.
lessons.bridge: For the film's final sum ending in zero, inspect the units column before guessing whole numbers. Its carry places a restriction on the next column.
lessons.recap: An equation alone may allow several digit assignments. Recheck the letter restrictions and any requested maximum or minimum.

example.prompt: In 6A − 27 = 38, what is A?
steps: The original number is 38 + 27 = 65.
Hence A is 5. Check the subtraction, which borrows one ten for the units.

questions.title: Borrowed units
questions.prompt: In 5A − 18 = 36, what is the digit A?
questions.hint: Undo the subtraction to recover 5A.

questions.title: A zero at the end
questions.prompt: Two-digit numbers 2A and 3A have the same nonzero units digit. Their sum ends in zero. What is A?
questions.hint: The units sum must be a positive multiple of ten.

questions.title: A constrained product
questions.prompt: In the multiplication 2A × 3 = B1, A and B are different digits. What is the two-digit product?
questions.hint: Find a units digit A for which 3A ends in 1.

questions.title: The mirror receipt
questions.prompt: A two-digit code AB and its two-digit reverse BA total a three-digit palindrome. The tens digit A is one less than twice B. What is AB?
questions.hint: The sum is below 200. What must its first and last digits be?

lessons.headline: Count hits in a shifted cycle
lessons.intro: For a long run, count complete blocks of the cycle and then inspect the leftover block. If the cycle has a lead-in, decide separately whether the target occurs during that opening stretch.
lessons.bridge: In the machine example, mark the first entry into the loop and the number of moves around it. Watch which of those two numbers belongs in the remainder calculation.
lessons.recap: Identify the first repeating day, count how many target states occur per block, and check both ends of the requested interval.

example.prompt: A machine reports X, then cycles A,B,A,C starting on day 2. How many As occur during days 1–10?
steps: Days 2–9 make two whole blocks with two As each. Day 1 is X.
Day 10 starts the next block with A. The total is five As.

questions.title: Two per block
questions.prompt: A warning sequence repeats R,G,R,B,B from day 1. How many R days are among days 1–18?
questions.hint: Separate complete five-day blocks and the remaining days.

questions.title: Starts before the loop
questions.prompt: A lamp shows white on days 1 and 2. From day 3 it repeats green, amber, red. What colour appears on day 101? Answer green, amber or red.
questions.hint: Take the offset from day 3.

questions.title: An interior interval
questions.prompt: A machine visits its check state on steps 5, 12, 19 and every 7 steps after that. How many visits occur from step 20 through step 96 inclusive?
questions.hint: Find the first and last check steps in the interval.

questions.title: The joint warning
questions.prompt: A sensor flashes on days 2,6,10,… . Another flashes on days 3,8,13,… . On how many days from 1 through 150 inclusive do they both flash?
questions.hint: Find the first match, then the period of the complete pair.

lessons.headline: Reconstruct a table from its margins
lessons.intro: Row totals and column totals describe the same entries from two directions. A missing cell can sometimes be recovered without knowing every other cell. Start with a row or column with only one blank.
lessons.bridge: As the film moves between its table and chart, identify what each row actually counts. You will use the same care when one observation is present in both a row and a column total.
lessons.recap: Use a row or column with one missing entry. Verify your reconstruction against the other margin.

example.prompt: A class has 12 walkers and 8 riders. Seven walkers and three riders wear hats. How many pupils do not wear hats?
steps: There are 20 pupils in all and 10 hat wearers.
The complementary count is 10. Equivalently, 5 walkers and 5 riders have no hat.

figure.alt: A table shows seven hat wearers among twelve walkers and three hat wearers among eight riders. Both no-hat cells are unknown.

questions.title: Blank table cell
questions.prompt: A team collects 35 tokens. There are 18 stars and the rest are circles. Seven circles are blue; all other circles are red. How many circles are red?
questions.hint: Recover the total number of circles first.

questions.title: A percentage row
questions.prompt: A display has 30 large tiles and 20 small tiles. Half the large and one-quarter of the small are blue. How many tiles are blue?
questions.hint: The two fractions use different row totals.

questions.title: Cross totals
questions.prompt: Forty packets are sweet or savoury, and each is small or large. There are 26 small packets and 18 savoury packets. Eleven are small and savoury. How many are large and sweet?
questions.hint: Complete the savoury column and the large row.

questions.title: Find the row size
questions.prompt: A survey table shows that half the children in group A and one-third in group B walk to school. The groups have 36 children altogether, with 15 walkers in total. How many children belong to A?
questions.hint: Try treating every child as belonging to B, then compare the walker total.

lessons.headline: Translate changes into an opening share
lessons.intro: Sequences of gifts, sales or spills can combine fractions with fixed amounts. Decide when the fixed amount enters and what the next fraction acts upon.
lessons.bridge: Watch where the fixed gift enters the film's pile of counters. Decide whether the next fractional instruction also changes the gift.
lessons.recap: Work backwards one instruction at a time. Test your answer forwards with the same order and the same whole at every step.

example.prompt: A box holds 18 pencils. Half are taken, then 3 new ones are added. How many are now in the box?
steps: Taking half leaves 9 pencils.
The fixed addition happens afterwards, bringing the box to 12.

lessons.videoTitle: Parts and wholes, including remaining fractions

questions.title: The gift first
questions.prompt: A jar contains 18 coins. Someone adds 6, then gives away a third of all the coins now in it. How many remain?
questions.hint: Find the amount at the moment the fraction is taken.

questions.title: Equal endings?
questions.prompt: Mia starts with 24 beads, removes half, then adds 4. Leo starts with 24, adds 4, then removes half. How many more beads does Mia end with than Leo?
questions.hint: Trace the two orders separately.

questions.title: The last nine
questions.prompt: A player spends one third of her counters and then loses 2 more. She gives half of the counters now left to a friend and finishes with 9. How many counters did she start with?
questions.hint: Undo the last halving first.

questions.title: Unexpected equal shares
questions.prompt: Two gardens have a combined area of 120 m². Half of the first and a quarter of the second are planted with peas. The pea areas are equal. What is the area of garden two in square metres?
questions.hint: Compare the whole gardens using their equal pea areas.

lessons.headline: A reverse step can have two candidates
lessons.intro: Some operations lose information. A square hides a sign, and an absolute difference hides which number was larger. After reversing, use every original restriction to test the candidates.
lessons.bridge: For the film's whole-number machine, test the reconstructed input forwards. In later puzzles a reverse step can give two candidates, so the original input restriction will matter.
lessons.recap: Keep all reverse candidates until a stated condition eliminates them. A forward check proves a candidate works; the restrictions explain whether it is unique.

example.prompt: A whole number from 1 to 9 is 3 units away from 8. What is it?
steps: The candidates are 8 − 3 = 5 and 8 + 3 = 11.
Only 5 lies in the permitted range.

questions.title: A square above zero
questions.prompt: A positive whole number is squared and 4 is added, giving 53. What is the number?
questions.hint: Undo the addition first.

questions.title: The negative input
questions.prompt: An integer less than zero is squared and then 1 is subtracted, giving 35. What was the input?
questions.hint: Both signs can lead to a square of 36.

questions.title: A distance from a target
questions.prompt: A positive whole number is doubled. The result is 5 units away from 19 and the original number is below 10. What was that original number?
questions.hint: List both possible doubled results.

questions.title: The last digit survives
questions.prompt: A positive two-digit number below 40 is tripled. Its product has last two digits 14. What is the original number?
questions.hint: Write all possible products in the allowed size range with that ending.

lessons.headline: Let the largest member lead
lessons.intro: Every nonempty set of distinct numbers has exactly one largest number. Counting by it often turns a restriction on the whole set into a small choice from the numbers below it.
lessons.bridge: During the exhibit puzzle, notice how fixing one room controls the remaining choices. Later, use a fixed largest member to give every set one home.
lessons.recap: Choose a defining feature that is unique. Recalculate the remaining pool inside each case instead of assuming it has constant size.

example.prompt: Choose two distinct numbers from 1 to 5 with largest number 4. How many pairs can you make?
steps: One number is fixed at 4.
Its partner can be 1, 2 or 3, giving three pairs.

questions.title: Top card
questions.prompt: Choose three different cards numbered 1 to 7, with largest card 6. How many hands exist?
questions.hint: Pick two cards from below 6.

questions.title: Odd maximum
questions.prompt: Two different integers are chosen from 1 to 8. How many unordered pairs have an odd larger number?
questions.hint: Use possible odd maxima 3, 5 and 7.

questions.title: Short-spread hands
questions.prompt: Choose three different integers from 1 to 8. How many sets have largest minus smallest equal to 4?
questions.hint: Fix the smallest number, then the largest is determined.

questions.title: Prize tokens
questions.prompt: Four different token numbers from 1 to 9 win if the largest is twice the smallest. How many winning sets are there?
questions.hint: The two middle tokens must lie strictly inside the endpoint interval.

lessons.headline: Keep two colours separate
lessons.intro: A cube may carry two colours because it lies on the meeting line of two painted faces. Opposite faces have no such meeting line in a solid more than one cube thick.
lessons.bridge: Watch which faces meet along each painted edge of the film’s cuboid. Then imagine labelling two of those faces with different colours.
lessons.recap: Translate colour conditions into intersections of positions, and check where the painted faces actually meet.

example.prompt: A 3-by-3-by-3 block has only its top red and its front blue. How many cubes carry both colours?
steps: The two large faces meet along the front top edge.
That edge contains 3 cubes, including both of its ends.

lessons.videoTitle: Painted faces, boundary and hidden cubes

questions.title: Two stripes across one face
questions.prompt: A 6-by-6 array of unit faces forms the top of a cube. The first two rows are coloured red and the first three columns blue. How many unit faces receive both colours?
questions.hint: Locate the rectangle shared by the selected rows and columns.

questions.title: A corner of three colours
questions.prompt: A cuboid is 5 cubes wide, 4 deep and 3 high. Its top face is red, its front face blue and its right face yellow, and no other face is painted. How many cubes have both red and blue but no yellow?
questions.hint: Follow the common edge of the top and front. What happens at its right-hand endpoint?

questions.title: Purple footprints
questions.prompt: A 4-by-4-by-4 cube has its two horizontal outside faces painted red and its four vertical outside faces painted blue. How many unit cubes have at least one face of each colour?
questions.hint: Inspect the boundary of each horizontal layer that received red paint.

questions.title: Replace the two-colour cubes
questions.prompt: A 5 × 4 × 3 block of unit cubes has its two 5-by-4 faces painted blue and the other four outside faces gold. Replace each small cube bearing both colours with an unpainted cube. How many painted unit faces are now visible?
questions.hint: Separate the two blue end layers from the middle layer. Which cubes in each layer keep their paint?

lessons.headline: Search backwards from the constraints
lessons.intro: In a longer search, reserve one value as the final check. Try the other values in an order that enforces the rules automatically. This can turn three loops of guesses into a handful of rows.
lessons.bridge: In the film’s box problem, inspect the moment when fixing two box counts forces the third. See which apparently possible choices then fail a bound.
lessons.recap: When one value is forced, verify its range and its order. A forced answer still has to satisfy every original condition.

example.prompt: Select three different numbers from 1 to 6 with sum 10. How can a third choice be forced?
steps: Choose the two smallest, in order. With 1 and 3 the third must be 6. With 1 and 4 it must be 5.
Starting with 2 gives 2,3,5. Larger first values overshoot. There are three sets.

questions.title: One number left
questions.prompt: Choose 3 different integers from 1 to 7 with sum 14. How many sets include 7?
questions.hint: With 7 fixed, work with pairs summing to 7.

questions.title: Unequal boxes
questions.prompt: Three positive whole numbers in increasing order multiply to 48. How many such triples exist?
questions.hint: Choose the smallest factor, then list factor pairs for the remainder.

questions.title: Routes through a gate
questions.prompt: A robot takes exactly four moves, each 1, 2 or 3 units forwards. It travels 8 units and lands on 4 immediately after move two. How many ordered move lists work?
questions.hint: Treat each half of the route as an ordered pair.

questions.title: The examiner’s shortlist
questions.prompt: A panel chooses four different integers from 1 to 9 whose sum is 20. Exactly two chosen numbers must be odd. How many shortlists are possible?
questions.hint: List the even pairs first, then match their sums with odd-pair sums.

lessons.headline: Track the area that changes
lessons.intro: Moving one boundary can alter only a strip or triangle, even if the whole figure looks different. Compare regions with the same height or the same base.
lessons.bridge: As the film adds a second shaded rectangle, trace only the area newly covered. This comparison will also work when a vertex moves.
lessons.recap: Ask which measure stayed fixed, then compute the area change before rebuilding the whole figure.

example.prompt: A triangle with base 6 cm has its height increased from 2 cm to 3 cm. What extra area appears?
steps: The common base stays 6 cm while the height gains 1 cm.
Half of 6 × 1 is 3 cm² of extra area.

questions.title: Slide a divider
questions.prompt: A rectangle is 10 cm wide and 6 cm high. A vertical line separates it into two panels. The line moves 2 cm to the right while staying inside the rectangle. By how many square centimetres does the left panel grow?
questions.hint: Picture the strip between the old position and the new one.

questions.title: Shorten only the base
questions.prompt: A triangle has area 24 cm² and base 8 cm. Slide one base endpoint 2 cm towards the other along the same line, leaving the top vertex in place. What is the new area in square centimetres?
questions.hint: Changing the base along the same line leaves the perpendicular height unchanged.

questions.title: Resize a display
questions.prompt: A rectangular display is 15 cm wide and 9 cm high. Its right edge moves 3 cm right and its top edge moves 2 cm down. By how many square centimetres does its area decrease?
questions.hint: The height of the added strip depends on which change you count first.

questions.title: The band between two outlines
questions.prompt: A parallelogram banner has area 96 cm². Join the midpoints of its four sides in order to form an inner parallelogram. Join the midpoints of that inner parallelogram to form a second one. What area, in square centimetres, lies inside the first outline but outside the second?
questions.hint: Compare each corner triangle with one half of the parallelogram before adding the four corners.

figure.alt: A parallelogram, an inner outline joining the side midpoints, and a second midpoint outline. The band lies between the inner outlines.

lessons.headline: Weight the different routes
lessons.intro: A random experiment can reach the same event by several routes. Multiply along each route and add the probabilities of disjoint successful routes. Different routes can have different probabilities.
lessons.bridge: At the film's bag of counters, track how different orders can produce the same final colour count. Watch the successful paths come together in the final probability.
lessons.recap: Keep the first-stage probability attached to every branch. If a later clue is supplied, compare branch weights within that event.

example.prompt: A fair coin selects a bag. Bag A contains two red tokens and bag B contains one red and one blue. What is the probability of red?
steps: Through bag A the red probability contributes 1/2 × 1. Through B it contributes 1/2 × 1/2.
The routes cannot both happen. Their sum is 3/4.

questions.title: Choose the jar
questions.prompt: One of two jars is chosen by a fair coin. Jar A has one green and three grey discs; B has three green and one grey. Draw one random disc. What is the probability of green? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Add the two contributions weighted by the jar choice.

questions.title: Unequal bag sizes
questions.prompt: One of two bags is chosen with equal chance. A has two blue counters and B has one blue and three white counters. A random counter is taken from the chosen bag. What is the probability of blue? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: The bags are equally likely even though they hold different numbers.

questions.title: Two-stage ticket
questions.prompt: A fair spinner has two A sectors and one B sector, all equal. In game A a fair die wins on 5 or 6. In B it wins on 6. What is the overall win probability? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Separate the two game routes.

questions.title: Trace the winning ticket
questions.prompt: A fair coin selects a machine. Machine A issues a winning ticket half the time and B a quarter of the time. Given that the ticket won, what is the probability it came from A? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Find how much of the total winning probability belongs to A.

lessons.headline: Use colour counts in every separate piece
lessons.intro: A colouring test becomes stronger when a board splits into parts. A domino cannot cross a missing row or jump a gap, so each connected piece must supply its own colour pairs.
lessons.bridge: In the film, compare the two removed corner squares with the two neighbouring squares. Why does removing the same number of squares permit one tiling but rule out the other?
lessons.recap: First mark the pieces a tile can reach. Apply the same invariant within each piece, then construct a layout if you claim the bound can be met.

example.prompt: Two separate strips each have three cells. Can three ordinary dominoes cover all six cells?
steps: A domino must stay inside one strip. Each strip can hold only one domino.
Two dominoes cover four cells. The even total of six does not guarantee a covering.

questions.title: The missing stripe
questions.prompt: A 2-by-5 board loses its entire middle column. What is the maximum number of dominoes that fit on the remaining board?
questions.hint: Look at the two pieces separately.

questions.title: Matching holes
questions.prompt: A 4-by-4 chess-coloured board loses two black cells. Can all the remaining cells be covered by ordinary dominoes? Enter yes or no.
questions.hint: Count the two colours after the holes.

questions.title: Separate strip bounds
questions.prompt: A single row has 12 cells numbered 1 to 12. Cells 4 and 9 are removed. What is the maximum number of dominoes that fit?
questions.hint: Find the lengths of the uninterrupted runs.

questions.title: Two disconnected gardens
questions.prompt: A rectangular 5-by-7 grid loses all five cells of its central column. What is the maximum number of ordinary dominoes that can cover the remaining cells without overlap?
questions.hint: In each side, prove a bound and show how to reach it.

lessons.headline: Use a third clue to separate three types
lessons.intro: Two totals can leave several possible collections. An extra relationship can reduce three unknown counts to two or even just one. Check all counts are whole and nonnegative.
lessons.bridge: For the three boxes in the film, note when the third condition becomes necessary. Your collections of three types also need enough clues to separate all three counts.
lessons.recap: A complete answer must obey the head count, the weighted total, and the relationship between the types. Check all three.

example.prompt: A box holds 6 shapes. It has equal numbers of squares and circles and exactly 2 triangles. How many circles are there?
steps: Set the two triangles aside.
Four shapes remain in equal square and circle groups, so there are 2 circles.

questions.title: Equal outer boxes
questions.prompt: Three drawers contain 24 beads. The middle has 4 and the outer drawers hold equal amounts. How many beads are in one outer drawer?
questions.hint: Subtract the middle drawer before halving.

questions.title: A double batch
questions.prompt: A box has red, white and blue balls. White equals blue and red is twice white. There are 36 balls. How many are red?
questions.hint: Draw the three counts as equal shares.

questions.title: Values on the discs
questions.prompt: There are 12 discs worth 1, 2 or 5 points. Exactly 3 are worth 5 and the total is 29 points. How many discs are worth 2?
questions.hint: Handle the known five-point discs first.

questions.title: Equal numbers of extremes
questions.prompt: An order contains 18 boxes holding 2, 4 or 8 cards each. The counts of 2-card and 8-card boxes are equal. There are 82 cards altogether. How many 4-card boxes are there?
questions.hint: Pair each small box with a large one and compare the pair with two middle boxes.

lessons.headline: Make every symbol appear
lessons.intro: If every kind of item must appear, count strings that miss particular kinds. These failure cases can overlap when a string misses two kinds at once.
lessons.bridge: As the film counts integers that avoid all the unwanted divisors, follow one that belongs to two excluded lists. The same correction will apply to a string missing two colours.
lessons.recap: Write the unwanted events as “missing this particular item”. Check whether something can satisfy two or more of those events.

example.prompt: A row of two beads uses black or white. How many rows use both colours?
steps: Four rows exist. All-black and all-white each miss a colour.
Remove these two rows, leaving BW and WB.

questions.title: Both digits
questions.prompt: A passcode has five positions, each 0 or 1. How many codes use both digits?
questions.hint: Are leading zeroes permitted in a passcode? Here every position has the same choices.

questions.title: Three flags in three spaces
questions.prompt: Fill three labelled spaces using red, blue or green flags. How many displays use all three colours?
questions.hint: How often must each colour appear?

questions.title: Four sounds
questions.prompt: A four-note tune uses the notes C, D and E and must include all three. How many tunes are possible?
questions.hint: Exactly one note repeats. Choose it and choose its positions.

questions.title: Map the deliveries
questions.prompt: Five different parcels each go to one of three labelled huts. Every hut must get a parcel. How many delivery plans are possible?
questions.hint: Exclude the plans missing each hut, then restore those missing two.

lessons.headline: Work with exact interval boundaries
lessons.intro: Timetables and counters use rules about the first and last instant. Write down whether an event exactly at either endpoint counts. A change of units does not change these boundaries.
lessons.bridge: The film's two signals both flash at time zero. Mark that flash separately and check the question's endpoints before including it in a count.
lessons.recap: Use the first eligible event and the last eligible event. The count is one more than the number of gaps between them.

example.prompt: A sensor records at 0, 10, 20 and 30 seconds. How many readings are strictly after 0 and strictly before 30 seconds?
steps: The endpoints 0 and 30 are excluded.
Only the readings at 10 and 20 count, giving 2.

questions.title: A one-minute recording
questions.prompt: A sensor records at time zero and every 5 seconds. How many readings occur from time zero to 60 seconds, including both ends?
questions.hint: A minute has 60 seconds.

questions.title: Excluding both ends
questions.prompt: A marker is placed every 8 metres along a 64-metre straight trail, starting at metre 0. How many markers lie strictly between the ends?
questions.hint: Remove the markers at 0 and 64.

questions.title: Shift the recording window
questions.prompt: A clock clicks every 7 seconds from time zero. How many clicks occur after second 20 and up to and including second 70?
questions.hint: Find the first allowed multiple of 7.

questions.title: Two counters, one beep
questions.prompt: A device beeps at multiples of 6 or 10 seconds from zero. If both rules apply at the same instant it makes just one beep. How many beeps occur strictly after time zero and up to 60 seconds?
questions.hint: Count both lists, then remove their shared instants once.

lessons.headline: Give a reason for the recurrence
lessons.intro: A recurrence is a compact proof only when its cases cover every object once. Define the count for an empty start, handle impossible cases explicitly, and check a small example before extending the table.
lessons.bridge: For the broken-rung puzzle, inspect the last jump of a valid route. Try explaining why every permitted route enters the total exactly once.
lessons.recap: Explain why no last-step case is missing or repeated. If a route has a compulsory stop, its prefix and suffix can often be counted separately.

example.prompt: A row is tiled with lengths 1 and 3. Why is there exactly one tiling of length 0?
steps: The single empty tiling allows a first tile to start the row.
It lets the “last tile has length 3” case produce exactly one all-long tiling when the row length is 3.

questions.title: The empty start
questions.prompt: How many ordered sequences of 2-unit and 3-unit jumps reach 7 units exactly?
questions.hint: A last jump of 2 comes from 5; a last jump of 3 comes from 4.

questions.title: Two colours of single tile
questions.prompt: A 4-cell strip can use red or green tiles of length 1 and uncoloured tiles of length 2. How many tilings are possible?
questions.hint: The two colours double the number of endings in a single tile.

questions.title: A compulsory landing
questions.prompt: A robot moves forwards 1 or 2 from 0 to 9. How many routes land on 4 along the way?
questions.hint: Split each route at its unique visit to 4.

questions.title: No return to the broken rung
questions.prompt: A staircase has rungs 0 through 10. Hops of 1 or 2 must go forwards. Rung 5 is broken and every route must land on 8. How many routes from 0 reach 10?
questions.hint: Find counts up to the compulsory rung, using zero for the broken rung, then count the final segment.

lessons.headline: Cut the board into manageable pieces
lessons.intro: A hole, notch or compulsory tile can leave independent regions. Draw what remains, then check each part for area, colouring and any forced boundary placements.
lessons.bridge: Look for the point where placing the first pair of dominoes leaves a shorter, familiar board. The same splitting idea applies when a piece in the middle is fixed.
lessons.recap: After making a forced placement, check whether the leftover parts have become independent before multiplying their counts.

example.prompt: A fixed vertical domino fills the middle column of a 2-by-5 board. What boards remain?
steps: The occupied column separates the squares on its left and right.
Each side is a 2-by-2 board. Each has two tilings, so the whole board has 4 tilings with that domino fixed.

questions.title: A compulsory tile in a corridor
questions.prompt: Eight cells form a straight corridor. A domino is permanently fixed over cells 4 and 5. What is the maximum number of additional dominoes that fit without overlapping it?
questions.hint: How long are the two free segments?

questions.title: Two rooms with one doorway
questions.prompt: Two 2-by-2 tiled rooms sit side by side with a wall between them. A domino may cross the wall only along the single doorway joining the top-right cell of the left room to the top-left cell of the right room. How many complete coverings of both rooms are possible?
questions.hint: If one domino crosses the doorway, how many cells remain inside each room?

questions.title: A single-cell passage
questions.prompt: A one-row corridor of three cells L, M and R has an additional cell directly above M. At its left end attach a separate 2-by-2 room, and attach another 2-by-2 room at its right end. Each room has just one doorway, between its one corner cell and its adjacent end cell of the corridor. Dominoes may cross those doorways. How many complete coverings exist?
questions.hint: Decide first whether a room of four cells can use its only connection once; then inspect the four cells outside the rooms.

questions.title: Which tiles straddle a boundary?
questions.prompt: Divide an 8 × 8 board into sixteen aligned 2 × 2 blocks. One corner cell is missing. Tile it by this rule: divide the current square into four equal quarters, place a central L-shaped tromino over one cell in each of the three quarters that lack a hole, and repeat in each quarter. A 2 × 2 square with one hole takes one tile. How many tiles use cells from more than one of the sixteen original blocks?
questions.hint: Track the size of the square when each central tile is placed.

lessons.headline: Recover a hidden cycle from common returns
lessons.intro: Knowing when two schedules first coincide gives a least common multiple. A hidden interval must divide that repeat time, but being a divisor alone may allow an earlier coincidence.
lessons.bridge: When the film works with a highest common factor and a lowest common multiple, watch how it strips off the common part before testing pairs.
lessons.recap: List possible divisors of the shared time, then test their least common multiple. Extra information may be needed for a unique interval.

example.prompt: One chime repeats every 4 minutes. Two chimes first repeat together after 12 minutes. Could the second chime repeat every 2 minutes?
steps: The least common multiple of 4 and 2 is only 4.
They would already coincide at minute 4, so an interval of 2 does not fit.

questions.title: A hidden small rhythm
questions.prompt: One lamp flashes every 4 seconds. Another has a whole-number interval greater than 4 and less than 10. They first return together after 12 seconds. What is the other interval in seconds?
questions.hint: The unknown interval must divide 12.

questions.title: Could there be two?
questions.prompt: One bell rings every 6 minutes. A second has a whole-number interval from 2 through 12 minutes. How many choices give a first shared return after 12 minutes?
questions.hint: Test divisors of 12 as possible intervals.

questions.title: A pair of packet counts
questions.prompt: Two positive whole numbers have highest common factor 4 and lowest common multiple 60. One number is 12. What is the other?
questions.hint: Multiply the HCF and LCM, or test divisors of 60.

questions.title: Missing gear
questions.prompt: Two gears return together to their starting marks every 84 clicks. The first makes one turn in 12 clicks. The second takes fewer than 40 clicks and a multiple of 7 clicks per turn. What is the largest possible turn length of the second gear, in clicks?
questions.hint: Its turn length must divide 84 and still produce a least common multiple of 84 with 12.

lessons.headline: Prove the minimum can be built
lessons.intro: A silhouette imposes lower bounds on stack heights. Sometimes a single high stack can satisfy both a row maximum and a column maximum. Always build a plan that attains a claimed minimum.
lessons.bridge: In the six-stack puzzle, check how the film confirms a minimum using an actual arrangement. A number alone cannot show that all the views can be met together.
lessons.recap: A lower bound needs a construction attaining it. Check every row, every column and the nonempty condition.

example.prompt: On a 2-by-2 footprint all stacks are nonempty. The row maxima and column maxima are both 3,1 in that order. What minimum works?
steps: Put 3 at the intersection of the first row and first column. This satisfies both tall maxima.
All three remaining stacks may be 1. The minimum is 6 cubes, and the proposed plan shows it can be built.

questions.title: Place the tallest witness
questions.prompt: Four nonempty stacks occupy a 2-by-2 footprint. Only the first row can contain a stack of height 4, and only the second column can contain height 4. At least one stack is height 4. How many footprint positions can contain such a stack?
questions.hint: A valid location must meet both position restrictions.

questions.title: An inventory bound
questions.prompt: A front view shows three nonempty stacks in a single row with heights 2, 5 and 3. A second row directly behind them may be empty at any position. The combined front silhouette must stay unchanged. What is the greatest number of cubes that can be added in the back row?
questions.hint: At each back position, find the tallest stack that its corresponding front stack could hide.

questions.title: Minimise occupied high cells
questions.prompt: Nine nonempty stacks form a 3-by-3 array. Every row and column must have maximum height exactly 3. What is the smallest possible total number of cubes?
questions.hint: Each row needs a height-3 stack. Can the same three stacks also cover all three columns?

questions.title: The least material for a skyline
questions.prompt: Nine nonempty stacks of unit cubes stand in a row. Neighbouring heights may differ by at most 1. Stack 3 is exactly 4 cubes high and stack 7 is exactly 5. What is the least total number of cubes that could form the skyline?
questions.hint: Work out the lowest possible height at each position from both known peaks. Then try building the row.

lessons.headline: Combine an order rule with a digit rule
lessons.intro: If digits must be different and obey an order or a divisibility test, first choose a pair of places that captures the strongest restrictions. Then count what can legally fill the rest.
lessons.bridge: In the film, the leading digit and the final pair obey different restrictions. Choose one end first, then check that building the other end has not reused its digits.
lessons.recap: Check that you counted orders when positions matter, and only one order when the digits were required to increase.

example.prompt: A two-digit number uses two different digits from 1, 3 and 6 and is divisible by 3. How many qualify?
steps: The digit sum must be divisible by 3. Only the pair 3 and 6 works.
Both orders work, giving 36 and 63: two numbers.

questions.title: End in five
questions.prompt: Form three-digit numbers using different digits from 1, 2, 5 and 8. How many end in 5?
questions.hint: Reserve the last digit first.

questions.title: Front exceeds back
questions.prompt: Using the digits 1, 4 and 7 once each, how many three-digit numbers have first digit larger than the last?
questions.hint: Pair each arrangement with its reversal.

questions.title: Ascending and even
questions.prompt: How many three-digit numbers have strictly increasing digits chosen from 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 and are even?
questions.hint: Fix the last digit, then choose two smaller digits.

questions.title: Divisible by six
questions.prompt: How many ordinary three-digit numbers use three different digits from 0, 1, 2, 3 and 6 and are divisible by 6?
questions.hint: An even final digit and a digit sum divisible by 3 are both required.

lessons.headline: Compare successive percentage changes
lessons.intro: A percentage change uses the value immediately before the change. Apply each percentage as a multiplier and check what price the second change acts on.
lessons.bridge: The film changes a price twice. Pause just before the second change and point to the amount that now represents one hundred percent.
lessons.recap: Divide the final amount by the combined multiplier to recover an earlier amount. Equal percentages in opposite directions usually use different starting values.

example.prompt: A $40 bag rises by 25% and then falls by 20%. What does it cost?
steps: The rise adds $10, giving $50.
The fall removes a fifth of $50, or $10. The bag returns to $40.

questions.title: The second discount
questions.prompt: A $100 tablet is discounted 20%, then a further 10% off its sale price. How many dollars does it cost?
questions.hint: Find the price after the first reduction.

questions.title: Restore the price
questions.prompt: A $60 pass falls to $48. What percentage increase on $48 would return the price to $60? Enter a number.
questions.hint: Compare the missing $12 to the current price.

questions.title: A club subscription
questions.prompt: After a 10% rise followed by a 20% reduction, a membership costs $88. What was the original price in dollars?
questions.hint: Find the multiplier for both changes together.

questions.title: Same sale price
questions.prompt: A red bicycle was discounted 20% and a blue one 25%. Both sold for $180. How many dollars higher was the blue bicycle's original price?
questions.hint: Reverse each discount using its own remaining fraction.

lessons.headline: Work backwards from a sequence total
lessons.intro: The average of a finite arithmetic sequence equals the average of its endpoints. When the total is given, use that relationship to recover a missing endpoint or number of terms.
lessons.bridge: In the theatre, watch how an evenly spaced list turns a total into endpoint pairs. Consider how to undo that calculation if the total is supplied first.
lessons.recap: Use an endpoint pair to recover a total, or use total and length to recover the endpoint pair. Verify that the resulting step fits the number of gaps.

example.prompt: Six shelves hold 90 objects in all. The first holds 5, and the shelf counts rise by a constant amount. How many are on the last?
steps: The mean shelf holds 90 ÷ 6 = 15.
The two endpoints must add to 30, so the last shelf holds 25.

questions.title: Find the last term
questions.prompt: Nine terms of an arithmetic sequence total 153. The first is 5. What is the last?
questions.hint: The endpoint mean equals the overall mean.

questions.title: Lost length
questions.prompt: An arithmetic sequence starts at 2 and ends at 34. Its sum is 162. How many terms does it contain?
questions.hint: Find the average term.

questions.title: Choose the middle
questions.prompt: Seven consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence total 140. The second of these terms is 12. What is the seventh?
questions.hint: An odd-length sequence has its mean at the middle.

questions.title: Two theatre wings
questions.prompt: Two wings each have ten rows. In wing A, row sizes start at 7 and increase by 2. Wing B starts at 9 and has a constant whole-number increase. Both wings together seat 430. What is wing B's increase?
questions.hint: Subtract wing A's total before recovering the endpoints of wing B.

lessons.headline: Ask what every solution shares
lessons.intro: The entire arrangement may remain uncertain even when the requested position is forced. Test the requested feature across all surviving cases.
lessons.bridge: When several places in the film still seem possible, concentrate on a single item. Which clue rules out its last alternative?
lessons.recap: To prove a feature is forced, rule out every alternative for that feature, even if the rest can vary.

example.prompt: Four desks form a row. Inez occupies an end, and Leo is immediately to her right. Which desk holds Inez?
steps: The right end has no desk to its right.
Inez must occupy the leftmost desk. The other two students can still swap.

questions.title: Two seats apart
questions.prompt: Four children sit in seats 1 to 4: Zed, Ana, Bea and Cleo. Zed is exactly two seat numbers before Ana. Cleo is in seat 1. Which seat number belongs to Bea?
questions.hint: Write every possible pair for the two numbered seats.

questions.title: A letter forced between
questions.prompt: Five cards stand in a row: A, B, C, D and E. A is first, E is last and C must be next to both B and D. Which position from the left does C occupy?
questions.hint: Consider the three middle places as a small row of their own.

questions.title: A bag in every solution
questions.prompt: Three bags each contain a different number of marbles from the set 2, 3, 5 and 7. Together they contain 12 marbles. The yellow bag is lighter than both other bags. How many marbles must the yellow bag contain?
questions.hint: Find which triple can total 12, then ask which of its values can be the smallest.

questions.title: Three failed keypad guesses
questions.prompt: A keypad code has three different digits from 1 to 5. Guess 123 contains exactly two of the code digits, guess 145 contains exactly one, and guess 234 contains exactly two. Across all three guesses, no digit that is present is in its correct position. What is the code?
questions.hint: The guesses 123 and 234 share two digits. What does their equal match count say about 1 and 4?

lessons.headline: Recover an integer from remainder clues
lessons.intro: A remainder can be converted into a distance from a convenient multiple. If two clues line up after the same adjustment, the whole search can move in large steps.
lessons.bridge: When the film adds one to a number before applying two divisibility clues, ask exactly what has become a common multiple. The ending condition still belongs to the original number.
lessons.recap: Write the candidates in a progression and apply the final range or digit clue to the original number. Verify by dividing the proposed answer both ways.

example.prompt: A number is one short of a multiple of both 4 and 5. What is the least such number above 40?
steps: Adding 1 must produce a multiple of 20.
The first multiple of 20 above 41 is 60, so the number is 59.

questions.title: A copying error
questions.prompt: A three-digit entry has digit sum 19. A clerk copies it but increases its units digit by 2, without a carry. What remainder does the copied entry leave on division by 9?
questions.hint: Find the digit sum after the copying change.

questions.title: A changed multiple
questions.prompt: A positive integer is 2 more than a multiple of 7. What remainder does three times that integer leave on division by 7?
questions.hint: Separate complete groups of 7 from the leftover.

questions.title: Find the sum remainder
questions.prompt: A leaves remainder 4 on division by 7 and B leaves remainder 5. What remainder does 2A + B leave on division by 7?
questions.hint: Replace each whole number with its remainder.

questions.title: The faulty counter
questions.prompt: A counter displays one less than the true count. The displayed number is divisible by 6 and by 8. The true number is between 70 and 100 and its digits add to 10. What is the true count?
questions.hint: Write the displayed candidates before adding the missing unit.

lessons.headline: Track overlapping neighbour requirements
lessons.intro: Two adjacency rules may share a letter. When they both hold, the shared letter can force a whole run. Identify that run before you add or subtract the case counts.
lessons.bridge: When the film considers two named pairs, sketch both adjacency rules at once. Later you will check how that sketch changes when the two rules share a letter.
lessons.recap: Sketch what it means for both conditions to occur. Shared objects cannot belong to two independent blocks.

example.prompt: In an order of A, B, C, D, how many have both AB and BC as consecutive pairs in either internal direction?
steps: B must touch A on one side and C on the other. The run is ABC or CBA.
The run and D have two orders, giving 2 × 2 = 4.

questions.title: A forced middle
questions.prompt: Arrange A, B, C, D and E with C immediately between A and B. How many arrangements are possible?
questions.hint: The run has length three and two internal orders.

questions.title: No circular shortcut
questions.prompt: Four different flags form a row. Its two ends count as neighbours only in this problem. In how many rows is A next to neither B nor C?
questions.hint: Think about A's two different neighbours.

questions.title: Exactly one neighbour
questions.prompt: How many orders of five different letters A–E put A next to exactly one of B and C?
questions.hint: Count the two adjacency sets and remove orders with both twice.

questions.title: Six display stands
questions.prompt: Six different art pieces A–F form a row. A must touch B, B must touch C, and D must stay apart from E. How many displays are possible?
questions.hint: Treat the forced run as one unit before imposing the last restriction.

lessons.headline: Look for fixed positions
lessons.intro: A turn can pair most positions yet leave a centre alone. Recognising fixed positions makes it easier to test whether a marked shape keeps its symmetry.
lessons.bridge: In the film’s two-mirror colour puzzle, identify the centre cell and cells on just one mirror. Compare the sizes of their forced groups.
lessons.recap: Check what happens to every mark, including any position whose image is itself.

example.prompt: In a row of seven seats, a half-turn reverses the order. Which seat counted from the left stays in the same position?
steps: The outer pairs are 1 with 7, 2 with 6 and 3 with 5.
Seat 4 has no distinct partner. It stays fixed.

questions.title: The circular dial
questions.prompt: A circular dial has twelve equally spaced points around its rim and one point at its centre. Markings must look the same after a 120° turn. How many independent groups of points can be marked separately?
questions.hint: The centre stays put. Find how many rim points join any chosen point under repeated turns.

questions.title: The balanced tray
questions.prompt: Six columns and two rows form a tray of twelve cells. Exactly two cells are red. How many different choices of red cells look unchanged after a half-turn about the tray centre?
questions.hint: A red cell forces one other cell to be red. Is there a fixed central cell?

questions.title: Three marks and a mirror
questions.prompt: A board has 5 columns and 3 rows. Exactly 3 cells are marked, and the pattern has mirror symmetry across the middle column. How many marked patterns are possible?
questions.hint: A mark off the mirror needs a partner, but a mark on the middle column can stand alone.

questions.title: Two diagonal mirrors
questions.prompt: On a 5-by-5 board, colour exactly one cell red and exactly four cells blue; the others are white. The pattern must be unchanged by reflection in either diagonal. How many colour patterns satisfy both mirrors?
questions.hint: Where could a single red cell lie? Sort the other cells into groups forced to share one colour.

lessons.headline: Check what a chart allows you to infer
lessons.intro: A graph may give endpoints, totals or an interval average. It does not automatically tell you how values were distributed between two observations. Test a claim by constructing a possible set of missing entries.
lessons.bridge: In the film’s graph of total counts, compare what the endpoints tell you with what would need an extra reading. Use that distinction before deciding a later table forces a unique answer.
lessons.recap: Translate every chart entry into a constraint. To claim a value is forced, rule out every competing value; for a maximum, also give an example reaching it.

example.prompt: A shop sells 12 books over three days. Does this force four books on day two?
steps: The daily counts 4,4,4 would fit.
The counts 2,9,1 also total 12. Day two is not determined from the total.

figure.alt: Two three-day examples give book sales of 4, 4, 4 and of 2, 9, 1. Both total 12.

questions.title: What is fixed?
questions.prompt: A counter increases from 12 at 9 am to 31 at noon and never goes backwards. What total increase is certain?
questions.hint: The shape of the rise between the readings does not affect its total.

questions.title: Smallest possible peak
questions.prompt: A shop sells 22 loaves over five days. Each day's count is a nonnegative whole number. What is the smallest possible value of the busiest day's sales?
questions.hint: Try an even spread before rounding.

questions.title: Unrecorded interval
questions.prompt: Four one-hour intervals account for 34 arrivals. The first has 8 and the last has 11. The third has at least as many arrivals as the second. What is the greatest possible number in the second interval?
questions.hint: Find the total left for the middle pair.

questions.title: A missing timetable
questions.prompt: At noon a bus terminal's cumulative arrivals and departures both read zero. By 3 pm it has 14 arrivals and 9 departures. At 1 pm it had 5 arrivals and 2 departures. What is the largest possible number of buses present at any time strictly between 1 and 3 pm? The terminal starts empty.
questions.hint: For an upper bound, ask which remaining events could occur first.

lessons.headline: Reconstruct a consistent grid
lessons.intro: A locally plausible number can force an impossibility elsewhere. Combine the line total, the allowed values and any symmetry before deciding a square is complete.
lessons.bridge: As the magic-square film completes its final cells, check both the line totals and whether any allowed value was used twice.
lessons.recap: Use all the conditions together. Finish by checking every required line and every allowed value.
