example.prompt: Three cells must total 14 using distinct numbers. Two are 3 and 7. Can the third be 7?
steps: The missing value is forced by 14 − 3 − 7 = 4.
Only 4 fits the sum. A second 7 would also break the distinctness rule.

lessons.videoTitle: Magic grids, symbolic rules and consistency

questions.title: Detect the altered entry
questions.prompt: A 3-by-3 magic square once had line sum 15. One entry increased by 3. Exactly one row and one column now total 18, and both main diagonals still total 15. How many cells of the square could be the changed cell if you do not know which row and column changed?
questions.hint: Mark the positions that lie on neither main diagonal.

questions.title: Consistent input order
questions.prompt: A machine uses the rule output = first input + twice the second input. The numbers 2, 3 and 5 may be used as inputs. How many ordered pairs of different inputs give output 8?
questions.hint: Try each permitted second input and work out which first input would be needed.

questions.title: One rule fixes the grid
questions.prompt: A 2-by-2 grid uses 1, 2, 4 and 5 once each. The top row totals 6, the left column totals 5, and the bottom-right entry is even. What number belongs in the top-left cell?
questions.hint: The row and column clues each allow two pairs. Try a potential top-left value in both.

questions.title: Ink over a rectangle of entries
questions.prompt: A 6-by-6 table has each row and each column totalling 30. Ink covers the six cells common to the top two rows and the left three columns. The twelve cells in the bottom four rows and the right three columns total 74. What is the sum under the ink?
questions.hint: Count the visible cells by combining all bottom rows with all right-hand columns. Which cells get counted twice?

figure.alt: Six rows and six columns. The top-left two-by-three region is obscured. The bottom-right four-by-three region has total 74.

lessons.headline: Recover the choices behind a total
lessons.intro: A frame count combines boundary choices. When a total or a change is given, reverse that product and ask which lines could have produced it.
lessons.bridge: At the film’s rectangle count, try reversing the argument: if a boundary were fixed first, how many choices would be left for the other three sides?
lessons.recap: Identify the family of frames changed by the new line or constraint, then use its known choices to recover the others.

example.prompt: A grid has exactly two horizontal lines. If you can choose the pair of vertical sides in six ways, how many rectangles result?
steps: Every rectangle must use both horizontal lines, giving one horizontal choice.
Each of the six vertical pairs supplies one rectangle, so there are 6.

questions.title: Rebuild the orchard plan
questions.prompt: An orchard plan has four columns of cells. Exactly 30 different grid rectangles have their bottom side on the southern outside edge. How many rows does the plan have?
questions.hint: The width interval can be chosen independently of the top side.

questions.title: Recover the lost width
questions.prompt: On a board four rows high, a 2-column by 3-row rectangle has 14 different placements. It cannot rotate. How many columns does the board have?
questions.hint: Count the possible bottom rows, then undo the horizontal sliding count.

questions.title: Two sizes of inspection stamp
questions.prompt: A panel is three cells high. Each possible 1-by-1 or 2-by-2 square position is marked once. There are 33 marks. How many columns does the panel have?
questions.hint: What does one extra column add to the two kinds of positions?

questions.title: The two changes to a grid
questions.prompt: A grid has at least two full vertical lines and two full horizontal lines. Adding one new full vertical line creates exactly 30 new rectangles. In a separate experiment on the original grid, adding one new full horizontal line creates 40. How many rectangles did the original grid contain?
questions.hint: With v original vertical lines and h horizontal lines, count the rectangles that must use each newly drawn line.

lessons.headline: Pair prime factors to make a square
lessons.intro: A square uses each prime an even number of times. A factor without a partner tells you what must be supplied or what can be removed.
lessons.bridge: In the film's perfect-square puzzle, pair the copies of every prime. Which unpaired copies dictate the smallest extra factor?
lessons.recap: To prove a multiplier is the smallest, show that every unpaired prime must occur in it. Check the final number has a whole-number square root.

example.prompt: What is the smallest positive whole number by which 18 must be multiplied to make a square?
steps: Eighteen is 2 × 3². The two 3s are already paired.
An extra 2 completes the unpaired factor, giving 36 = 6².

questions.title: One missing partner
questions.prompt: What is the smallest positive whole number that makes 12 a perfect square when the two numbers are multiplied?
questions.hint: Factor 12.

questions.title: Largest square divisor
questions.prompt: What is the greatest perfect square dividing 108?
questions.hint: Factor the number and keep as many complete pairs as you can.

questions.title: Square after division
questions.prompt: What is the smallest positive divisor you can divide 180 by to leave a perfect square?
questions.hint: Which primes occur an odd number of times?

questions.title: The smallest square shipment
questions.prompt: A square number of beads can be packed into groups of 12 or 18 with none left over. It must exceed 100. What is the least possible bead count?
questions.hint: Start from the least common multiple and test square multiples, or constrain the square root.

lessons.headline: Partition by a remainder, then check the cases
lessons.intro: A divisibility condition can turn a long search into a few short rows. Record the remainders that can go together, count each row, and explain why it cannot overlap another.
lessons.bridge: In the exhibit problem, watch how one feature places each legal display in a single case. In your final problem, remainders will give the cases and a counterexample will test a claim.
lessons.recap: A complete argument needs both directions: every counted choice passes the test, and every passing choice belongs to one listed case.

example.prompt: Pick two distinct labels from 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 so their sum is divisible by 3. Which remainder pairs can work?
steps: The remainders must be 0 and 0, or 1 and 2. Only one label has remainder 0, so the first case is empty.
The remainder-1 labels are 1 and 4. The remainder-2 labels are 2 and 5. Each first choice has two partners, giving 4 pairs.

questions.title: Remainder partners
questions.prompt: Pick two different tokens from 1 through 8. How many unordered pairs have sum divisible by 3?
questions.hint: Separate pairs with two multiples of 3 from pairs with remainders 1 and 2.

questions.title: Product test
questions.prompt: Two different cards from 1 through 8 are chosen. How many unordered pairs have product divisible by 12?
questions.hint: The product needs a factor of 3 and two factors of 2. Separate pairs containing 3 from those containing 6.

questions.title: Three remainder cases
questions.prompt: Choose three different labels from 1 through 8. How many sets have a sum divisible by 3?
questions.hint: Three residues summing to a multiple of 3 must all match or all differ.

questions.title: Counterexample audit
questions.prompt: A pupil claims that any three different labels from 1 through 9 with sum divisible by 3 must contain a multiple of 3. How many unordered counterexamples are there?
questions.hint: Exclude all multiples of 3 and ask which remainder triples can still work.

lessons.headline: Eliminate first, then compare by ratio
lessons.intro: A pair of totals may fix an item's value before a ratio question can be answered. Match the equal quantities, subtract, and keep track of what the difference measures.
lessons.bridge: In the film's two kinds of packs, note which order to scale so one kind cancels. Keep the recovered unit values available for the equal-mass ratio question in your practice.
lessons.recap: Check each recovered mass in both weighings. For an equal-mass question, compare total masses rather than merely comparing the item counts.

example.prompt: Two identical bags and a tin weigh 17 kg. One bag and the same tin weigh 11 kg. What is the bag-to-tin mass ratio?
steps: Subtract to find one bag weighs 6 kg. The tin therefore weighs 5 kg.
The ordered ratio of bag mass to tin mass is 6:5.

figure.alt: First weighing: bag plus bag plus tin equals seventeen kilograms. Second weighing: bag plus tin equals eleven kilograms.

questions.title: Cancel the crate
questions.prompt: A crate and four plates weigh 29 kg. The same crate and two plates weigh 19 kg. How many kilograms does one plate weigh?
questions.hint: The extra two plates account for the difference.

questions.title: Equivalent bundles
questions.prompt: A red parcel weighs 6 kg and a blue parcel weighs 4 kg. What is the smallest positive number of blue parcels with the mass of a whole number of red parcels?
questions.hint: Find the least common mass.

questions.title: How many blue blocks?
questions.prompt: Two red blocks and one blue block weigh 16 g. Two red blocks and three blue blocks weigh 24 g. How many blue blocks have the mass of four red blocks?
questions.hint: Find blue from the difference, then recover red.

questions.title: A counterweight box
questions.prompt: Three washers and two pins weigh 31 g. One washer and four pins weigh 27 g. A kit must contain washers and pins with equal total mass, and at least one of each. What is the least possible mass of the whole kit, in grams?
questions.hint: Match the pin counts in the weighings. Then find the least mass each type can contribute.

lessons.headline: Use a fraction of a known area
lessons.intro: A length fraction can become an area fraction when the perpendicular height stays fixed. This lets you solve a shaded-region puzzle without measuring its picture.
lessons.bridge: The film subtracts two overlapping shaded rectangles from a whole board. Keep track of which whole is being divided, then use that same care with the area fractions after the film.
lessons.recap: Name the whole used by each fraction. Check that the areas of all the pieces restore the original region.

example.prompt: A triangle of area 24 cm² has its base split into lengths in the ratio 1 to 3. Join the split to the opposite vertex. What is the smaller area?
steps: Both pieces have the same height, so their areas also have ratio 1 to 3.
The smaller is one of four equal shares of the original area: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 cm².

questions.title: A base in three shares
questions.prompt: A triangular sail has area 42 m². A seam runs from the top to a point one third of the way along its base from the left. What is the area of the piece beside the left end, in square metres?
questions.hint: The seam gives both triangles the same altitude.

questions.title: A fraction of what remains?
questions.prompt: A 12 cm by 8 cm card has a corner triangle removed with perpendicular legs 6 cm and 4 cm. One quarter of the remaining card is painted. How many square centimetres receive paint?
questions.hint: First find the area that the fraction refers to.

questions.title: Window and crossbar
questions.prompt: A rectangular stained-glass panel has area 120 cm². A horizontal band covers one third of the panel and a vertical band covers one quarter. Each band crosses the whole panel at uniform width. How many square centimetres lie outside both bands?
questions.hint: Identify the fraction of each dimension still uncovered.

questions.title: The field beyond the triangle
questions.prompt: A rectangular field is 18 m wide and 10 m high. A triangle joins the lower-left corner, a point one third of the way from the lower-right corner up the right edge, and the top-right corner. What fraction of the whole field lies outside this triangle? Give an exact fraction.
questions.hint: Use its vertical side as the base. How far is the third vertex from that line?

lessons.headline: State exactly what a route may remember
lessons.intro: Two routes reaching the same point may have different legal futures when a condition refers to earlier steps. Include the relevant fact, such as whether a marker was visited, when combining route totals.
lessons.bridge: Watch the film mark both closed intersections. Before the count is revealed, work out whether one route can pass through both and how to account for that group.
lessons.recap: Count all routes, then classify forbidden or required visits. When two forbidden sets overlap, account for their shared routes once.

example.prompt: A robot may finish by entering a gate from the west or from the south. There are five routes in total and two enter from the west. How many enter from the south?
steps: Sort the routes by their final step. Every route belongs to exactly one group.
The south group has 5 − 2 = 3 routes.

questions.title: Sort the first steps
questions.prompt: From (0,0) to (3,3), move right or up one unit. How many routes begin with an up-step?
questions.hint: Fix that step and count orders of the remaining five.

questions.title: Missing only the bridge
questions.prompt: A robot moves right or up from (0,0) to (4,2). The horizontal edge from (1,1) to (2,1) is broken, but both intersections can be visited. How many routes remain?
questions.hint: Count routes using that one step, rather than crossing out both endpoints.

questions.title: One checkpoint only
questions.prompt: A route from (0,0) to (4,3) uses only right and up unit steps. How many routes visit exactly one of A=(1,1) and B=(3,2)?
questions.hint: Routes through both belong to both single-checkpoint counts, but must contribute nothing.

questions.title: Dispatch with priority gates
questions.prompt: A delivery robot travels from (0,0) to (5,3), stepping one unit right or up. It must pass gate A=(2,1) or gate B=(3,2), or both. How many different command strings are allowed?
questions.hint: Write the totals for A, for B, and for the route visiting both in order.

lessons.headline: Choose a region whose parity you can track
lessons.intro: On a changing grid, the total board may be the wrong thing to count. Look for a small selected set of cells that every legal move touches an even number of times. Its parity then survives.
lessons.bridge: In the film's number-line moves, the position can change while its parity survives. After the film, try applying that test to selected squares of a grid instead of to a single number.
lessons.recap: Mark the cells used in your count and check every kind of move. For a maximum or minimum, also show a pattern of moves that reaches your claimed bound.

example.prompt: Four lamps mark the corners of a rectangle. One move switches both lamps on its top edge. Starting with all four off, how many corners are lit after that move?
steps: The two top lamps turn on together.
There are two lit corners. Turning any pair of corners changes the lit count by 0 or 2 in either direction, preserving evenness.

questions.title: Two lights change
questions.prompt: All 8 lamps are off. Every move switches exactly two distinct lamps. Is it possible to finish with precisely 5 lamps on? Enter yes or no.
questions.hint: What parity does a move preserve?

questions.title: Mark opposite corners
questions.prompt: A 3-by-3 board has a counter on its top-left square. Each step moves one cell up, down, left or right. Can it reach the bottom-right corner in exactly 5 steps? Enter yes or no.
questions.hint: Colour the board like a chessboard.

questions.title: Overlapping switches
questions.prompt: On an initially dark 4-by-4 display, switch on an entire row by toggling its four lamps. Then toggle one entire column. How many lamps are now on?
questions.hint: The intersection is switched twice.

questions.title: The smallest beacon
questions.prompt: A 4-by-4 lamp board begins dark. Any move toggles a whole row or a whole column. You need the top-left lamp on. What is the fewest OTHER lamps that must be on?
questions.hint: For each of the other three diagonal lamps, mark the four corners of the rectangle joining it to the top-left lamp. What does a row or column move do to their parity?

lessons.headline: Rebuild a journey from its finish
lessons.intro: A final time and speed can reveal a distance. Treat that distance as the starting clue and undo the earlier operations in reverse order.
lessons.bridge: The film adds the leg times and the stop on a return journey. As you watch, try reading one leg backwards: if its time and speed are known, which distance can you restore?
lessons.recap: Check backwards reasoning by reconstructing each leg forwards. Add the leg times, including stops if the total is elapsed time.

example.prompt: A rider covers half a route, then rides its last 6 km at 12 km/h. How long does the final leg take and how long is the route?
steps: Six kilometres at 12 km/h takes half an hour.
The last 6 km is half the route, so the route is 12 km long.

figure.alt: Two equal route halves. The second half is six kilometres, travelled at twelve kilometres per hour.

questions.title: A final run
questions.prompt: A rider's final 15 minutes are spent at 16 km/h. How far does she travel during that time in kilometres?
questions.hint: Express 15 minutes as part of one hour.

questions.title: Restore the lost distance
questions.prompt: A walker finishes by covering one third of her whole route in 24 minutes at 5 km/h. How many kilometres was the entire route?
questions.hint: Find the final distance before expanding from a third.

questions.title: A detour and a half
questions.prompt: A van first covers 10 km. It then covers half of the distance still to go. The last leg takes 18 minutes at 50 km/h. What is the whole route in kilometres?
questions.hint: Restore the two equal final parts before adding the opening 10 km.

questions.title: Recover the first speed
questions.prompt: A runner covers one quarter of a route, rests 6 minutes, then covers the other three quarters in 36 minutes at 10 km/h. The whole outing took 1 hour. What was the runner's speed on the first leg in km/h? Give an exact fraction or decimal.
questions.hint: Use the final distance to recover the route length, then find the first leg's time.

lessons.headline: Show that no better shape exists
lessons.intro: An optimum needs two pieces of evidence: a legal shape reaching it and a reason that every other legal shape does no better. Organise the full range of possible widths before comparing results.
lessons.bridge: When the film finds a promising pen beside a wall, look for the argument that excludes all better whole-number dimensions. You will need both a construction and a complete check.
lessons.recap: Give a bound or an exhaustive ordered list. Then name dimensions that attain the claimed optimum.

example.prompt: A rectangle must have integer sides, area 12 cm² and width smaller than length. What is its least perimeter?
steps: List factor pairs with width no greater than the square root: (1,12), (2,6), (3,4).
Their perimeters are 26, 16 and 14 cm. The list is complete, so 14 cm is minimal.

lessons.videoTitle: Optimising areas and lengths under constraints

questions.title: List the legal sides
questions.prompt: A rectangle has whole-number side lengths and perimeter 22 cm. How many distinct unordered side pairs are possible?
questions.hint: Put the shorter side first and bound it by half the side sum.

questions.title: One side must be even
questions.prompt: A rectangle has perimeter 28 cm, whole-centimetre sides and at least one even side. What is its greatest area in square centimetres?
questions.hint: The unconstrained best pair may not be allowed.

questions.title: Half the wire buys the width
questions.prompt: Two adjacent rectangular runs share one dividing fence. Together they form a large rectangle, and the divider is parallel to its width. Exactly 30 metres of fencing are used for the four outer sides and the divider. The large rectangle has positive whole-metre dimensions. What is its largest possible area in square metres?
questions.hint: If width is w, the fence equation is 3w + 2l = 30.

questions.title: A shelter beside the rock wall
questions.prompt: A rectangular shelter has a rock wall as its back. Exactly 28 m of netting cover the front, both ends and one divider parallel to an end. All lengths are positive whole metres. The front length must also be divisible by 4. What is the greatest covered area in square metres?
questions.hint: Express the front in terms of the depth. Which depths leave a positive multiple of 4?
